INTERNATIONAL SHIP AND PORT FACILITY SECURITY
 
25.       The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has introduced new maritime security regulations called International Code for the
 Security of Ships and of Port Facility (ISPS Code) which was adopted as an amendment to 'Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS)' by the conference
 of Contracting Governments on 12/12/2002.  The ISPS Code embodies a number of functional requirements which include:
 
(i)         gathering and assessing information with respect to security threats and exchanging such information with appropriate Contracting
 Governments;
(ii)        requiring the maintenance of communication protocols for ships and port facilities;
(iii)       preventing unauthorized access to ships, port facilities and their restricted areas;
(iv)       preventing the introduction of unauthorized weapons, incendiary devices or explosives to ships or port facilities;
(v)        providing means for raising the alarm in reaction to security threats or security incidents;
(vi)       requiring ship and port facility security plans based upon security assessments; and
(vii)      requiring training, drills and exercises to ensure familiarity with security plans and procedures.
 
26.       The code was introduced as a fall out of 11 th September 2001 terrorist attack incident in the US, after which the need to tighten up
 security for all modes of transport, was realised.  Therefore, the 22 nd Session of the Assembly of the IMO in November, 2001 unanimously
 agreed to the development of new measures relating to the security of ships and of port facilities for adoption by a Conference of Contracting
 Governments to the SOLAS (Safety of Life at Sea) 1974.  The ISPS Code provides for the international framework through which ship and
 port facilities can cooperate to detect and deter acts which threaten security in the maritime transport sector. The Code has become mandatory
 with effect from 1st July, 2004 in respect of the contracting parties to SOLAS 1974 including India.
 
27.       Giving the details of efforts made to implement the new security regulations in India the Ministry informed the Committee that the
 ISPS Code in India covers all Major Ports, Minor Ports catering to international trade, and Ships.  Under the Code if an ISPS compliant Ship
 enters a non-compliant Port, it will have problems in its next voyage which will affect international trade and business.  India is one among
 the first few countries to complete implementation of ISPS Code, ensuring that there will be no hindrance in Indian exports and imports.
 
28.       All Indian Ships, Major Ports and Minor Ports in the country have since been completed and Port facility security plans (PFSP) have
 also been prepared by the DG(Shipping).
 
29.       During the course of oral evidence, the Secretary informed the Committee that;
"the international code for security of ships and ports facility was a fall-out of 9/11 attack in US on the World Trade center.  IMO
 introduced the ISPS Code which has come into effect from 1.7.2004.  In India too, we have covered all major and minor ports catering to
 international trade and all ships above 500 GT.  The DG(S) has been made the designated authority for this purpose and the Indian Register of
 Shipping the recognized organisation for this purpose. Accordingly, all the 12 Major Ports, 34 minor ports and 191 ships flying the Indian
 Flag have become ISPS-complaint;"
           
30.       The Committee appreciates the Ministry for complying the ISPS code for all 12 Major Ports, 34 minor ports catering to international
 trade and 191 Indian Flagged ships in the country.  The Committee notes that the new maritime security regulations will provide international
 framework for ships and ports facilities besides detecting the deterring acts, which threaten security in the maritime transport sector.  The
 implementation of ISPS code, will also do away the hindrances in Indian export and imports.  The Committee, however, recommends that a
 task force be formed in the Ministry to observe strict compliance of international safety and security code/regulations.

 Committee feels that any delay in cabinet approval of this programme will adversely affect the modernization alongwith capacity expansion
 of ports network in the country.  However, the Committee is constrained to note that there is very little activity in the Inland Water Transport
 sub-sector.  This raises the question that how investment on infrastructure building will yield commensurate economically viable rate of
 returns.  The Committee was also disturbed to note that the IWAI is yet to develop the infrastructure for capacity building both in terms of
 human resources for proper technology appraisal, R&D and design inducement packages.  Therefore, the Committee concludes that this is a
 task, which should be urgently addressed.    The Committee, therefore, recommends that an early approval to launch Sagar Mala programme
 should be given and the Ministry should initiate action for setting-up of Sagar Mala Development Authority on the pattern of National
 Highways Authority of India.
 
INTRODUCTION OF TONNAGE TAX
37.       As regards implementation of Tonnage Tax in lieu of Corporate Tax, the Ministry had been taking up the matter with Ministry of
 Finance since 2002. Now, the Government has announced the introduction of Tonnage Tax for the Shipping Industry with an option for the
 shipping companies to opt for either tonnage tax or corporate tax in the finance bill for the year 2004-05. 
 
38.       During the course of oral evidence, the Secretary deposed before the Committee that;
            "the lack of conducive fiscal environment has been one of the reasons for Indian shipping not increasing its tonnage.  With
 the present introduction of the Tonnage Tax option for the Indian shipping companies, the shipping tonnage under the Indian flag would
 further increase.  This is in line with more maritime nations who have introduced tonnage-based taxation.  Some of the basic features of the
 proposed tonnage tax scheme are as follows:
·
  It is a scheme of presumptive taxation whereby the notional income arising from the operation of a ship is determined based
 on the tonnage of the ship.
·  The national income is taxed at the normal corporate rate applicable for the year.

INDIAN SEAFARERS WORKING ON FOREIGN FLAGGED SHIPS
 
40.       Indian seafarers working on foreign flagged vessels enjoy tax free status, as they are in more advantageous position to comply with
 the requirements to become eligible to NRI status when they are employed on Indian ships.  Even when they do no comply with the
 requirements to become eligible for NRI status, they are not subject to TDS in India, because the foreign ship owners employing Indian
 seafarers are outside the jurisdiction of the Indian Tax authorities. 
41.       On a question of exempting the Indian seafarers from paying taxes so as to retain qualified and trained officers, the Ministry
 informed that as a measure of preventing the large-scale drift of qualified and experienced personnel, Sec.6 of I.T. Act was amended in
 1990 to provide for tax exemption in respect of income received by the Indian crew serving on Indian ships outside India for 182 or more
 days in a year. The provision was aimed specifically to help Indian shipping companies to retain the services of Indian crew employed on
 their ships.  However, this intent could not be achieved because of an interpretation of the relevant provision namely, Explanation (a) to
 Sub-Section (1)(c) of Sec.6 by CBDT Circular No.586 of 28-11-1990 that the period of the seafarers’ service when the ships are in Indian
 territorial waters is to be treated as period of service in India, in a year.  A communication dated May 7, 1996 received from CBDT clarified
 this point.  As Indian ships generally operate in international waters and also call frequently at Indian ports, a large number of the crew
 employed on Indian ships though trading outside India cannot comply with this eligibility criteria to have NRI status, resulting in denial of
 tax exemption benefits to most of Indian seafarers working on Indian ships.
 
42.       An expert committee under the chairmanship of Dr. Rakesh Mohan, the then Adviser to the Finance Minister was constituted in
 August, 2001. The committee considered this issue after taking into consideration various alternatives and recommended “In order to make
 employment on Indian ships attractive vis-à-vis foreign ships, it is essential that Indian nationals serving on board Indian flag ships be
 treated equally as those Indians employed on foreign ships. The Committee also recommended for insertion of appropriate provision in
 Sec.10 of the Income Tax Act and the alternative, the Board in exercise of its power under Sec.119 of the Act may issue a Circular that
 would put an end to the discriminatory consequences of the CBDT Circular of 28-11-1990, though such discrimination was unintended”.
 
43.       In line with the recommendation of the committee, following provision/clarification (as a sub-section inserted in Section 10 of the
 I.T. Act) is suggested for consideration of CBDT:
“In case of an Indian citizen who is a member of the crew of an Indian ship as defined in clause (18) of section 3 of the Merchant
 Shipping Act, 1958, any income chargeable under the head “Salaries” received by or due to any such individual being a non-resident as
 remuneration for services rendered in connection with his employment on such ship where his total stay in India does not exceed in the
 aggregate a period of 182 days in the previous year and where actual period/s of stay outside India of such individual while serving on such
 ship/s is determined as under :-          
“His stay in India may be determined from the embarkation date stamped by the Immigration authority on his passport or by the
 Master of vessel on the Articles of Agreement (Foreign Going), whichever is earlier, to the disembarkation date stamped on the passport or
 on CDC while signing-off from the ship, whichever is later.”
 
44.       The Ministry has been taking up the recommendation of the committee with the Ministry of Finance at various levels since 2002 and
 has suggested necessary amendments in the Income Tax Act so as to provide necessary relief to the deprived Indian seafarers.  Response
 from Ministry of Finance is still awaited in the matter.
 
45.       During the course of evidence, the Secretary deposed before the Committee that;
"the request of seamen to get exemption from Income tax deserves consideration.  This will encourage seafaring profession in India,

 and help to promote merchant navy, and help Indian owners and charterers to get good Indian crew.  Otherwise the Indian seafarer prefers
 to go on board the foreign-flag vessels.  Today he gets the income exemption while working on the Indian ships- only, and only if he
 becomes an NRI i.e. goes out of India for more than half the year.  It is understood that most of the Indian seamen on foreign-flag vessels do

INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
 85.      Inland waterways comprises of rivers, creeks, canals, backwaters and lakes etc. which extend to about 14,500 kms length in the
 country out of which about 5,700 kms are navigable by mechanised vessels.  However, the potential of this important mode of transport has
 not been exploited so far to its desired level. Inland Water Transport (IWT) schemes mainly relate to development of waterways and
 augmentation of the traffic carrying capacity through expansion and modernization of I.W.T. vessels.  Whereas the Inland Waterways
 Authority of India (IWAI) is responsible for the development of National Waterways, responsibility for the development of State
 Waterways rests with the State Governments.  The Central Government have declared three Waterways, viz., Allahabad – Haldia Stretch
 (1620 kms.) Sadiya and Dhubri Stretch (891 kms.)  and  West Coast Canal from  Kollam to Kottapuram stretch along with  Udyogamandal
 and Champakara canals  (total 205 km) as National Waterways. Amongst the major initiatives, during the 10th Plan, it has been planned to
 construct Permanent Terminals at Gaighat, Patna, in N.W.- I and at Pandu, Assam, in NW-II. During the Financial Year 2004-05, a sum of
 Rs.145.57 crores (including Rs.47.5 crore from NE Pool) has been earmarked towards Plan Support to IWAI.
                       
86.       IWAI undertakes various schemes related to development of IWT infrastructure on these three National Waterways namely, Fairway
 Development, Terminals and Navigational Aids.  The Committee desired to know about the status of the proposal for declaration of four
 Waterways as National Waterways on the basis of techno-economic feasibility studies conducted by IWAI. The Ministry informed that the
 National Transport Policy Committee (NTPC) had identified 10 waterways.  Out of these three waterways namely the Ganga-Bhagirathi-
Hooghly, the Brahmaputra and the West Coast Canal have already been declared as National Waterways.  The Ministry further informed
 that a view was earlier taken by the Ministry that no new waterways  would be declare as National Waterways until the existing National
 Waterways are made fully operational. The policy has since been reviewed by the Ministry. Accordingly, the following three proposals for
 declaration as National Waterways are being pursued:
 
(i)         Godavari-Krishna and the integrated canal system including Buckingham            Canal in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu –
1074 kms.
(ii)        The Barak River in the Silichar Valley in North-East – 140 km.
(iii)       The East Coast Canal alongwith Brahmani river and Mahanadi Delta in Orissa – 623 kms.
 
87.       The declaration proposals are being finalized by IWAI in respect of (i) and (iii) only. As regards, the proposal at Barak River in
 North-East, the same will be considered in order of its priority.

            Inland Water Transport is a potential area and should receive national priority.  The question is often asked why we are not
 witnessing large scale movement of cargo through Inland Water Transport.  My answer to this, would be that in our country the
 investment needed for reviving the Inland Water Transport mode o transport has been inadequate.  World-wide, it has been experienced
 that with the growth of efficient road and rail network, traditional mode of Inland Water Transport declines.  But it may be revived if
 Government comes out with necessary policy support and adequate investments.  In our country, this support has been sub-optimal.  For
 the declared 3 NWs, we have so far spent Rs.292.74 crore only in the last 18 years.  If we have to achieve the stated objective of making
 these 3 NWs fully operational even by the end of 10 th Five Year Plan, there is a need of additional Rs.293 crore of plan funds over and
 above the available provision of Rs.301 crore in the remaining period of 10th Five Year Plan."

94.       The Committee expresses its concern over the slow pace of development of Inland Water Transport sector in the country.  The
 Committee feels that the potential of this important mode of transport has not yet been exploited to its desired level.  The Committee is
 surprised to note that inspite of the efforts of the Government only Rs.292.74 crore was spent during the last 18 years for development of
 the existing three National Waterways.  The Committee disapproves the lackadaisical approach of the Ministry towards the development of
 this important mode of transport. The Committee however, notes that a policy frame-work for the Inland Water Transport system has been
 approved by the Government to mobilize the required resources by attracting private investments and forming joint ventures for developing
 waterways infrastructure and cargo handling facilities. The Committee is however, constrained to express its doubts over the participation
 of private sector unless the Government has focused approach for providing basic infrastructural facilities for Inland Water Transport.
 
95.       The Committee is constrained to note that cargo transportation by Inland Water Transport mode has not shown significant
 improvement on these three National Waterways.  The Committee also expresses its displeasure over the fact that no comparative cost-
output evaluation for transportation of cargo through this alternate mode of transport has been carried out by the Ministry. The Committee is
 of the view that such evaluation would further establish the support of Inland Water Transport over other mode of transports. Therefore, the
 Committee recommends that a detailed study should be carried out by the Ministry in this regard. The Committee also recommends the
 Ministry to look into the possibility of formation of the taskforce to oversee the progress of the projects so that these could be completed in
 a time bound manner for development of Inland Water Transport in country.   The Committee feels that there is a need to strengthen R&D
 facilities particularly in the design of vessels, night navigation facilities, identification of economically viable routes and issues of mutual
 benefits with neighbouring countries like Bangladesh.  In this context, the Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation contained in
 its 70th Report of Demands for Grants (2003-04) of the Ministry of Shipping, which is reproduce below;
"The Committee also does not approve the strategy of the Ministry to make investment for development and regulation of Inland
 Waterways without fixing the physical targets to be achieved vis-à-vis financial parameter. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Ministry while coming up with target of investment must have a realistic physical target for cargo transportation, year-wise for the entire
 10th Plan period and beyond."
 
96.       The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should approach the Ministry of Finance to enhance allocation by Rs.293 crore
 as requested by the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping for the remaining period of 10 th Plan so as to achieve the objectives of making the
 existing three National Waterways fully operational.

CAPACITY AND TRAFFIC IN MAJOR PORT
         The Committee notes that the Ministry is taking capacity building major schemes for improving the capacity and productivity of all
 Major Ports.  The Committee appreciates the Ministry for adding capacity of 46.05 MTPA to Ports in the first two years of the 10 th Plan,
 making the aggregate cargo handling capacity of Port to 390 MTPA as against the total traffic of 344.53 MT.  The Committee observes that
 aggregate capacity of the Major Ports exceeds the traffic targets.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to initiate action for
 the modernization and capacity expansion of the port network across India's maritime zone so as to enable the Ports to utilise the additional
 capacity vis-à-vis traffic smoothly.
(Para 24)
INTERNATIONAL SHIP AND PORT FACILITY SECURITY
            
The Committee appreciates the Ministry for complying the ISPS code for all 12 Major Ports, 34 minor ports catering to international
 trade and 191 Indian Flagged ships in the country.  The Committee notes that the new maritime security regulations will provide international
 framework for ships and ports facilities besides detecting the deterring acts, which threaten security in the maritime transport sector.  The
 implementation of ISPS code, will also do away the hindrances in Indian export and imports.  The Committee, however, recommends that a
 task force be formed in the Ministry to observe strict compliance of international safety and security code/regulations.
(Para 30)
SAGAR MALA
            The Committee is happy to note that Sagar Mala programme has been initiated to cover all facets of maritime transport including Ports,
 Shipping and Inland Waterways with the aim to fully realise the potential of sea-borne trade and Inland Water Transport system.  The
 Committee feels that any delay in cabinet approval of this programme will adversely affect the modernization alongwith capacity expansion
 of ports network in the country.  However, the Committee is constrained to note that there is very little activity in the Inland Water Transport
 sub-sector.  This raises the question that how investment on infrastructure building will yield commensurate economically viable rate of
 returns.  The Committee was also disturbed to note that the IWAI is yet to develop the infrastructure for capacity building both in terms of
 human resources for proper technology appraisal, R&D and design inducement packages.  Therefore, the Committee concludes that this is a
 task, which should be urgently addressed.    The Committee, therefore, recommends that an early approval to launch Sagar Mala programme
 should be given and the Ministry should initiate action for setting-up of Sagar Mala Development Authority on the pattern of National
 Highways Authority of India.
(Para 36)
INTRODUCING OF TONNAGE TAX
            
The Committee notes that the Government has since introduced the tonnage tax in lieu of the corporate tax as per its
 recommendation.  The Committee hopes that with the introduction of tonnage tax and other fiscal incentives, the Indian Shipping
 companies will be able to acquire more tonnage.  However, the Committee is constrained to note that at present, the tonnage tax scheme is
 proposed for the vessels registered under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 only and vessels registered under the Indian Vessels Act, 1917,
 Indian Coastal Act 1838 and Dredgers have not been included for the purpose.  The Committee, therefor, recommends that in order to
 promote Inland Water Transport in the country, the Ministry should pursue the matter with Ministry of Finance for extending the benefit of
 tonnage tax to Dredgers and vessels registered under Indian Vessels/Indian Coastal Vessels Acts. 
(Para 39)
INDIAN SEAFARES WORKING ON FOREIGN FLAGGED SHIPS
           
The Committee expresses its deep concern regarding continuing drift of personnels away from employment on Indian ship to foreign
 flagged ships.  The Committee notes that the drift is due to lack of uniform tax regime i.e. Indian officers on Indian Ships have to pay
 income tax whereas, Indian officers on foreign flagged vessels are enjoying tax free status.  The Committee feels that there is some lacunae
 in the CBDT circular dated 28.11.90.  The Committee, recommends, the Ministry to revisit the whole issue in order to make employment on
 Indian ships attractive vis-à-vis foreign ships, and if necessary, impress upon the Ministry of Finance for amendment in the Income Tax
 Act.
(Para 46)
SHIPPING CORPORATION OF INDIA

REPORT
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/81streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:02:02]
The Committee notes with concern that the share of Shipping Corporation of India for transportation of crude oil imports has been
 declining due to non-avability of tanker tonnage while crude oil transportation in India has been increasing.  The Committee feels that
 Government's decision to disinvest the Shipping Corporation of India led to halt in making capital investments and accordingly, the
 Shipping Corporation of India could not pursue its vessel acquisition plan.  However, the Committee notes with satisfaction the
 Governments decision for not going in for disinvestment of the Shipping Corporation of India as this will clear the atmosphere of
 uncertainty.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Shipping Corporation of India should take steps to arrest the declining share of
 crude oil imports and to recover the lost market share besides augmenting and modernizing tanker tonnage significantly during the 10
th
 Plan.
(Para 57)
KOLKATA DOCK LABOUR BOARD
The Committee notes with anguish that the Kolkata Dock Labour Board has not yet revised the pension and liberalisation of post
 retirement benefits in terms of wage settlement and the pensioners have not been paid their pensionary and other post retirement dues for
 long.  The Committee notes that Kolkata Dock Labour Board, a body corporate, was constituted in terms of Section 5 (A) of the Dock
 Workers (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1948 in September 1952.  However, the Committee is constrained to note that the employees of
 the Board are not being treated as a Government employees so far as payment of pension and pensionary benefits to the employees of
 Kolkata Dock Labour Board is concerned, which is a matter of right of the Government employees.  The Committee also notes with
 constrained that Kolkata Dock Labour Board has also not been provided financial assistance out of the National Revival Fund. The
 Committee notes that a proposal for release of one time grant of Rs.42.96 crore to Kolkata Dock Labour Board was sent to the Ministry of
 Finance but the Ministry of Finance has not acceded to the request for release of grants to Kolkata Dock Labour Board.  The Committee is
 of the view that it is the sole liability of the Government to pay pension to the pensioners in time and it will be sheer discrimination on the
 part of the Government to withhold pension and post retirement benefits in the name of financial crisis that prevailed in Kolkata Dock
 Labour Board.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that no injustice should be meted to the pensioners of Kolkata Dock Labour
 Board in the payment of pension and pensionary benefits and the Ministry of Shipping should impress upon the Ministry of Finance for
 release of one time grant for the implementation the pensionary and other benefits to the pensioners.   In fact even Voluntary Retirement
 Scheme could be implemented to address this serious problem.  The Committee also recommends the Ministry to keep it informed about the
 progress in the matter regularly.
(Para 63)
            
INDIAN INSTITUTE OF MARITIME STUDIES (IIMS)
           
The Committee is not satisfied with replies of the Ministry regarding setting up of Indian Maritime University, terms and conditions
 of employees creation of Pension Fund and retention of Government accommodation etc. and convey its dismay over the delay in
 finalisation of terms and conditions of service of Indian Institute of Maritime Studies and confusion is still prevailing in this regard, this has
 certainly affect the morale of the employees.  The Committee is of the view that the creation of trust for the Indian Institute of Maritime
 Studies has resulted in ambiguity with respect to the management of funds of Indian Institute of Maritime Studies.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that Government must expedite their effort for formation of university for Indian Institute of Maritime Studies. In
 this connection, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation contained in the 70th Report
of Demands for Grants 2003-04 of the Ministry of Shipping which is reproduce below:
 
"The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry should go for establishing the University by an Act of Parliament so as to
 provide considerable operational freedom and a qualitative boost to the Maritime training in the country.  The Committee, however, notes
 with concern that the terms and conditions of services are being changed against the interest of the employees.   The Committee
 recommends that before taking any action with regard to the terms and conditions of the service of employees of erstwhile Maritime
 Institutes, the unions of the employees be consulted and it should be ensured that the terms and conditions of service of employees who
 have been transferred on deemed deputation to IIMS remain unchanged. Also, the interests of employees particularly relating to pension,
 CGHS facilities and retention of Government accommodation should be safeguarded."
(Para 69)
MISAPPROPRIATION OF SEAMEN'S PROVIDENT FUND
            The Committee is constrained to note that the matter of recouping the shortage to the tune of Rs.92.78 crore is pending for long time
 with the Ministry of Finance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should pursue the matter vigorously
 with Ministry of Finance for providing a grant to the extent of Rs.92.78 crore to recoup the shortage in the Seamen's Provident Fund.  More
 so, because the Fund was managed by the Government and the responsibility of irregularity in the management of that Fund cannot be
 borne by the seamen's who's life-long savings stands in uncertainty, if not, outrightly jeopardize.
(Para 73)
HINDUSTAN SHIPYARD LIMITED
            The Committee notes that Hindustan Shipyard Limited has been making consistent efforts to utilise the installed capacity for
 increasing shiprepairs turnover and its aggressive marketing efforts is gaining result due to which the order book position of the company
 has increased. The Committee also notes that fresh financial restructuring of the company is under active consideration of the Government.
 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take steps to improve the performance of the shipyard besides impressing

REPORT
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/81streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:02:02]
 upon the Ministry of Finance for the capital restructuring of the Company.
(Para 84)
INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
           
The Committee expresses its concern over the slow pace of development of Inland Water Transport sector in the country.  The
 Committee feels that the potential of this important mode of transport has not yet been exploited to its desired level.  The Committee is
 surprised to note that inspite of the efforts of the Government only Rs.292.74 crore was spent during the last 18 years for development of
 the existing three National Waterways.  The Committee disapproves the lackadaisical approach of the Ministry towards the development of
 this important mode of transport. The Committee however, notes that a policy frame-work for the Inland Water Transport system has been
 approved by the Government to mobilize the required resources by attracting private investments and forming joint ventures for developing
 waterways infrastructure and cargo handling facilities. The Committee is however, constrained to express its doubts over the participation
 of private sector unless the Government has focused approach for providing basic infrastructural facilities for Inland Water Transport.
 
            The Committee is constrained to note that cargo transportation by Inland Water Transport mode has not shown significant
 improvement on these three National  Waterways.  The Committee also expresses its displeasure over the fact that no comparative cost-
output evaluation for transportation of cargo through this alternate mode of transport has been carried out by the Ministry. The Committee is
 of the view that such evaluation would further establish the support of Inland Water Transport over other mode of transports. Therefore, the
 Committee recommends that a detailed study should be carried out by the Ministry in this regard. The Committee also recommends the
 Ministry to look into the possibility of formation of the taskforce to oversee the progress of the projects so that these could be completed in
 a time bound manner for development of Inland Water Transport in country.   The Committee feels that there is a need to strengthen R&D
 facilities particularly in the design of vessels, night navigation facilities, identification of economically viable routes and issues of mutual
 benefits with neighbouring countries like Bangladesh.  In this context, the Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation contained in
 its 70th Report of Demands for Grants (2003-04) of the Ministry of Shipping, which is reproduce below;
"The Committee also does not approve the strategy of the Ministry to make investment for development and regulation of Inland
 Waterways without fixing the physical targets to be achieved vis-à-vis financial parameter. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Ministry while coming up with target of investment must have a realistic physical target for cargo transportation, year-wise for the entire
 10th Plan period and beyond."
            The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should approach the Ministry of Finance to enhance allocation by Rs.293 crore
 as requested by the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping for the remaining period of 10 th Plan so as to achieve the objectives of making the
 existing three National Waterways fully operational.
(Paras 94, 95 & 96)
 
CENTRAL INLAND WATER TRANSPORT CORPORATION
           
The Committee notes that the Central Inland Water Transport Corporation is presently implementing four year restructuring schemes
 involving Government assistance of Rs.139 crore.  However, the Committee also note that there is a dispute over the time-frame of
 restructuring plan, the exact time of starting of the scheme and availability of funds. Given the fact that inspite of substantial investment for
 infrastructure building in Inland Water Transport sector and the insignificant participation of private sector in utilizing infrastructure for the
 restructuring the Central Inland Water Transport Corporation to a proper health is an urgent task.  Therefore, the Committee is of the view
 that the future of IWT operations including that of CIWTC holds immense possibilities for establishing a well-defined multimodal
 transportation network in the country and recommends that Government should consider a fresh financial restructuring of the company. 
     (Para 103)

R E P O R T
 
Roads are the very arteries of the nation, carrying the lifeblood of trade and commerce to all corners of the country,
 promoting and sustaining a robust national economy.  They also play an important role in national integration, which is
 particularly important in a country of the size of India.
 
2.         The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is responsible for development, formulation and implementation of
 policies relating to Road Transport and National Highways.  Its main function relate to road development and maintenance
 including Border Roads, Planning and co-ordination and Road Transport. The Ministry is administratively divided into two

D R A F T R E P O R T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/82ndreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:03:03]
 wings namely Transport Wing and Roads Wing.
 
3.         Transport Wing is concerned with the formulation of broad policies relating to Road Transport, Motor Vehicles Act,
 legislation relating to Road Transport Corporations, besides making arrangements for movement of motor vehicular traffic with
 the neighbouring countries.
 
            Roads Wing is mainly concerned with the matters relating to:-
(i)                  Advising Government on all general policy matters relating to Highways;
(ii)                Development & Maintenance of roads declared as National Highways;
(iii)               Roads other than National Highways in Union Territories;
(iv)              Administration of Central Road Fund (CRF) pertaining to State Roads other than rural roads;
(v)                Evaluation of standards for roads and bridges and formulation of specifications;
(vi)              Performance of road research;
(vii)             National Highways Authority of India and National Institute for Training of Highway Engineers.
 
4.         The following autonomous bodies function under the administrative control of the Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways: -
 
(a)                National Highways Authority of India (NHAI); and
(b)                National Institute of Training of Highway Engineers (NITHE).
 
5.         Demand No.79 containing the details of budget allocation of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways for the
 financial year 2004-05, was considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism
 and Culture at its meeting held on the 13 th August 2004.  During the meeting, the Committee took oral evidence of the
 Secretary and other officers of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. 
 
PLAN PROVISIONS
6.         The Tenth Plan (2002-2007) provides an outlay of Rs.59,490 crore for development of Roads under Central Sector
 including National Highways.  This comprises of Rs.34,790 crore as Gross Budgetary Support and Rs.24,700 crore as Internal
 and Extra Budgetary Resources   (IEBR).
 
7.         The Annual Plan 2004-2005 of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways envisages Gross outlay of Rs.10,814.00
 crore in respect of Central and Centrally Sponsored Schemes in Transport Sector within the jurisdiction of the Ministry: -

9.         While making presentation before the Committee during his evidence, the Secretary, Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways brought out that the National Highway system in the country suffers from deficiencies of capacity constraint,

D R A F T R E P O R T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/82ndreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:03:03]
 inadequate pavement crust etc.  The resource requirement for removing deficiencies during Tenth Plan is around Rs.1,65,000
 crore.  However, the Tenth Plan allocation is only Rs.59,490 crore.  The Committee was further informed that the length of
 National Highway network other than NHDP is 51,290 kilometers and the pro-rata funds for maintenance and development for
 these highways are inadequate.  The Secretary also expressed the apprehension that National Highways Development Project
 (NHDP) may slide if funds assured for the project are not provided in future.
 
10.        According to the Tenth Five Year Plan, roads are the key to the development of an economy.  However, the allocations
 made for the road sector do not indicate their importance in the economic development of the country.  The Committee notes
 with concern that there is a huge resource gap of around Rs.1,06,000 crore in the road sector during the Tenth Plan.  A good
 road network constitutes the basic infrastructure that propels the development process through connectivity and opening up the
 backward regions to trade and investment.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to achieve the objective of
 Tenth Plan in road sector, the budget allocation of Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should be substantially increased at
 RE stage.  The Committee notes that the Government has not been able to attract private investment as anticipated.  Therefore,
 the budgetary allocations of the Ministry should be adequately increased during the remaining years of the Tenth Plan so as to
 reduce the resource gap in this sector to some extent. 
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
11.        India has a vast road network of 3.32 million kilometers of which the National Highways and the State Highways
 together account for 1,95,000 km.  As on 31
st March 2004, the length of National Highways network is only 65,569 km
 constituting about 2% of the total road network in the country and carrying about 40% of the total traffic across the length and
 breadth of the country.
 
12.        The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways is primarily responsible for the construction and maintenance of National
 Highways (NH). All roads, other than National Highway in States, fall within the jurisdiction of respective state governments. 
 The development and maintenance of National Highways are being done on agency basis.  The National Highways Authority
 of India (NHAI), State Public Works Departments (PWDs) and the Border Road Organisation (BRO) are the main agencies.
 Out of the total National Highway length of 65,569 km, about 14,279 km have been entrusted to National Highways Authority
 of India (NHAI) for improvement under National Highway Development Project (NHDP), Port Connectivity Schemes and
 other schemes.  The 7,457 km length of new National Highways is yet to be entrusted to agencies.  The balance lengths of
 about 39,129 km and 4,704 km of non-NHDP sections of National Highways are mainly entrusted to State PWDs and Border
 Road Organisation (BRO) respectively, as agencies of the Ministry. 
 
13.        Ministry of Road Transport & Highways has also decided to upgrade stretches of NH-34 from km 31 at Barasat and 398
 Km at Raiganj in West Bengal by availing assistance from Asian Development Bank.  While the total project size is around
 Rs.1085.70 crore, the outlay for the year 2004-05 is Rs.113.50 crore.  Separately, Rs.3210 crore has been earmarked for NHAI
 for Externally Aided Project out of which Rs.2568 crore is being provided as Grant and Rs.642 crore as EAP-loan.
 
14.        National Highways (Original) Works are capital works on Non-NHDP highways such as two laning, four laning,
 construction of bye-passes, construction of Rail over-Bridges, construction of Bridges, widening of roads etc. Budgetary
 provision for National Highway Works (O) for the year 2004-05 is Rs.1487 crore out of which Rs.1338.80 crore is for the
 States and Union Territories other than Sikkim and North Eastern States and a sum of Rs.148.20 crore has been earmarked for
 2004-05 for Sikkim and North Eastern States.
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP) 
15.        The Committee was informed by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways that the Government has embarked upon
 a massive programme to develop highways through the National Highways Development Project (NHDP) in the country.  The
 NHDP is the largest highway project ever undertaken in the country.  This is being implemented by NHAI.  The NHDP
 consists of Golden Quadrilateral, North-South and East-West Corridors, Port Connectivity and other Projects.  The total length
 under NHDP is about 14,279 km.  The details relating to NHDP are as under:-
(i)
                  Golden Quadrilateral (GQ) comprising National Highways connecting four metro cities viz., Delhi, Mumbai,
 Chennai and Kolkata.  Total length of GQ is 5846 km.  As on 31 st March 2004, four-laning of 2082 km has
 already been completed and work is under various stages of implementation on the entire balance length of
 3764 km under 78 different contracts.

(ii)                North-South and East-West corridors comprising the National Highways connecting Srinagar to Kanyakumari
 including Kochi-Salem spur and Silchar to Porbandar.  The total length of the corridors is about 7300 km.  As

24.        The Committee observes that the main objective relating to the road sector for the Tenth Plan is balanced development
 of the total network.  The task would include widening of roads, improvement in riding quality and strengthening and road
 safety measures to cater to the growing demand for road services.  However, the Committee notes with dismay that out of
 43,833 kilometer of non-NHDP National Highways, only 1.95 per cent are four or more laned whereas 62.55 per cent of such
 National Highways are two-laned and 35.49 per cent of such National Highways are only single/intermediate laned.  The
 Committee cannot accept the wishful thinking of the Ministry that "this is intended to be implemented mostly through private
 sector participation on Build Operate Transfer (BOT) basis" without being supported by any specific facts.  Going by the past
 records, the Committee also feels it is not suggestive that such course will be available to the Government.  The allocation
 made for these National Highways is also meagre  when compared to the allocations made for National Highways under
 NHDP.  There is a mismatch between NHDP and non-NHDP Highways in terms of lanes, surface quality and funds. 
 Therefore, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should give equitable weightage to the
 non-NHDP National Highways and provide adequate budgetary allocation required for their development as envisaged in the
 Tenth Plan.  A balanced approach should be adopted for increasing the lane width and improving the riding quality of these
 National Highways.  This will ensure that those parts of the country which are not connected with National Highways under
 NHDP also get due attention.  The development of National Highways in these areas will also help improve the economic
 development of such places.
 
VALUE ADDITION TO THE LAND ADJOINING NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
25.        During the course of the evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, the Committee
 observed that construction of National Highways results in appreciation of economic value of land on both sides of the road.  
 Hence while creating world-class roads, the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways adds value to the lands adjoining the
 roads and there is a price appreciation of these lands.  As a result, the owners of the land adjoining National Highway get
 advantage without investing any money. 
26.        The Committee feels that in view of the resource crunch being faced by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways,
 there is a genuine need for generation of additional revenue by the Ministry.  Whenever any National Highway is constructed, it
 leads to huge value addition to the land adjoining the National Highway and these benefits of addition in value have so far been
 enjoyed by private agencies only.   The Government should also get advantage of the appreciation of land value because it is
 the taxpayer's money that has led to the value addition of that property.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Government may explore the possibility of imposing some cess/tax on land adjoining National Highways which is being
 utilized for commercial purpose on annual basis.  This could serve as a permanent source of income for the Government and the
 revenue so generated could be ploughed back only for the construction and maintenance of National Highways in the country. 
 Provision of ducting at the time of construction of National Highways for laying telephone and electric cables also leads to
 value addition and can be explored for generating more funds for the road sector. These measures may go a long way to meet
 the resource gap for maintenance and construction of National Highways in the country.

29.        During the course of the evidence, the Committee brought to the notice of the representatives of the Ministry of Road
 Transport & Highways and BRO that high-intensity explosives are being used while constructing the roads in the hilly areas. 
 This often results in landslides which lead to washing away of roads, bridges and residential areas.  The Committee sought the
 response of BRO in the matter.  Replying to the query, the representative of the BRO agreed with the view expressed by the
 Committee.  The Committee was informed that so far the executing agencies in the hilly areas were using high-intensity
 explosives.  The Committee was further informed that in view of the adverse effects of the high-intensity explosives, the
 Government of India has directed the manufacturing agencies to try for other alternatives.  The BRO was trying to switch over
 to some other system in this respect.  
 
30.        The Committee is of the opinion that hilly areas have a delicate ecological system and there is a need to reduce blasting
 in these areas so that the hill slopes do not destabilize or fall.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the BRO should
 switch over to using  low-intensity explosives while making roads in such areas.   The BRO should also consider constructing
 tunnels in hilly areas, wherever required.
 
31.        The Committee also enquired from the representatives of BRO as to whether they had any Research and Development
 facility within their own organisation to address such problems.  The Committee was informed that BRO had no specific
 Research and Development facility available with them.  However, it was mentioned that BRO had a huge experience of over
 forty years in road construction in hilly areas.
 
32.        The Committee is aware that Border Roads Organisation is a well disciplined, motivated construction organisation in
 the country equipped with proven capability and expertise developed over more than forty years in the area of construction of
 roads, national highways, permanent bridges etc. in the border and hilly areas.  However, the Committee is surprised to know
 that no Research and Development facility is available in the BRO.  The Committee is of the opinion that R&D should be an
 integral part of any organisation working in a field where technological advancements are bound to take place.  Practical
 experience of BRO of making roads in hilly areas is no doubt an added advantage for them but having an institutional
 mechanism for research and development is absolutely essential in the contemporary age.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the BRO should develop a Research and Development facility of their own so that they can have access to the
 modern technology and they could stay in touch with technological advancements in the field of making roads on hilly areas.

ROAD SAFETY
47.        Road Safety is a area of serious concern.  An allocation of Rs.29.00 crore was made for this sector in BE 2003-2004
 which was reduced to Rs.28.16 crore at the RE stage.  However, the actual expenditure during the year was to the tune of
 Rs.28.24 crore.  Now an amount of      Rs.33.20 crore has been allocated in BE 2004-05.  Under this scheme, a number of
 activities such as publicity and awareness campaign on road safety, grants-in-aid to Non Governmental Organisations (NGOs)
 to create awareness on road safety/administer road safety programmes, assistance in the form of equipment for accident relief
 and refresher training to drivers in the unorganized sector are being undertaken.
           
48.        The Committee brought to the notice of the Ministry that in recent year, more than 80,000 persons had been killed in
 accidents on Indian roads annually.  The Committee further pointed out that the Delhi-Jaipur and Delhi-Agra Highways were
 the most accident prone of the five highways leading out of Delhi.  The Committee enquired as to whether Ministry of Road
 Transport & Highways had conducted any survey to identify the factors which have been the cause of higher rate of accidents
 on the two highways and taken remedial measures. 
 
49.        In response, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways that a study had been
 conducted by a private consultant for the NHAI to identify the requirement of improvements related to road safety on NH-2
 (Delhi-Agra section) and NH-8 (Delhi-Jaipur section).  The consultant has suggested some of the remedial measures for
 enhancing the road safety on these two highways such as road markings, delineators, road signs, improvement of junctions,
 improvement of median openings, provision of service road etc.  The total estimated cost of these works as submitted by the
 consultant is Rs.121.22 crore.  The reports are being scrutinized and further action for execution of these works will be taken
 thereafter keeping in view the availability of the resources.   The Committee enquired from the Ministry regarding the steps
 taken for increasing public awareness about road safety.  In response, the Committee was informed that the Ministry works
 with the different State Governments and NGOs in the following areas:-
·
               refresher training for heavy vehicle drivers
·               evacuation of accident victims from the accident spot to the nearest hospital by assisting States and NGOs with
 ambulances
·               removal of vehicles involved in accidents on National Highways by providing a crane to States and NGOs
·               checking overloading of vehicles
·               NGOs and institutions are also given financial assistance for conducting refresher training to drivers of heavy
 commercial vehicles in the unorganized sector
·               providing non-recurring financial assistance to State Government / NGOs for setting up model driver training
 schools.
·               publicity and awareness on road safety through campaigns in print and electronic media.
50.        The Committee observes that the mortality rate due to the road accidents in the country is too high.  The rate of
 accidents has gone up after the improvement in the riding quality of our highways.  The Committee feels that so far the
 measures taken by the Government to contain road accidents have proved to be inadequate.  Hence there is an urgent need to
 re-devise the strategy for taking remedial measures and minimize road accidents.  The Committee recommends that the
 Government should introduce road safety devices and launch awareness programmes for the public and transport users in a big
 way.  The Committee takes note that a consultant has suggested some remedial measures for enhancing the road safety on some
 highways.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should adopt a proactive
 approach in this regard and there should be wider and effective use of fast improving applications of information technology
 and communication technology to monitor technical deficiencies on the roads.  The Committee suggests that the Ministry of
 Road Transport & Highways should involve their R&D wing and before constructing National Highways, road safety features
 should be incorporated in the design of the road at the detailed project report stage itself. 
 
51.        During the course of the evidence, the Committee observed that there had been frequent digging of National Highways
 by various local and central agencies.  This exercise is mostly undertaken for laying of cables etc.  However, the roads are not
 laid properly after that and are merely filled up with mud.  In some cases the process goes on in a very haphazard way.  Such
 portions of the road sink inside during rains.  The drivers of the vehicles passing through the roads are not aware of the puddles
 and the potholes so created.  This often leads to serious accidents which result in loss of precious lives and property.
           
52.        The Committee is of the view that with the development and improvement in riding quality of the roads in the country,

D R A F T R E P O R T

 the speed of the vehicles has also gone up.  Non-uniformity of the quality of the surface because of indiscriminate digging and
 non-compliance of rules by other departments while digging, presence of slow moving vehicles particularly in densely
 populated areas, straying of animals in the carriageways lead to fatal accidents.  Therefore, the Committee feels that availability
 of service roads/underpasses in densely populated areas is of immense importance.  The Committee further feels that laying
 ducts is not only beneficial for value addition and resource mobilization but also for avoiding indiscriminate digging.  The
 Committee is of the view that lack of telecommunication facility on the National Highways is also responsible for higher death
 rate.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should ensure the availability of adequate
 telecommunication for availing medical facility.  The Committee further recommends that in view of the growing number of
 accidents, adequately equipped trauma centers should be opened at reasonable distances on National Highways.
           
53.        The Committee also desired to know from the representatives of Ministry of Road Transport & Highways whether there
 was any monitoring mechanism which ensured that the dug up roads were restored to their original position.  In response, the
 Committee was merely informed that all efforts were being made in this direction.
           
54.        The Committee is of the view that if ever the roads are required to be dug up, they must be restored to their earlier
 position.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should make it mandatory
 that the quality of National Highways should be restored by the authority undertaking the digging work to a workable condition
 so as to be able to cope up with the traffic load till repair work is undertaken by the NHAI or concerned PWD.  The violators in
 this respect should be punished adequately. 
MODEL DRIVER TRAINING SCHOOL
55.        As per Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, an analysis of data of accidents reveals that about 83.5% of accidents
 are attributed to the fault of the drivers.  Hence a scheme for setting up a Model Driver Training Schools has been formulated
 for development of right attitude towards driving and to instill understanding of traffic regulations.  Under the scheme,
 assistance is given for setting up of Regional Schools in the country aimed at imparting training to drivers and improving their
 driving skills.  The State Government is required to provide land free from all encumbrances.  Central Government provides
 financial assistance as capital grant for building and other infrastructure.  It is the responsibility of the concerned State
 Government or NGO recommended by the State Government to bear the recurring and maintenance costs.  A budget provision
 of Rs.6.5 crore has been kept for this scheme in the budget for 2004-05.  The allocation during the years 2003-04 and 2004-05

56.        During the financial year 2003-04, a total of 30,015 drivers had been imparted training with the help of various
 ogranisations/institutions, as against 21999 drivers during 2002-03.  The objective during the Tenth Plan is to set up at least one
 such school in each of the five zones.  During 2002-03, proposals for setting up of Driver Training Institutes in Assam, West
 Bengal, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh were sanctioned.  During 2003-04 efforts were made to complete the already
 sanctioned Drivers Training Schools.  It is expected that all the four training schools will become functional by the end of

DIFFERENTIAL PRICING SYSTEM FOR PRIVATE VEHICLES
59.        During the course of the oral evidence, the Committee observed that the automobile population in the country had been
 growing disproportionately with respect to the infrastructure created and the roads were under undue pressure.  In view, the
 Committee was of the opinion that there was a need to adopt a policy which discourages owning of multiple vehicles.  The
 efforts of the Government should focus on developing the public transport.  In order to discourage owning multiple vehicles,
 the Government should adopt a methodology whereby the rich and the affluent are asked to pay more for keeping more than
 one vehicle.  Acquiring more than one vehicle in a family should invite financial disincentives.  This would certainly
 discourage owning of multiple vehicles.  Further, it would also help release the pressure on the surface of the roads and also
 help positively to reduce vehicular pollution.
 
RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT 
60.        The National highway works are being executed following the standard specifications and manuals besides guidelines
 issued from time to time.  To build a sustainable road infrastructure comparable to the best in the world, the updation and
 standardization of specifications including design parameters of road and bridge structures need the support of R&D base.  The
 various components of this strategy are improvement in design, modernization of construction techniques, introduction of
 improved material conforming to latest trends, evolving better and appropriate specifications, encouraging development and use
 of new technologies etc.  The areas covered are roads, road transport, bridges, traffic and transportation techniques etc. 
 
61.        The Ministry does not have R&D organisation of its own.  The research schemes sponsored by the Ministry are
 generally 'applied' in nature which once completed, would enable them to be adopted by user in their work in the field.  The
 Ministry takes the help of various research institutions, academic institutions and universities to implement the schemes.  The
 Ministry invites the proposals from various research/academic institutions including Council of Scientific and Industrial
 Research (CSIR) Laboratories, Indian Roads Congress (IRC) and reputed public/private institutions engaged in R&D activities

OBSERVATION/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
AT A GLANCE
 
PLAN PROVISIONS
According to the Tenth Five Year Plan, roads are the key to the development of an economy.  However, the allocations
 made for the road sector do not indicate their importance in the economic development of the country.  The Committee notes
 with concern that there is a huge resource gap of around Rs.1,06,000 crore in the road sector during the Tenth Plan.  A good
 road network constitutes the basic infrastructure that propels the development process through connectivity and opening up the
 backward regions to trade and investment.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to achieve the objective of
 Tenth Plan in road sector, the budget allocation of Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should be substantially increased at
 RE stage.  The Committee notes that the Government has not been able to attract private investment as anticipated.  Therefore,
 the budgetary allocations of the Ministry should be adequately increased during the remaining years of the Tenth Plan so as to
 reduce the resource gap in this sector to some extent. 
(Para 10)
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP)
The Committee notes that about 90% of the Golden Quadrilateral is proposed to be completed by December 2004.  The
 Committee recommends that the Government should take all necessary steps to make sure that the works proposed to be
 completed by December 2004 are completed within that period.  However, the Committee is not satisfied with the reasons
 given by the Ministry for delay in completion of NHDP programme.  The reasons are general in nature and could have been
 anticipated well in advance whereby the time of one year could have been saved.  This clearly shows the lack of proactive
 approach on the part of the Ministry. The Committee also recommends that the Government should evolve a monitoring
 mechanism to ensure quality of construction, making officials accountable for failure, transparency in implementation process,
 penalising defaulting contractors etc. so that the remaining part of the project is also completed within the revised targeted
 period.
(Para 20)
STATUS OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS NOT COVERED UNDER NHDP
The Committee observes that the main objective relating to the road sector for the Tenth Plan is balanced development
 of the total network.  The task would include widening of roads, improvement in riding quality and strengthening and road
 safety measures to cater to the growing demand for road services.  However, the Committee notes with dismay that out of
 43,833 kilometer of non-NHDP National Highways, only 1.95 per cent are four or more laned whereas 62.55 per cent of such
 National Highways are two-laned and 35.49 per cent of such National Highways are only single/intermediate laned.  The
 Committee cannot accept the wishful thinking of the Ministry that "this is intended to be implemented mostly through private
 sector participation on Build Operate Transfer (BOT) basis" without being supported by any specific facts.  Going by the past
 records, the Committee also feels it is not suggestive that such course will be available to the Government.  The allocation
 made for these National Highways is also meagre  when compared to the allocations made for National Highways under
 NHDP.  There is a mismatch between NHDP and non-NHDP Highways in terms of lanes, surface quality and funds. 
 Therefore, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should give equitable weightage to the
 non-NHDP National Highways and provide adequate budgetary allocation required for their development as envisaged in the
 Tenth Plan.  A balanced approach should be adopted for increasing the lane width and improving the riding quality of these
 National Highways.  This will ensure that those parts of the country which are not connected with National Highways under
 NHDP also get due attention.  The development of National Highways in these areas will also help improve the economic
 development of such places.
(Para 24)
VALUE ADDITION TO THE LAND ADJOINING NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
The Committee feels that in view of the resource crunch being faced by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways,
 there is a genuine need for generation of additional revenue by the Ministry.  Whenever any National Highway is constructed, it
 leads to huge value addition to the land adjoining the National Highway and these benefits of addition in value have so far been
 enjoyed by private agencies only.   The Government should also get advantage of the appreciation of land value because it is
 the taxpayer's money that has led to the value addition of that property.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Government may explore the possibility of imposing some cess/tax on land adjoining National Highways which is being
 utilized for commercial purpose on annual basis.  This could serve as a permanent source of income for the Government and the
 revenue so generated could be ploughed back only for the construction and maintenance of National Highways in the country.

 Provision of ducting at the time of construction of National Highways for laying telephone and electric cables also leads to
 value addition and can be explored for generating more funds for the road sector. These measures may go a long way to meet
 the resource gap for maintenance and construction of National Highways in the country.
(Para 26)
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS ENTRUSTED WITH BORDER ROADS ORGANISATION (BRO)
The Committee is of the opinion that hilly areas have a delicate ecological system and there is a need to reduce blasting
 in these areas so that the hill slopes do not destabilize or fall.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the BRO should
 switch over to using low-intensity explosives while making roads in such areas.   The BRO should also consider constructing
 tunnels in hilly areas, wherever required.
(Para 30)
 
The Committee is aware that Border Roads Organisation is a well disciplined, motivated construction organisation in
 the country equipped with proven capability and expertise developed over more than forty years in the area of construction of
 roads, national highways, permanent bridges etc. in the border and hilly areas.  However, the Committee is surprised to know
 that no Research and Development facility is available in the BRO.  The Committee is of the opinion that R&D should be an
 integral part of any organisation working in a field where technological advancements are bound to take place.  Practical
 experience of BRO of making roads in hilly areas is no doubt an added advantage for them but having an institutional
 mechanism for research and development is absolutely essential in the contemporary age.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the BRO should develop a Research and Development facility of their own so that they can have access to the
 modern technology and they could stay in touch with technological advancements in the field of making roads on hilly areas. 
(Para 32)
DEVELOPMENT OF NEWLY DECLARED NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
The Committee is concerned to note that certain lengths of state roads had not been handed over to the Ministry of Road
 Transport & Highways for taking over the roads for development even after a period of nearly six months after their declaration
 as National Highways.  The Committee feels that once the roads are declared as National Highways, the physical possession of
 the roads should be immediately taken over by the central agencies for their development as National Highways.  The
 Committee recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should adopt a proactive approach in this regard. 
 Before declaring a state road as National Highway, such lengths of the road must fulfil the criterion for declaration as National
 Highway.  The guidelines for declaration of state roads as National Highways should also be so revised that the State
 Governments fulfil the required criterion before any road is declared as National Highway.
(Para 34)
CENTRAL ROAD FUND
The Committee is dismayed to note that the fund accruing due to additional cess on petrol and diesel to support the
 implementation of National Highway Development Project is yet to be provided to Ministry of Road Transport & Highways
 and the amendment in the relevant Act for the purpose is yet to be introduced in the Parliament.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the necessary legislation facilitating the transfer of the above fund to the Central Road Fund should be
 introduced at the earliest, so that the funds earmarked for NHDP do not remain idle and are utilized for the purpose.   The
 Committee would also like to be apprised of the total amount earmarked for National Highways and the details of its
 component coming from Central Road Fund and Consolidation Fund of India.
(Para 39)

The Committee is not convinced with the replies furnished by the Ministry regarding the introduction of High Security
 Registration Plates and getting the technology required for the purpose from a single source.   The Committee is constrained to
 note that at a time when, during the 10
th Plan, the road transport sector is faced with a resource gap of over Rs.1,00,000 crore,
 the Ministry has not been able to prioritise its programmes.  The Committee feels that through a Government regulation, the
 Government is forcing the people in the country to switch over to the much expensive HSRP.  The Committee is not able to
 understand the reasons which necessitated the Government to make a compulsory financial burden on the people by introducing
 the HSRP.  Though the Government has no indication to have single technology provider, however, the Committee has
 apprehension that given the specifications of HSRP, there is very likelihood of monopolistic regime deciding the course of
 development in the matter.  The Committee further recommends that given the development of the information technology and
 its induction in this sector, the Government should have focused attention on capacity building towards the choice of the
 appropriate technology-model and encourage the emergence and promotion of multiple players.

 INTRODUCTION
 
         I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture,
 having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this Eighty-third report on
 “Functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety”.
 
2.      The Committee considered the subject and held discussions with the representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation
 and Commission of Railway Safety at Bangalore and Lucknow during its study visits in September 2001 and
 September 2002 respectively.  The Committee took oral evidence of the officers of Ministry of Civil Aviation and
 Commission of Railway Safety at its meeting held on    20
th May 2003.  The Committee also took oral evidence of the
 representatives of Ministry of Railways at its meeting held on the 14th July 2003.
 
3.         3.         In order to get wider views on the subject, the Committee invited the views of individuals and institutions
 interested in the subject through advertisement in all major national dailies and vernacular newspapers all over the
 country.  The advertisement evoked tremendous public response and the Committee received memoranda on various
 aspects of the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety from a lot of people including many retired
 Commissioners/Chief Commissioners of Railway Safety.  The Committee also heard the views of Shri Prakash Narain
 and Shri R.N. Malhotra, both former Chairmen, Railway Board and Shri Arya Bhushan, former Chief Commissioner of

REPORT
 
The Commission of Railway Safety deals with matters pertaining to safety in rail travel and operation.  For
 discharge of these functions, the Commission derives certain statutory powers from the Railways Act, 1989 and the
 rules framed thereunder.  While the Railway Board in the Ministry of Railways are the safety controlling authority and
 are responsible for laying down and enforcing safety standards for the Indian Railways, the main task of the
 Commission is to direct, advise and caution the railway executives through its regulation, inspection, audit,
 investigatory and advisory functions and thereby assist them in ensuring that all stipulated measures are taken in regard
 to the soundness of rail construction and safety in train operation.  The most crucial function of the Commission of
 Railway Safety is to ensure that any new Railway line to be opened for passenger traffic should conform to the
 standards and specifications prescribed by the Ministry of Railways and the new line is safe in all respects for carrying
 of passenger traffic.  Similar job is also performed in respect of other works such as gauge conversion, doubling of lines
 and electrification of existing lines.  Another important function of the Commission is to conduct statutory inquiry into
 serious train accidents occurring on the Indian Railways and to make recommendations for improving Railway Safety.  
 
2.         Since Railway safety is of paramount importance to all and the fact that there had been a spurt in train accidents
 during the recent past, the Committee decided to study the functioning of Commission of Railway Safety.  Since the
 Commission of Railway Safety is under the administrative control of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Committee
 asked the Ministry of Civil Aviation to furnish a status note on the functioning of Commission of Railway Safety for its
 consideration. 
 
3.         In the status note submitted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Committee was informed about the genesis of
 the Commission of Railway Safety.  It was brought out that formerly the Commission of Railway Safety was called the
 Railway Inspectorate and it functioned under the control of the Railway Board till May 1941. In the wake of a serious
 accident in 1937, the Central Legislature considered that the Commission, which was charged with the responsibility
 for conducting inquires into serious railway accidents as also for the inspection of Railways, should not function under
 the administrative control of the same executive authority whose work it was required to inspect and comment upon. 
 The principle of separation of the Railway Inspectorate from the Railway Board was endorsed in 1940 by the Central
 Legislature who recommended that "Senior Government Inspectors of Railways should be placed under the
 Administrative control of some authority of the Government of India other than the Railway Board."  The Railway
 Inspectorate was then separated from the control of Railway Board to secure its independence from the authority
 administering the Railways.  After its separation, the Railway Inspectorate was placed under the administrative control
 of the then Department of Communications with effect from 12
th May 1941.  On 9 th July 1942, this Department of
 Communication was bifurcated into two Departments viz (i) Post & Air Department and (ii) War Transport
 Department.  The Railway Inspectorate was kept under the administrative control of Posts & Air Department and
 continuously thereafter under whichever Ministry that held the portfolio of Civil Aviation.  It was re-designated as the
 Commission of Railway Safety on 1.11.1961.  It came under the administrative control of the Ministry of Tourism and
 Civil Aviation in May 1967 subsequently re-designated as the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
 
ORGANISATIONAL SET UP & JURISDICTION

APPOINTMENT TO THE CADRE OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
7.         The Deputy Commissioners of Railway Safety are appointed on deputation/absorption from the applicants drawn
 from Signaling, Electrical, Mechanical, Operating and Civil Engineering Departments of Indian Railways.  The period
 of deputation as per extant recruitment rules is five years.  During the period of deputation the officers are entitled to
 deputation allowance as per the instructions of Ministry of Finance.  However, in their case the restriction that pay plus
 deputation allowance shall not exceed the maximum of scale has been relaxed.  The officers are governed by Railway
 TA rules and are eligible for free passes and Privilege Ticket Orders (PTOs) on the same lines as other Railway
 Officers of corresponding status. 
 
8.         The Commissioners of Railway Safety are selected by the Union Public Service Commission on absorption basis
 from amongst the applicants who are senior officers drawn from Civil Engineering Department of the Indian Railways
 and once confirmed cannot return back to railway service, but are governed by Railway TA rules and are eligible for
 free passes and PTOs on the same lines as other Railway Officers of corresponding status. 
 
9.         The Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety is selected by the Union Public Service Commission from amongst
 the existing Commissioners who have put in a minimum of three years of service in the grade.
 
10.       The supporting staff of the Commission is appointed in the Commission itself through Employment Exchange
 and Staff Selection Commission etc. and are governed by civil rules for TA etc. and are not entitled for free passes and
 PTOs.
FUNCTIONS
11.       The responsibility for safety in the working and operation of Railway rests solely with Railway Board and the
 Zonal Railway authorities.  The main task of the Commission of Railway Safety is to direct, advise and caution the
