 Railway executives with a view to ensure that all reasonable precautions are taken in regard to soundness of rail
 construction and safety of train operation.  The Railway Board refers to the Commission matters relating to
 modification or enhancement of standards in respect of operation of trains, track, locomotive, rolling stock and revision
 of rules embodied in the General Rules, Rules for the opening of New Lines, Manuals, IRCA Regulations, Schedules of
 Dimensions and other publications.  Suggestions made by the Commission of Railway Safety are duly considered by
 the Railway Board before necessary revisions are notified.
 
12.       The duties and functions of the Commissioners are laid down in the Railways Act, 1989 and rules framed
 thereunder, and executive instructions issued from time to time.  These are briefly:
·
              to conduct statutory inquires into serious railway accidents and suggest safeguards.
·              to inspect new railway lines with a view to determining whether they are fit to be opened for the
 public carriage of passenger, and to sanction their opening after inspection on behalf of the Central
 Government.
·              to sanction the execution of all new works and installations on the running track affecting the
 safety of the traveling public such as rebuilding of bridges, remodeling of station yards, line
 capacity works, resignalling works, etc.
·              to make periodical inspections of railways and report to the Central Government on any condition
 which may endanger the safety of the traveling public and make recommendations.
·              to examine the technical aspects of new rolling stock and advise on their sanctions and increase in
 speeds.
·              to authorize the carriage of oversized consignments stipulating the conditions for their movements.
·              to recommend and sanction infringements to the schedule of dimensions prescribed by the
 Government of India.
·              to grant dispensation from general rules under approved special instructions subject to stipulated
 safeguards.
·              to oversee the accident prevention efficacy of the zonal railway administrations by reviewing the
 reports of departmental enquiries into less serious accidents.
 
13.       Field duties of the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety consist of inspections of sections of Railways, visits
 to the Railway Headquarters and Divisional Offices, Railway installations and Circle Offices.  If considered necessary
 by him, he may himself hold inquiries into important accidents.   The Chief Commissioner submits an annual report on
 the working of the Commission which is laid on the table of both the Houses of Parliament.
 
14.       The Committee took the oral evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation and Chief Commissioner of
 Railway Safety at its meeting held on the 20
th May 2003 to get an indepth insight into the functions of the Commission
 and to discuss the essential aspects of the working of the Commission.  On the basis of the information furnished by the
 Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation and Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety, the Committee also elicited the views
 of the Chairman, Railway Board on the subject at its meeting held on the 14th July 2003.  In order to get wider views on
 the subject, the Committee, at its meeting held on the 4 th September 2003, decided to invite the views of individuals
 and institutions interested in the subject through advertisement in all major national dailies and vernacular newspapers
 all over the country.  The advertisement evoked tremendous public response and the Committee received memoranda
 on various aspects of the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety from a lot of people including many retired
 Commissioners/Chief Commissioners of Railway Safety.
 
15.       The issues pointed out by the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Commission of Railway Safety, the response of
 the Ministry of Railways thereon and the observations/recommendations of the Committee have been discussed in the
 succeeding paragraphs.
 
ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
16.       The Committee observed that the Commission of Railway Safety had been working under the administrative
 control of Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The Committee enquired from the Commission of Railway Safety as to whether

 there were any difficulties in the existing arrangement.  The Committee also sought suggestion of Chief Commissioner

 Accidents, and certain other duties connected with safety of railway operation as required under the Railways Act

 cases and hence it will not be in the interest of the impartial working of the Commission to keep it attached with the

 they are able to discharge their duties impartially.  In response to the query as to whether the Commission of Railway
 Safety should remain with the Ministry of Civil Aviation or should it be attached to any other organization, other than
 Ministry of Railways, Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety stated that for the past more than 50 years, the
 Commission of Railway Safety has been attached with that Ministry which deals with Civil Aviation.  The Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety stated that the Commission could as well be attached, with any other Ministry.  The

·        Railway Accidents Enquiry Committee 1968 (Wanchoo Committee)
·        Railway Accidents Enquiry Committee 1978 (Sikri Committee)
 
17.       All these Committees went into great depth and after considering their recommendations, the Government every
 time decided that the Commission of Railway Safety should not be with the Ministry of Railways but remain outside it
 and decided to keep the Commission of Railway Safety under the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The Appointments
 Committee of the Cabinet re-considered this issue in 1998 and decided to maintain status quo i.e. to keep Commission
 of Railway Safety under administrative control of Ministry of Civil Aviation.
 
18.       As regard the suggestion to make the working of the Commission more effective, the Chief Commissioner of
 Railway Safety was of the view that the Commission should enjoy the autonomy as available with the Election
 Commission, Central Vigilance Commission, Union Public Service Commission or Comptroller and Auditor General. 
 In that event the Commissioners of Railway Safety will be able to assert themselves in ensuring that their
 recommendations and observations are enforceable and do not remain merely recommendatory.  The Commission
 needs to be given active support and assistance in the pursuit of its objectives.  Also the budget provisions for the
 Commission of Railway Safety should be delinked from the budget of Ministry of Civil Aviation and it should be on
 the lines of other autonomous bodies like Election Commission, Union Public Service Commission, Central Vigilance
 Commission, or Comptroller and Auditor General.
           
19.       During the evidence of the representatives of Ministry of Railways, the Committee sought the opinion of the
 Chairman, Railway Board as to whether the Commission of Railway Safety should be an independent body like the
 Election Commission of India.  The Chairman, Railway Board opined as under:-
 
"Sir, I personally feel that we should maintain the creditability of the Deputy Chief Commissioners of Railway

 definitely enhance the confidence and credibility of the Commission.  There is no doubt about it."
           
20.       To a further query on the subject, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Railways vide their O.M. No.

 sent on deputation, rather they should go on absorption terms to the Commission to avoid unfavourable allegations

21.       The Committee is of the opinion that the mandate of Ministry of Civil Aviation is altogether different from the
 mandate of the Commission of Railway Safety.  Therefore, the Ministry of Civil Aviation is not in a position to address
 the administrative problems of the Commission of Railway Safety adequately.  In order to ensure the impartial working
 of the Commission of Railway Safety, it is essential that the Commission works outside the control of both the
 Ministries of Railways and Civil Aviation.  In order to make the functioning of the Commission more effective, it is
 strongly felt that the Commission should be provided greater powers and independence.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Commission of Railway Safety should be made an autonomous statutory body like Election
 Commission and Union Public Service Commission.  The Committee also agrees with the contention of the Ministry of
 Railways that officers below the rank of Commissioner of Railway Safety should also not be sent on deputation, rather
 they should go on absorption terms to the Commission.   The Committee is of the firm view that this would make the
 Commission independent, powerful and vigilant to the fullest extent.   This would definitely go a long way in dispelling
 the general impression that the Ministry of Railways unduly influences the Commission in its functioning as it is rightly
 said that justice should not only be done but it should also appear to have been done.
EFFECTIVENESS OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
22.       The Committee then enquired about the nature of the recommendations made by the Commission and whether
 the recommendations of the Commission were recommendatory or mandatory.  The Committee also enquired so to
 whether the Ministry of Railways had been accepting the advice given by the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety,
 particularly in matters relating to Railway Safety.  In response, the Committee was informed by the Commission of
 Railway Safety that their recommendations were recommendatory and not mandatory.  It was also informed that the
 recommendations were mostly honoured or accepted by the Ministry of Railways.  However, the Commission could not
 force the Railway Administration to accept the recommendations because they were only a recommendatory body.  
 The responsibility for acceptance and implementation of the measures recommended by the Commission rests solely
 with the Railway Board and the Zonal Railway Administrations.  The Commission, however, does not have the
 wherewithal to monitor the status of implementation of these measures by the Railways. 
23.       The Committee was further informed that the question regarding the nature of the recommendations of the
 Commission was also raised by the Appointment Committee of Cabinet (ACC) in 1998 when they asked the Ministry
 of Railways to categorically state whether the recommendations of the Commission should be mandatory or not.  In
 response, Appointment Committee of Cabinet was assured by the Ministry of Railways that  "Every recommendation of
 the Commission is scrutinized at various levels before taking a final decision.  In case, Railways have any reservation
 regarding a particular item, the same is discussed with the Commission by the Railway Board before a final decision is
 taken.  In case of non-acceptance of any of the recommendations, personal approval of the concerned Board Member is
 taken.  This ensures that before turning down any recommendation, it is thoroughly scrutinized from all aspects."  
 
24.       It was pointed out by the Commission that inspite of the above commitment, with the passage of time, the
 Ministry of Railways changed their stand from discussing the issues with the Commission before taking final decision
 on a particular recommendation of the Commission, to discussions only in serious cases of dispute, to no discussions on
 any serious issue raised by the Commission. Ministry of Railways had also communicated to the Commission of
 Railway Safety that if any recommendation of the Commission is not accepted by the Railway Board, the Commission
 may reflect such issues in their Annual Report.
 
25.       The Commission further pointed out that the commitment made by the Ministry of Railways to the Appointment
 Committee of Cabinet was not being honoured.   Many times their recommendations were neither accepted nor any
 reason was given for the non-acceptance.  The Ministry of Railways had not even been discussing with the Commission
 before rejecting their recommendations.  It was further informed that the recommendations once accepted by the
 Ministry of Railways were either diluted or revoked at a later stage unilaterally by the Ministry of Railways without
 prior consultation and approval of the Commission or without even informing the Commission.  In some cases the
 Commission is kept in the dark where the Railway Board withdraws or overrules some conditions insisted by the
 Commission.
 
26.       The Committee brought the observations made by the Commission of Railway Safety to the notice of Ministry
 of Railways and sought their comments thereon.  In response, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Railways

27.       The Committee is of the view that although the recommendations of the Commission of Railway Safety are not
 mandatory for the Ministry of Railways yet the situation brought out by the Commission of Railway Safety is highly
 unsatisfactory.  The Committee is of the view that the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway Safety
 should receive utmost importance from the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee takes exception to the fact that, on
 certain occasions, the Ministry of Railways neither consults the Commission of Railway Safety before rejecting a
 recommendation nor furnishes reasons for not accepting the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway
 Safety.  The Committee strongly feels that the Commission of Railway Safety is a watch dog on behalf of the public at

29.       The Committee brought the above position to the notice of Ministry of Railways and sought comments thereon. 
 In response, the Ministry of Railways replied that before any new train is introduced, certification of available
 maintenance infrastructure at either end is given by two SAG (Joint Secretaries) Officers, in-charge of operation and
 maintenance, after consulting all concerned agencies.  A checklist of items has been circulated to all concerned by the
 Railway Board.  The recommendation of the Railway Safety Review Committee 1998 regarding certification by the
 Commissioner of Railway Safety in cases of introduction of new trains was not found feasible for acceptance as the
 Railway Board is the final safety controlling authority and necessary certificate from respective Departments are

32.       The Committee observes that a large number of new passenger trains are introduced every year to meet the
 demand of the traveling public.  While it does fulfil the requirements of the public, it has to be examined as to whether
 such an action is in the interest of safety and convenience of the traveling public.  The present system in the country is
 already overstressed and it is important to ensure that all infrastructure facilities cater to the safe running of additional
 trains with due safety margins.  It is essential that such facilities are in position before adding any burden of additional
 trains.  The introduction of additional trains involves the safety of the passengers.   The Committee is not convinced
 with the reply furnished by the Ministry of Railways with regard to not seeking the concurrence of Commission of
 Railway Safety before introduction of a new passenger train.  The Committee gives due weightage to the reply of the
 Ministry of Railways that before any new train is introduced, certification of available maintenance infrastructure at
 either end is given by two SAG (Joint Secretaries) Officers, in-charge of operation and maintenance, after consulting all
 concerned agencies.  Ministry of Railway have also pointed out that concurrence of every new train does not fall under

 Commission is to direct, advise and caution the railway executives through its regulation/inspectional/audit and
 investigatory/advisory functions and thereby assist them in ensuring that all stipulated measures are taken in regard to
 the soundness of rail construction and safety in train operation.   The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the
 sanction of Commission of Railway Safety must be necessary for Ministry of Railways before introducing any new
 passenger train.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that it should be made mandatory for Ministry of Railways to
 seek the concurrence of Commission of Railway Safety before introduction of any new passenger train, so as to ensure
 that the safety of the passengers is not compromised by amending the existing statutory provisions in this regard.

 the rank of a Principal Head of Department to accompany the Commissioner of Railway Safety on his inspection, the
 Ministry of Railways replied that it has been decided to modify the rules as under:-
"Chief Administrative Officer (Construction) (Higher Administrative Grade/Principal Head of the Department)
 should normally accompany the Commissioner of Railway Safety in unavoidable circumstances when the
 General Manager is not in a position to do so.  However, due to any unavoidable or compelling reason, if the
 Chief Administrative Officer (Construction) is himself unable to accompany the Commissioner of Railway
 Safety, an officer not below the level of Senior Administrative Grade should accompany Commissioner of
 Railway Safety".
 
37.       The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Railways has, on the insistence of Commission of Railway
 Safety, decided to make necessary amendments in the present 'Rules of 2000' to include the 'one month notice' to the
 Commissioner of Railway Safety before any line is intended to be opened.  The Committee recommends that the
 necessary amendment should be carried out at the earliest.  The Committee further notes that the Ministry of Railways
 have decided to modify the extant rules so that an officer of the level of Senior Administrative Grade should
 accompany the Commissioner of Railway Safety only in case the General Manager or the Principal Head of the
 Department are not able to accompany him due to unavoidable circumstances.  However, the Committee would like to
 advise that an officer of the level of Senior Administrative Grade accompanying the Commissioner of Railway Safety
 on his inspection should remain an exception, as envisaged under the said provisions, than becoming the rule.
 
PUBLICATION OF REPORTS ON RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
38.       The Committee pointed out to the Commission of Railway Safety that after completion of the report on accidents
 by Commission of Railway Safety, it is submitted to the Ministry of Railways.  However such reports are not
 published.  The Committee enquired from the Commission of Railway Safety as to why reports on accidents by
 Commission of Railway Safety are kept confidential and not made public at the earliest.  The Committee also sought to
 know whether there were any hindrances in the publication of the reports.
           
39.       In response, the Committee was informed by the Commission of Railway Safety that as soon as their
 Preliminary Report on an inquiry into an accident is submitted, a press note is issued by them in which the cause of the
 accident as found by the Commission of Railway Safety, is advised.  For this purpose, the cause is categorized in one or
 more of the following types:
i)
                    Sabotage
ii)                   Failure of Railway Staff

iii)                 Failure of other than Railway staff
iv)                 Failure of Railway equipment
v)                  Sudden convulsion of nature
 
40.       However press notes are issued only in the case of Commission of Railway Safety inquiries into accidents where
 there is death of a passenger or where sabotage is the cause of the accident.  Thus it may be appreciated that the cause
 of the accident is made known at the earliest opportunity through a press release.
 
41.       Only selected final reports of the Commission of Railway Safety inquires are recommended for publication if
 they fulfill any one of the following criteria:
a)
                        The accident has resulted in large scale deaths or injuries involving wide media attention and public
 criticism.
b)                        A number of important technical issues has been dealt, needing action of Railway Administration.
c)                        The standard of investigation (Technical or otherwise) was of a high order.
 
42.       The Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety and Railway Board together decide upon the publication of the
 report.  However no report can be published till such time, all prosecutions, if launched in a court of Law against
 Railway Staff held responsible in the report have been concluded, including the disposal of appeal as the case may be. 
 Thus, the accident reports are kept confidential till such time all prosecutions connected with the accident cases come to
 an end.
           
43.       It was pointed out by the Commission of Railway Safety that the Railway Safety Review Committee 1998 had
 recommended that the reports of Commission of Railway Safety can be published immediately after their submission,
 provided, the following are ensured through introduction of provisions in the relevant Act and Rules:-
A clause should be included in the relevant laws that no railway servant can be prosecuted without the sanction
 of the authority competent to appoint him or a higher authority.   Further, it should be stipulated that the
 Commissioner of Railway Safety or any other investigating authority who has powers of a civil court for
 conduct of inquiries cannot be called as witness or for examination by any court in cases which arise from
 investigations done by them.  Finally, the report and the findings of the Commission of Railway Safety should
 not be allowed to be used as an evidence.
 
44.       The Commission of Railway Safety further emphasized that the Commissioner of Railway Safety, while
 conducting accident inquiries has been given powers of civil judge as per Railway Act.  However these powers are not
 adequate.  Therefore, as per Railway Safety Review Committee recommendations, the immunity available to judges
 need to be extended to Commissioner of Railway Safety.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation has agreed with these
 recommendations and has taken up the matter with the Ministry of Railways who deal with the Railways Act, to make
 necessary amendments to provide legal protection to the Commissioner of Railway Safety. 
           
45.       The point relating to the inadequacy of the powers of the Commissioner of Railway Safety was also emphasized
 by many retired Chief Commissioners of Railway Safety.  It was brought out that the Commission of Railway Safety
 cannot prevent interference by the police in the smooth conducting of the enquiry.  Very often the police try to seize
 documents and other evidence relating to the accident, on the grounds that an act of criminal negligence had been
 committed and they had registered a criminal case.  Such action of the police affects the Commissioner of Railway
 Safety's enquiry.  Very often the Commissioner of Railway Safety is reduced to having to plead with higher officials in
 the police in order to progress with the enquiry. 
           
46.       The Committee was further informed that the Commission of Railway Safety is forced to conduct his accident
 enquiries in camera and not hold them as public enquiries.  This is because the proceedings do not enjoy the privileges
 of a judicial enquiry, and are not protected by provisions such as contempt action.  This leaves ground for interested
 parties and the media to provide false or prejudiced reports about the enquiry. 
 
47.       The comments of the Ministry of Railways were sought in the matter.  The Ministry of Railways informed the
 Committee that Section 186 of the Railways Act, 1989 provides that no suit, prosecution and other legal proceedings
 shall lie against the Central Government, any railway administration, a railway servant or any other person for anything

 which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Act or any rules or orders made there under. 
 Section 8 of the Railways Act, 1989 further provides that the Commissioner of Railway Safety shall be deemed to be a
 public servant within the meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.  From the perusal of the said provisions it
 appears that the Commissioner of Railway Safety is fully protected from being prosecuted or being used for anything
 which he has done in good faith or intended to do in pursuance of the Railways Act or any rules/orders made
 thereunder.
           
48.       As far as the question of the Commissioner of Railway Safety or any investigating authority should not be called
 as witness or for examination by any court, is concerned, this power of the court flows from the Code of Criminal
 Procedure and Code of Civil Procedure.  The Court is free to summon any person to give evidence in any case pending
 before it.
 
49.       Article 361 of the Constitution of India provides that the President or Governor of a State shall not be
 answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers/duties of his officers or for any act done or
 purposed to be done by him in the exercise and performance of those powers and duties.
           
50.       Under Section 121 of the Indian Evidence Act, it has been provided that no judge or magistrate shall be
 compelled to answer questions as to (a) his conduct in court as such judge or magistrate; or (b) anything which came to
 his knowledge in court as such judge or magistrate except upon an order of the court to which he is subordinate.
           
51.       In accordance with the provisions of the Evidence Act, even the judge or magistrate is not exempted from being
 called as a witness in a court of law.  Section 133 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for exempting of certain
 persons from personal appearance in a court of law.  There is a provision that if any witness is not able to come to
 court, his statement can be recorded in the commission.  The fact remains that the judge of a civil court can also be
 called as a witness to testify any fact.  Only exception to this rule are the provisions of Article 361 of the Constitution. 
 The Commissioner of Railway Safety does not fit into this exception.  He is deemed to be a public servant within the
 meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.  He is only entitled to the privileges which are available to a public
 servant under section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.
 
52.       The Committee is constrained to note that the inquiry reports of the Commission of Railway Safety on accidents
 are either not published or published too late and the people at large do not come to know of the reasons for
 concurrence of a particular accident.  The Committee is of the view that the public needs to know the reasons for the
 railway accidents and it will serve the larger interest of the public if the accident reports are published at the earliest. 
 The Committee also notes the impediments faced by the Commission of Railway Safety in undertaking the enquiries. 
 The Committee feels that it is essential to provide legal protection to Commission of Railway Safety.  The Committee
 is in agreement with the recommendations made by Railway Safety Review Committee 1998, quoted at para 43 above. 
 The Committee recommends that these recommendations should be accepted and the relevant acts and rules should be
 amended at the earliest.  The Committee also recommends that when the Commission of Railway Safety proposes to
 take up an inquiry, inquiries initiated by police or magistrate should be stopped and the civil and police authorities
 should co-operate in the Commission's inquiry.  The Committee feels that the implementations of the steps suggested
 by the Committee will enable the Commissioners of Railway Safety in undertaking their inquiries without any
 hindrances.  Thereby, the inquiry reports of the Commissioners on accidents could also be published as soon as the
 inquiry is over and the public at large would not be deprived of their vital right to information.

 the Commission do not get an equal opportunity to get exposed to the technologies which were developing abroad.  The
 Committee was also informed that Railway Board has given its officers the facility to become members of five
 professional institutions including two foreign institutions.  Again, no such facilities were available to the officers of
 Commission of Railway Safety.  The Committee was also informed that the requests of the Commission to the Railway

 matter.  In reply, the Committee was informed by the Railway Board that the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety
 had requested Ministry of Railways for training of his personnel in technology familiarization programmes abroad,
 alongwith other Indian Railway officers at Railways' cost.  The issue was examined and it was felt that dependence of
 the Commission on the Ministry of Railways for financial assistance will impair the independent identity of the
 Commission, and to maintain it, it is desirable that the Commission should be financially independent of Railways.  It

 familiarization programmes abroad on Railway expenses.

ANNOUNCEMENT OF PRIMA-FACIE CAUSE OF ACCIDENTS BY RAILWAY ADMINISTRATION
70.       The Committee observes that whenever a train accident occurs, the railway administration is quick to announce
 the prima-facie cause of the accident, even when the officials concerned are aware of the enormity of the accident and
 that, as provided in the Railway Act, Commissioner of Railway Safety would hold an enquiry to determine the exact
 cause of the accident.  However, if at a later date, the findings of the Commissioner of Railway Safety happen to
 coincide with the version earlier advanced by the railway officials, the Commission of Railway Safety is accused of a
 bias in favour of the Railways. Such actions affect the credibility of Commissioner of Railway Safety.
 
71.       The Committee is of the opinion that the unwritten convention that no one would give the cause of an accident,
 when an enquiry is pending, needs to be followed by the Railway administration.  The Committee recommends that the
 Railway administration should refrain from speculating and giving the prime-facie cause of an accident, which is
 required to be statutorily enquired by the Commissioner of Railway Safety.  This will ensure that the credibility of the
 Commission of Railway Safety is maintained and the Commissioners are not suspected of prejudice or bias in
 conducting their enquiries.
 
CONCLUSION
72.       The Committee is of the opinion that the Commission of Railway Safety is an important organisation of the
 Government and, in the prevailing circumstances, the Commission's hands need strengthening in all possible ways. The
 Committee recommends that the Government should bring a comprehensive legislation incorporating the suggestion
 made by the Committee in this Report so that the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety could improve in
 the interest of the public travelling by Indian Railways.

The Committee is of the opinion that the mandate of Ministry of Civil Aviation is altogether different from the mandate
 of the Commission of Railway Safety.  Therefore, the Ministry of Civil Aviation is not in a position to address the
 administrative problems of the Commission of Railway Safety adequately.  In order to ensure the impartial working of
 the Commission of Railway Safety, it is essential that the Commission works outside the control of both the Ministries
 of Railways and Civil Aviation.  In order to make the functioning of the Commission more effective, it is strongly felt
 that the Commission should be provided greater powers and independence.  The Committee, therefore, recommends
 that the Commission of Railway Safety should be made an autonomous statutory body like Election Commission and
 Union Public Service Commission.  The Committee also agrees with the contention of the Ministry of Railways that
 officers below the rank of Commissioner of Railway Safety should also not be sent on deputation, rather they should go
 on absorption terms to the Commission.   The Committee is of the firm view that this would make the Commission
 independent, powerful and vigilant to the fullest extent.   This would definitely go a long way in dispelling the general
 impression that the Ministry of Railways unduly influences the Commission in its functioning as it is rightly said that
 justice should not only be done but it should also appear to have been done.

EFFECTIVENESS OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
 
The Committee is of the view that although the recommendations of the Commission of Railway Safety are not
 mandatory for the Ministry of Railways yet the situation brought out by the Commission of Railway Safety is highly
 unsatisfactory.  The Committee is of the view that the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway Safety
 should receive utmost importance from the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee takes exception to the fact that, on
 certain occasions, the Ministry of Railways neither consults the Commission of Railway Safety before rejecting a
 recommendation nor furnishes reasons for not accepting the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway
 Safety.  The Committee strongly feels that the Commission of Railway Safety is a watch dog on behalf of the public at
 large.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Railways, should honour the commitment made by
 them to the Appointment Committee of Cabinet regarding consulting the Commission before rejecting a
 recommendation.   The Committee further recommends that it should be made mandatory for the Railway
 Administration not to reject or overrule any recommendations made by the Commissioners without a meeting between
 the Chairman, Railway Board and the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety, where the matters can be discussed
 threadbare and agreements reached.  The Committee further recommends that while expressing their inability to accept
 the recommendations, the Railway Board should give detailed reasons for not accepting the recommendations.  The
 Committee also recommends that any decision taken by the Railway Board in consultation with the Commission of
 Railway Safety must not be revoked unilaterally by the Railway Board or Zonal Railway, without prior consultation
 and approval of the Commission.
(Para 27)
 
The Committee observes that a large number of new passenger trains are introduced every year to meet the demand of
 the traveling public.  While it does fulfil the requirements of the public, it has to be examined as to whether such an
 action is in the interest of safety and convenience of the traveling public.  The present system in the country is already
 overstressed and it is important to ensure that all infrastructure facilities cater to the safe running of additional trains
 with due safety margins.  It is essential that such facilities are in position before adding any burden of additional trains. 
 The introduction of additional trains involves the safety of the passengers.   The Committee is not convinced with the
 reply furnished by the Ministry of Railways with regard to not seeking the concurrence of Commission of Railway
 Safety before introduction of a new passenger train.  The Committee gives due weightage to the reply of the Ministry of
 Railways that before any new train is introduced, certification of available maintenance infrastructure at either end is
 given by two SAG (Joint Secretaries) Officers, in-charge of operation and maintenance, after consulting all concerned
 agencies.  Ministry of Railway have also pointed out that concurrence of every new train does not fall under the legal
 duties of Commission of Railway Safety, as enumerated in the Railway Act, 1989.  The main task of the Commission is
 to direct, advise and caution the railway executives through its regulation/inspectional/audit and investigatory/advisory
 functions and thereby assist them in ensuring that all stipulated measures are taken in regard to the soundness of rail
 construction and safety in train operation.   The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the sanction of Commission of
 Railway Safety must be necessary for Ministry of Railways before introducing any new passenger train.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that it should be made mandatory for Ministry of Railways to seek the concurrence

83rd report of Committee on Transport,Tourism and Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/83rdreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:04:05]
 of Commission of Railway Safety before introduction of any new passenger train, so as to ensure that the safety of the
 passengers is not compromised by amending the existing statutory provisions in this regard.
(Para 32)
REVISION OF 'RULES FOR OPENING, 1933'
 
The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Railways has, on the insistence of Commission of Railway Safety,
 decided to make necessary amendments in the present 'Rules of 2000' to include the 'one month notice' to the
 Commissioner of Railway Safety before any line is intended to be opened.  The Committee recommends that the
 necessary amendment should be carried out at the earliest.  The Committee further notes that the Ministry of Railways
 have decided to modify the extant rules so that an officer of the level of Senior Administrative Grade should
 accompany the Commissioner of Railway Safety only in case the General Manager or the Principal Head of the
 Department are not able to accompany him due to unavoidable circumstances.  However, the Committee would like to
 advise that an officer of the level of Senior Administrative Grade accompanying the Commissioner of Railway Safety
 on his inspection should remain an exception, as envisaged under the said provisions, than becoming the rule.
(Para 37)
 
PUBLICATION OF REPORTS ON RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
 
The Committee is constrained to note that the inquiry reports of the Commission of Railway Safety on accidents are
 either not published or published too late and the people at large do not come to know of the reasons for concurrence of
 a particular accident.  The Committee is of the view that the public needs to know the reasons for the railway accidents
 and it will serve the larger interest of the public if the accident reports are published at the earliest.  The Committee also
 notes the impediments faced by the Commission of Railway Safety in undertaking the enquiries.  The Committee feels
 that it is essential to provide legal protection to Commission of Railway Safety.  The Committee is in agreement with
 the recommendations made by Railway Safety Review Committee 1998, quoted at para 43 above.  The Committee
 recommends that these recommendations should be accepted and the relevant acts and rules should be amended at the
 earliest.  The Committee also recommends that when the Commission of Railway Safety proposes to take up an
 inquiry, inquiries initiated by police or magistrate should be stopped and the civil and police authorities should co-
operate in the Commission's inquiry.  The Committee feels that the implementations of the steps suggested by the
 Committee will enable the Commissioners of Railway Safety in undertaking their inquiries without any hindrances. 
 Thereby, the inquiry reports of the Commissioners on accidents could also be published as soon as the inquiry is over
 and the public at large would not be deprived of their vital right to information. 
(Para 52)
 
 
UPGRADATION OF STATUS OF OFFICERS OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
 
The Committee is constrained to note that vacancies continue to exist in the Commission of Railway Safety for fairly
 long periods because of non-availability of eligible officers from the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee
 recommends that any vacancy arising in the Commission of Railway Safety should be filled up at the earliest so that the
 functioning of the Commission does not suffer.  The Committee is also constrained to note that the recommendations
 made by Railway Safety Review Committee 1998 are yet to be implemented by the Government.  The Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety, being the Principal Technical Advisor to the Government of India on matters
 concerning rail safety, is the highest technical official in the Ministry of Civil Aviation for dealing with railway safety. 
 The Committee is of the view that upgradation of the post of Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety to the level of
 Secretary to the Government of India is absolutely essential so that he can effectively and forcefully interact with the
 nine Secretary level officers of Railway Board.  Lack of such a status to the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety
 works as a serious deterrent to him in discharging his duties effectively in a hierarchy conscious bureaucracy.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the status of Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety should be equal to that of
 the Chairman of Railway Board in rank and pay.  Likewise the status of Commissioner of Railway Safety should be
 equal to that of General Manager of a Zonal Railway in rank as well as pay.  The posts of Deputy Commissioners of
 Railway Safety should be manned by Senior Administration Grade Officers.   The Commissioners of Railway Safety
 should also be provided with the assistance of Deputy Commissioners. The Committee further recommends that, as
 recommended by the Fifth Central Pay Commission, the tenure of the Chief Commissioner should be five years, taking

83rd report of Committee on Transport,Tourism and Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/83rdreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:04:05]
 him beyond normal retirement age and upto 62 years.  The Committee is of the firm view that these measures would
 bring to an end the current scenario of shortage of volunteers opting to join the Commission of Railway Safety.   Also
 these measures will significantly enhance the status of the Commission, make it more dynamic and enable it to
 discharge its functions more effectively and its views heard and acted upon, with due importance by Railway
 Administration.
(Para 60)
 
EXPOSURE TO TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCEMENTS
 
The Committee feels that there is a genuine need of the officers of Commission of Railway Safety to get exposed to the
 latest technological advancements taking place in the railway sector in India and abroad.  Otherwise there is a real
 danger that the technical knowledge of the officers of the Commission will get obsolete.  The Committee recommends
 that the officers of the Commission should be exposed to latest technologies through trainings in the country and
 abroad, so that they are in a position to perform their role effectively.  The officers of the Commission should also be
 given full facilities to become members of professional institutions, at par with the facilities extended by the railway
 administration to railway officers.  This will help in keeping the officers of the Commission updated in their technical
 knowledge.  However, for this purpose, the Commission should not depend upon the financial assistance of the
 Ministry of Railways.  The Committee recommends that the Government should ensure that the budget of the
 Commission of Railway Safety is suitably increased so that these requirements could be taken care of by the
 Commission itself.
(Para 63)
 
SUPPLY OF RAILWAY CIRCULARS ETC. TO COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
 
The Committee is of the view that unless the Commission of Railway Safety is kept aware of the latest instructions with
 respect to railway safety issued by the Railway Board or Zonal Railways, it cannot discharge its duties effectively. 
 Ministry of Railways have admitted that copies of all important policy orders are endorsed to the Chief Commissioner
 of Railway Safety.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Railways should ensure that Commission of
 Railway Safety is on the permanent mailing list of Railway Board and Zonal Railways for all policy Circulars having
 bearing on safety and all Circulars/Orders affecting safety.  The Committee further recommends that the Commission
 of Railway Safety should be supplied with the proceeding of the Technical Committees of Railway Board so that the
 Commission remains informed of the safety problems encountered in the working of the railways and the measures
 taken to solve these problems.
(Para 67)
 
LACK OF OFFICE INFRASTRUCTURE
 
The Committee notes with concern the constraints faced by the officers of the Commission of Railway Safety in
 performing their duties due to lack of budgetary allocations and proper infrastructure and office machinery.  The
 Committee feels that the Commission of Railway Safety need adequate budgetary support from the Government so that
 it does not have to look upon the Ministry of Railways for being able to effectively discharge its duties.  The
 Committee recommends that the budget allocation of Commission of Railway Safety should be substantially increased
 so that the Commission could take care of its essential requirements such as funds for foreign training, air travel within
 India, nominations to various training courses, membership to professional institutions etc. 
(Para 69)
 
 
ANNOUNCEMENT OF PRIMA-FACIE CAUSE OF ACCIDENTS BY RAILWAY ADMINISTRATION
 
The Committee is of the opinion that the unwritten convention that no one would give the cause of an accident, when an
 enquiry is pending, needs to be followed by the Railway administration.  The Committee recommends that the Railway
 administration should refrain from speculating and giving the prime-facie cause of an accident, which is required to be
 statutorily enquired by the Commissioner of Railway Safety.  This will ensure that the credibility of the Commission of
 Railway Safety is maintained and the Commissioners are not suspected of prejudice or bias in conducting their

file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/83rdreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:04:05]
 enquiries.
(Para 71)
 
CONCLUSION
 
The Committee is of the opinion that the Commission of Railway Safety is an important organisation of the Government
 and, in the prevailing circumstances, the Commission's hands need strengthening in all possible ways. The Committee
 recommends that the Government should bring a comprehensive legislation incorporating the suggestion made by the
 Committee in this Report so that the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety could improve in the interest of
 the public travelling by Indian Railways.
(Para 72)

R E P O R T
In June 2001, the erstwhile Ministry of Surface Transport was bifurcated into two Ministries viz. Ministry of

 Road Transport & Highways and Ministry of Shipping.  These two Ministries have been reconstituted into one Ministry,
 viz. Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport and Highways in September 2004 with two Departments i.e. Department of
 Road Transport and Highways and Department of Shipping.
 2.         The Department of Road Transport and Highways is responsible for the formulation and implementation of
 policies relating to Road Transport and National Highways, Central Sector Road Schemes, administration of Central
 Road Fund and sponsoring of research pertaining to road works.  The two major divisions of the Department are the
 Transport Division and the Road Division.
 
3.         The Road Transport Division of the Department is concerned with the formulation of broad policies related to
 road transport besides, making arrangements for the movement of vehicular traffic with the neighboring countries. 
 
4.         The Road Division is concerned mainly with matters relating to:-
(i)                    Advising Government on all general policy matters relating to Highways
(ii)                  Development and maintenance of roads declared as National Highways
(iii)                 Development and maintenance of roads other than National Highways in   Union Territories.
(iv)                Administration of Central Road Fund (CRF) pertaining to state roads other than rural roads.
(v)                  Evaluation and specification of Standards for roads and bridges
(vi)        Research on roads. 
 5.         The following autonomous bodies function under the administrative control of the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways:-
(a)                National Highways Authority of India
(b)               National Institute of Training of Highway Engineers (NITHE).

10.       The Committee had in its 82 nd Report on Demands for Grants 2004-05 of the Ministry of Road Transport and
 Highways observed that there is a huge resource gap of around Rs.1,06,000 crore in the road sector during the Tenth
 Plan and had, therefore, recommended that the budgetary allocations of the Ministry should be substantially increased at
 RE stage.  Also the allocations of the Ministry should be adequately increased during the remaining years of Tenth Plan
 so as to reduce the resource gap in this sector to some extent.  In their Action Taken Replies furnished to the Committee,
 the Department of Road Transport and Highways replied that the suggestion of the Committee has been noted for
 compliance and Planning Commission shall be approached for allocations during the remaining years of the Tenth Plan. 
 As desired by the Committee, the budget allocation for the road sector has been projected as Rs.13948.32 crore in RE
 2004-05 as against the budget provision of Rs.10770 crore.
 
11.       However, from a perusal of the Demands for Grants 2005-06 of the Department of Road Transport and
 Highways, the Committee observed that the BE 2004-05 of the Department was reduced from Rs.9637 crore to Rs.8566
 crore at RE stage.  The Committee asked the Department of Road Transport and Highways about the reasons that the
 budget provisions of the Department were reduced at RE stage inspite of its increased projection by the Department.
 
12.       In response, the Department of Road Transport and Highways explained to the Committee that the Budget
 Estimate for 2004-2005 for the Department including the provision for Road Transport was Rs.7912 crore as ‘Plan’
 provision and Rs.1725 crore as ‘Non Plan’ provision.  In addition to the ‘Plan’ provision, there was an IEBR component
 of Rs.3300 crore making a total Plan provision of Rs.11,212 crore.  At the RE stage, the plan provisions were brought
 down from Rs.7912 crore to 6766 crore and IEBR of Rs.3300 crore to ‘Nil’ and accordingly indicating total of Rs.6766
 crore.  The Non Plan provision was enhanced from Rs.1725 crore to Rs.1800 crore.  The plan provisions came down on
 account of slow implementation of Externally Aided projects by NHAI and the Department.  The Externally Aided
 component of NHAI came down from Rs.3210 crore to Rs.2000 crore and the provision for the Department for
 Externally Aided Project came down from Rs.113.50 crore to Rs.30 crore.  However, there was an increase of the outlay
 under NH (O) of Rs.147.5 crore which was provided out of the surrenders made on account of the Externally Aided
 Projects (EAP).   The reasons for the reduced demand for the EAP have been explained below.
 
13.       The Ministry had projected a requirement of Rs.13,948.32 crore (only for the ‘Road’ sector) at the RE stage on

16.       There was delay in the finalization of the loans and obtaining approvals for the procurement of the externally
 aided project component of the Corridor Project of NHDP (Phase-II), being financed by the Asian Development Bank
 (ADB).  Therefore, the requirement of fund for the RE 2004-05 was assessed considering that these projects might not

 Quadrilateral (Phase-I) due to various problems like delay in land acquisition, law & order problems, non performance
 by foreign partners (lead partners of the contractors), etc.  Due to this, it was assessed that the projected level of
 expenditure might not be incurred.  Accordingly, the external assistance component was reduced to the level of Rs.2000
 crore at the RE stage.
 
17.       The development of NH-34 in West Bengal  has been taken up from the loan assistance of the ADB.  There was
 delay in award of works to the contractors and consultants.  Therefore, it was assessed that the requirement of funds for
 2004-05 for this project could be only Rs.30 crore, against BE provision of Rs.113.50 crore.  The projected RE included
 this reduced amount.
18.       The Committee observed that the construction of flyover at Murthal in Sonepat on NH-I had been going on since
 2001, but there had been no progress in the work during the last four years.  The Committee enquired from the
 Department of Road Transport and Highways as to when the work of construction of flyover started at Murthal and
 what were the reasons for delay in execution of the projects.
 
19.       In response, the Committee was informed by the Department of Road Transport and Highways that the flyover at
 Murthal (Sonepat) was being constructed under the road project of six laning of km 44.300 to 66.000 of NH-1 in the

st May 2001 for a total contract value of Rs.69.82 crore.  This work was started on 30.08.2001 and was to be
 completed by 30.08.2003.  The work could not be completed in time due to delay in shifting of utilities / cutting of trees
 and extension of time was granted up to 29.04.2004.  The contract agreement between NHAI and M/s Maharia Raj (JV)

20.       The Committee regrets to note that BE Plan Provision of Rs.7912 crore of Department of Road Transport and
 Highways was brought down to Rs.6766 crore on account of slow implementation of Externally Aided Projects by
 NHAI and the Department.  Further, there was delay in finalisation of the loans and obtaining approvals for the
 procurement for the externally aided component of the Corridor Project of NHDP (Phase-II) being financed by the
 Asian Development Bank (ADB).  Also, there was delay in award of works to the contractors and consultants for
 development of NH-34 in West Bengal.  These instances clearly bring out that on the one hand, the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways emphasizes that funds for development and maintenance of National Highways are inadequate
 while, on the other hand, the Department is not able to utilise the higher allocation made to it at BE stage.   The
 Department has failed to make optimal utilization of the funds at its disposal. The reasons for shortfall mentioned are
 delay in land acquisition, poor performance of the contractors, law and order problem etc. are very general in nature and
 are repeated every year. As a result of these, the budgetary allocations of the Department were reduced at RE stage.  The
 Committee is of the view that there is a lack of monitoring system in the Department of Road Transport and Highways. 
 The lack of a proper monitoring system in the Department is exemplified by the delay and non-completion of the
 construction of flyover at Murthal in Haryana and the failure of the Department of Road Transport and Highways in
 verifying the credentials of the contractors who had submitted forged bank guarantees.  The Committee observes that
 the budget allocations of the Department of Road Transport and Highways have been substantially increased during
 2005-06. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should devise
 strategies, whereby they are able to fully utilize the funds at their disposal.  They should also evolve some mechanism to
 identify bottlenecks causing delays and work towards resolving all such hindrances in coordination with all the
 concerned agencies.  This would also help them to avoid time overrun and consequential cost overrun of the projects to
 be executed by them.
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
21.       India has a vast road network of 3.32 million kilometers of which the National Highways and the State Highways
 together account for 1,95,000 km.  As on 31
st March 2004, the length of National Highways network is only 65,569 km
 constituting about 2% of the total road network in the country and carrying about 40% of the total traffic across the
 length and breadth of the country.
 
22.       The Department of Road Transport & Highways is primarily responsible for the construction and maintenance of
 National Highways (NH). All roads, other than National Highway in States, fall within the jurisdiction of respective
 state governments.  The development and maintenance of National Highways are being done on agency basis.  The
 National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), State Public Works Departments (PWDs) and the Border Road
 Organisation (BRO) are the main agencies. Out of the total National Highway length of 65,569 km, about 14,279 km
 have been entrusted to National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) for improvement under National Highway
 Development Project (NHDP) Phase I & II, Port Connectivity Schemes and other schemes.  The balance lengths of
 about 46,586 km and 4,704 km of non-NHDP sections of National Highways are mainly entrusted to State PWDs and
 Border Roads Organisation (BRO) respectively, as agencies of the Ministry. 
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP)
23.       The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways informed the Committee that the Government has embarked upon a
 massive programme to develop highways through the National Highways Development Project (NHDP) in the country. 
 The NHDP is the largest highway project ever undertaken in the country.  This is being implemented by National
 Highways Authority of India.  The NHDP consists of Golden Quadrilateral, North-South and East-West Corridors, Port
 Connectivity and other Projects.  The total length under NHDP is about 14,279 km.  The details relating to NHDP are as
 under:-
(i)                  Golden Quadrilateral (GQ) comprising National Highways connecting four metro cities viz., Delhi,
 Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.  Total length of GQ is 5846 km.  As on 28
th February 2005, four-laning of

24.       The Committee noted that the Golden Quadrilateral project was originally targeted for completion by December
 2003.  As per revised schedule, 90 per cent of the project was proposed to be completed by December 2004.  The
 Committee sought to know as to whether the proposed target was achieved by the end of December 2004 or whether
 there was any shortfall in achieving the targets.  The Committee also enquired about the estimated cost escalation of the
 project. 
 
25.       In response, the Committee was informed by the Department of Road Transport and Highways that progress of 4-
laning under the Golden Quadrilateral project as on December 2004 was 74%.   It has been assessed that the actual
 expenditure on Golden Quadrilateral will be within the estimated cost, which also allows for escalation. Since the
 project is being implemented through a number of contractors, the exact quantum of escalation can be assessed only
 after the completion of the contracts.   The Committee noted that the revised target date of completion of Golden
 Quadrilateral is December 2005.
 
26.       The Committee further enquired whether there had been instances of delay in completion of jobs due to the
 defaulting contractors and, if so, what action had been taken against such contractors?  The Committee was informed by
 the Department of Road Transport and Highways that a review of performance of various contractors implementing the
 on-going contract packages in NHAI was made. It was found that the performance of 17 contractors (8 foreign and 9
 Indian) was very poor. These 17 contractors have been informed that they will not be pre-qualified for NHAI work, till
 their performance improves.
 
27.       The Committee was also informed by the Department of Road Transport and Highways that following steps had
 been taken for early completion of Golden Quadrilateral:-
(a)          On the request of NHAI, State Governments have nominated nodal officers of the rank of Principal
 Secretary /Secretary to coordinate with other Departments to resolve the issues related to land
 acquisition, shifting of utilities, tree cutting etc.  Regular meetings are being held to resolve these
 problems.
(b)         The progress of projects is being monitored on regular basis by independent supervision consultant,
 NHAI officials and the Department of Road Transport and Highways.
(c)          To expedite the construction of Railway Over Bridges (ROBs), monthly co-ordination meetings are
 being held with Zonal Chief Bridge Engineers of Railways with the officers of the NHAI.  It is also
 being pursued regularly with the Railway Board.
(d)         Forest and environment related matters are being taken up with State Governments as well as
 Ministry of Environment and Forest.
 
28.       The Committee was further informed that NHAI has appointed independent supervision consultants for
 monitoring the quality of construction. The defaulting contractors are penalized on the recommendations of the
 supervision consultants.  The NHAI has also appointed an independent agency M/s Engineers India Limited for quality
 audit and surveillance for 77 on-going contracts of which 61 contracts pertains to Golden Quadrilateral.  NHAI has also
 constituted a cell, headed by a General Manager, to make random check, among other things, of the quality of works
 being implemented under NHDP.

NATIONAL HIGHWAYS NOT COVERED UNDER NHDP
30.       The Committee had discussed the status of National Highways not covered under NHDP in its 82
nd Report on
 Demands for Grants 2004-05 of Department of Road Transport and Highways.  The Committee had noted that out of
 43,833 kilometer of non-NHDP National Highways, only 1.95% are four or more laned whereas 62.55% of such
 National Highways are two-laned and 35.49% of such National Highways are only single/intermediate laned.  The
 Committee felt that there was a mismatch between NHDP and non-NHDP Highways in terms of lanes, surface quality
 and funds.  The Committee had recommended the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways to give equitable
 weightage to the non-NHDP National Highways and provide adequate budgetary allocation required for their
 development.
 
31.       In their Action Taken Replies furnished to the Committee the Department of Road Transport and Highways
 informed that out of the total National Highways network of about 65,569 km, 14279 km have been have been taken up
 under NHDP Phase I & II, comprising the Golden Quadrilateral, North-South & East-West corridors and other projects,
 including connectivity to major ports. The implementation of NHDP Phase I & II is targeted for completion by
 December 2007. The balance length not covered under NHDP (Phase-I & Phase-II) is about 51,000 kms of National
 Highways.  The development of National Highways which are not covered under NHDP are being taken up according to
 the availability of fund, condition, inter-se priority and traffic.  The fund available is not sufficient to take up large
 development works.  Therefore, the Ministry is considering other programmes, using public private partnership, cess
 fund from petrol and diesel for development of National Highways which are not on NHDP.  The development of these
 balance length are being considered under NHDP Phase-III and NHDP Phase-IV and Special Accelerated North East
 Road Development Programme.
 
32.       The rehabilitation and upgradation of about 10,000 km length of existing National Highways to 4 lane, dual
 carriageway on Build, Operate and Transfer (BOT) basis has been proposed to be taken up as NHDP Phase III (A&B).  
 The programme generally comprises stretches of National Highways carrying high volume of traffic, connecting state
 Capitals with NHDP Phase I & II network and providing connectivity to places of economic, commercial and tourist
 importance.  The Government has approved the proposal of NHDP Phase IIIA (4,000 km) at an estimated cost of
 Rs.22,000 crore (2004 prices) and has directed for initiating advance action in the form of preparation of Detailed
 Project Reports  for Phase IIIB (6,000 km). The implementation of NHDP Phase IIIA and IIIB is targeted for
 completion by December 2009 and December 2012 respectively.  For this purpose Rs.1400 crore has been provided in
 the year 2005-06. 
 
33.       Considering the status of development of the roads in North Eastern region, an Accelerated North-East Road
 Development Project for a length of 3251 km of National Highways is under consideration which will mainly provide
 connectivity to all the State Capitals and District Headquarters in the North-East Region including 4-laning of 315 kms
 of National Highways between Nagaon and Dibrugarh and 2/4 laning of 288 kms of National Highways in Meghalaya,
 Nagaland and Sikkim. The proposal would also include up-gradation of other stretches of National Highways and State
 Highways considered critical for economic development of the North-East region.  An amount of Rs.450 crore has been
 provided for the purpose during 2005-06. 
 
34.       Out of the balance length of 38,000 kms, the proposal for approval of upgradation of the length of about 20,000
 kms of National Highways with two-lane paved shoulders is in formulation stage under NHDP Phase IV.

NEED FOR AN INTEGRATED TRANSPORT POLICY
64.       During the meeting of the Committee held on 31
st March 2005, the Committee impressed upon the Department
 of Road Transport and Highways the need to have an integrated transport policy in the country.  The Committee pointed
 out the availability of various types of transport systems in the country and that passenger traffic was not
 proportionately distributed.  The Committee sought the opinion of the representatives of Department of Road Transport
 and Highways in the matter.  In response, while agreeing to the need to have an integrated transport policy, the
 Secretary of the Department stated as under:-
“There is definitely a need to have an integrated transport policy.  This kind of policy one has to see.  We deal
 with roads; the Shipping deals with shipping; the Civil Aviation deals with it.  One has to see it either the
 Planning Commission can do it or we can come up with an integrated transport policy for the road sector.   But,
 we are in touch with the Planning Commission on this issue.  Whatever decision is taken by the Government as a
 whole, we will abide by that.”
 65.       The Committee observes that one of the objectives for the Tenth Plan for the road sector is ‘Development of
 roads to be considered an integral part of the total transport system supplementing other modes, integrating the
 development plans with railways and other modes of transport’.   This objective of the Tenth Plan reinforces the need to
 have an integrated transport policy in the country.  The Committee is of the view that the modal-mix in terms of
 transport is very adverse in the country inspite of the fact that we have long inland waterways, a fairly large railway
 network and the recent upsurge in the aviation and road transport sector.  However, in absence of the right kind of
 modal-mix the country is not making optimum utilization of all those resources.  There is, therefore, a need to have a
 more balanced and equitable distribution of passenger and freight traffic in the country.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Government must come forward with an integrated transport policy to make optimum utilization
 of the various transport facilities available in the country.

DAMAGE IN TSUMANI HIT AREAS
66.       The Tsunami waves hit the coastal regions of the country in December 2004 and caused a major loss of life and
 property there. The Committee desired to know from the Department of Road Transport and Highways about the
 damage caused to the road network and the relief measures undertaken by the Department in the southern parts of the
 country and Andaman & Nicobar Islands. In response, the Department of Road Transport and Highways informed the
 Committee that the Tsumani waves that hit the coastal regions of south India in December 2004 caused huge loss of life
 and property and extensive damage to road network and bridges.  Five teams of officers from the Department inspected
 the affected areas to assess the damages to road infrastructure.  About 242 km of National Highways and 520 km of
 state roads, 14 bridges and 78 culverts have been damaged in the states of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and
 Union Territories of Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Pondicherry.   The total cost of repairs to damaged National
 Highways and state roads has been assessed at about Rs.200 crore (Rs.31.5 crore for short term and Rs.168.5 crore for
 long term measures).  The following relief measures were undertaken by the Department:-
A Control Room was set up by the Department which functioned from         28 th December 2004 to 28th January
 2005.  It was done with the help of all the concerned field agencies as well as other Ministries.
 
The Arasalar Bridge on NH-45A near Karaikal in the Union Territory of Pondicherry was damaged. A bailey
 bridge has been provided for immediate restoration of traffic.  A bridge by the side of the existing bridge is to be
 constructed as a permanent measure.
 
There have been extensive damages to the road network and bridges in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands also. 
 The Andaman and Nicobar Public Works Department (PWD) had requested for the supply of six power saws,
 eight generators, 20 water pumps, 6000 metre G.I. Pipes, 10 plate compactors, 100 metric tonne cement, 100
 pieces RCC Hume Pipes, 10 hand rammers, 500 metre flexible hose, 1000 metre ERW steel pipes, etc. for
 restoration works.  These items were sent by air/ship.
 
67.       The Committee was further informed that the superstructure of a 160 metre  long bridge over the Pazhyar river in
 Tamil Nadu was washed away by the tsunami waves.  The Department of Road Transport and Highways provided relief
 measures by operationalising a ferry service pending installation of a temporary steel bridge and installing a temporary
 steel bridge within 6 weeks for immediate restoration of traffic.  In addition, a permanent bridge was also proposed to be
 constructed within one and a half years.
 
68.       The Department further stated that 23 proposals amounting to Rs.80 crore had been received from the states of
 Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Union Territories of Pondicherry for restoration of the above damages.  All
 these proposals are still under examination.
 
69.       The Committee observes that the Tsunami waves caused extensive damage to the road network and bridges in the
 Southern Parts of the country.  The Committee appreciates the promptness with which the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways responded to the situation and carried out the relief measures in the tsunami hit areas.  The
 Committee strongly recommends that the Department should consider the proposals submitted by the State
 Governments for restoration of the damages on priority basis so that construction/repair works could be carried out at
 the earliest.  The Committee further observes that damage to the National Highways has badly affected the tourism
 potential in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, which is the lifeline of these islands.  The Committee recommends that

POLLUTION TESING AND CONTROL
81.       In order to combat the problem of vehicular pollution, a scheme to provide central assistance in the shape of
 reimbursement of actual cost of the pollution testing equipment purchased by the State Governments had been made
 effective from 1.4.1993. Funds have been released under this scheme to various State Governments restricting the
 purchase of pollution testing equipment to two equipment per RTO.  The scheme was later on modified with effect from
 01.06.97 to provide the facility of reimbursement of only 75% of the cost of equipment to the States as well as to
 accommodate NGOs within the purview of this scheme.   Since no proper proposal was received from any NGO during
 the financial year 1997-98, the scheme was again modified w.e.f. 1.6.1998 to restrict the facility only to the State
 Governments. 
 
82.       The Committee noted that the allocation for Pollution Testing Equipment had been reduced from Rs.2.00 core in
 2004-05 to Rs.1 crore in 2005-06.  The Committee enquired about the reasons for the decreased allocation in 2005-06. 
 In response the Committee was informed by the Department of Road Transport and Highways that in the year 2004-05,
 the BE amount under the scheme of Pollution Testing Equipment was reduced from Rs.2.00 crore to Rs.1.00 crore at RE

84.       Vehicular pollution has been gaining alarming proportions in the country.  The Committee enquired from the
 Department of Road Transport and Highways regarding the steps taken by them for controlling vehicular pollution and
 monitoring pollution levels.  The Department of Road Transport and Highways apprised the Committee of some of the
 important steps taken by them to control vehicular pollution which are as under:-
·        From 1.4.2000, unleaded petrol has been made available in the country.
·        Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG) have been  permitted to be used as
 alternate auto fuels.
·        India 2000 (India stage I) which are akin to Euro I norms have been made effective from 1.4.2000 throughout
 the country.
·        Bharat Stage II emission norms  which are akin to Euro II norms have already been introduced in the eleven
 mega cities and are envisaged to come into force all over India from 1.4.2005. 
·        Bharat Stage III emission standards which are akin to Euro III norms, have been notified  to come into force in
 11 mega cities from 1.4.2005.
·        The emission norms for tractors were first notified in the year 1999 and the next stage emission norms  for
 these vehicles have also come into force from 1.6.2003.  Further, even tighter emission norms for new tractors 
 are coming into force w.e.f. 1.10.2005.
·        Stricter Pollution Under Control norms have been introduced for on-road motor vehicles from 1.10.2004. 
 Apart from tighter norms for Carbon Mono Oxide (CO), the measurement of Hydro Carbon (HC) in respect of
 petrol driven vehicles have also been introduced.  Further, the testing protocol in respect of diesel vehicles has
 also been defined. States have also been empowered to prescribe tighter norms in specific areas, if there is such
 a need and the infrastructure available enables doing so.  
 
85.       The Department of Road Transport and Highways further stated that monitoring and enforcement of these norms
 for on-road vehicles comes under the purview of respective State Governments.
 
86.       The Committee is of the view that vehicular emission has become one of the major sources of environmental
 pollution and the share of the transport sector in total emissions is a matter of serious concern.  The Committee
 appreciates the steps taken by the Department of Road Transport and Highways in controlling vehicular pollution.  The
 Committee recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should impress upon the State
 Governments the need for effective monitoring and enforcement of these norms for on-road vehicles so as to minimize
 its ill effects.
DIFFERENTIAL PRICING SYSTEM FOR PRIVATE VEHICLES
87.       The Committee had, in its 82
nd Report on Demands for Grants 2004-05 of the Ministry of Road Transport and
 Highways observed that the automobile population in the country had been growing disproportionately with respect to
 the infrastructure created and the roads were under undue pressure.  In view, the Committee was of the opinion that
 there was a need to adopt a policy which discourages owning of multiple vehicles.  Accordingly, the Committee had
 recommended that acquiring more than one vehicle in a family should invite financial disincentives. The Committee had
 expressed hope that this would discourage owning of multiple vehicles and  also help release the pressure on the surface
 of the roads and also help positively to reduce vehicular pollution.

95.       The Committee understands that Automotive Research Association of India, Pune has been set up by the Indian

 members of this institute.  The Committee is at a loss to understand as to why Government of India's emission norms

 Road Transport & Highways does not have any administrative control.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that
 either the Department of Road Transport & Highways should have control on the Automotive Research Association of
 India, Pune or the Association should be divested of the power of fixing emission norms as apex certification agency.  It
 is a direct case of the manufacturers themselves being the regulators, which promotes the scope of corruption in the
 functioning of the Institute.  The Committee desires that a proper enquiry may be instituted in the functioning of this
 institute.

 Rs.7.00 lakh for Research & Development out of the total allocation of Rs.7.9 crore during 2004-05, which makes
 evident as to how much priority the Department of Road Transport & Highways attaches to the Research &
 Development activities.  The Committee is dissatisfied that the Department of Road Transport & Highways has no
 Research & Development mechanism of its own and the Department has to depend upon other organisations for its
 Research & Development activities.  The Committee recommends that Department of Road Transport and Highways
 should develop an institutional mechanism to undertake research and development activities.  The Department should
 also create a regulator of its own with the requisite technical wherewithal for fixing emission norms, product design and
 development etc.  The Committee also recommends that the Research & Development activities should also be used for
 developing technology for creating cost-effective high quality road network such as existing in Malaysia and some other
 countries.

 promotion of use of information technology in the highway sector is one of the objectives of the Government in the

 Technology can also be used as an effective tool for monitoring the implementation of the projects undertaken by the
 Department.    They should also make efforts to integrate research and development activities with their monitoring
 system so that proper monitoring could be kept on the projects undertaken by them, which will also help them to keep
 tab on time overrun and cost overrun of such projects.   The Committee also recommends that efforts cited by the
 Department of Road Transport & Highways like creation of Ministry's chair in the area of development of highway
 system at Indian Institutes of Technology and creation of independent testing facilities for bridges on National
 Highways at Central Road Research Institute, New Delhi may be pursued more vigorously and in case of any difficulty,
