9.         The Committee notes that Ministry of Civil Aviation has failed to fully utilize the outlay approved during 2004-
05.  The Ministry anticipates to utilize an amount of Rs.1473.03 crore out of the approved allocation of Rs.1620.98
 crore during the year 2004-05, which exemplifies the poor financial management in the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The
 Committee feels that there is a lack of proper planning in the various organisations of Ministry of Civil Aviation, as a
 result of which the Ministry was unable to utilize optimally the approved outlays at its disposal.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress upon the concerned agencies to make a
 realistic assessment of their financial requirements so that the allocations made do not remain unutilized. 
ANALYSIS OF THE AVIATION POLICY
10.       The Committee notes that the civil aviation sector has grown in the country during the recent years.  As per the
 aviation policy being pursued by the Government, the Ministry of Civil Aviation has taken a number of steps which
 have affected the airlines and the airports in the country.  The Government has taken decision to allow Air India and
 Indian Airlines to proceed with the acquisition process of aircraft. The Government has allowed private domestic
 carriers to fly on international routes also.  With respect to the airport sector, the Government has taken steps for
 modernization and restructuring of the Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Government has also taken steps towards the
 development of Greenfield airports at Bangalore and Hyderabad. 
 
11.       The aviation policy being pursued by the Government will have a bearing on the various aspects of the civil
 aviation sector in the country in general and the public sector airline companies in particular.   The Committee analysed
 the effect of the aviation policy of the various aspects of the civil aviation sector such as opening of international routes
 to private airlines, requirement of trained manpower, infrastructure and maintenance facilities at airports, modernization
 and restructuring of the Delhi and Mumbai airports, development of Greenfield airports at Bangalore and Hyderabad,
 high cost of air turbine fuel (ATF), review of Route Dispersal Guidelines, impact of Fringe Benefit Tax, requirement of
 an eastern hub at Kolkata etc. The details of the analysis of the Committee have been discussed in the succeeding
 paragraphs of the report.

REVIEW OF ROUTE DISPERSAL GUIDELINES
40.       The Committee had, in its 78
th Report on Demands for Grants 2004-05 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 observed that like Indian Airlines, private airlines should also fulfil their social commitments and not prefer to operate
 mostly on lucrative routes and complete the formality of fulfilling their social obligation by flying to the prescribed
 minimum flights to the North-East region under the Route Dispersal Guidelines.  The Committee had noted that Route
 Dispersal Guidelines had been manipulated by the private airlines to the disadvantage of the backward regions.   The
 Committee had recommended that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should evolve some mechanism to ensure that private
 airlines in the country fulfil their social obligation by operating more number of flights in the North-East region.  The
 Committee had also expressed the view that the Route Dispersal Guidelines should be reviewed with a view to making
 them full proof so that no private airline is able to violate them and any such violation should entail heavy disincentive
 to that airline.
 
41.       In their Action Taken Replies furnished to the Committee, the Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the
 Committee that the Ministry had constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of DGCA vide  order dated 23-09-
2003 to review the Route Dispersal Guidelines.  The Committee had been mandated to submit its report within two
 months of issue of the order.  The review committee and its members had been provided with the contents of the
 observations of the Committee in this regard so as to incorporate these views while reviewing the present Route
 Dispersal Guidelines.  The committee had been requested to expedite its report.  During the course of the examination
 of Demands for Grants 2005-06 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, it was informed that the Committee under DGCA to
 review the Route Dispersal Guidelines had submitted its report on 18.3.2005 which was being examined. 
 
42.       The Committee is of the view that the present aviation policy being followed by the Government has not been
 effective in making the private airlines share the social obligations of the country.  The Committee feels that the private
 airlines have been focusing on lucrative trunk routes only.  These airlines have been operating only on the basis of
 commercial terms and tend to follow the bare minimum of what is mandatory for them under the Route Dispersal
 Guidelines. The Committee recommends that the Route Dispersal Guidelines should be revisited to ensure that the
 private domestic airlines also share the social obligation of connecting remote parts of the country in the true sense and
 not by merely completing the formalities in this regard.

66.       During the course of the oral evidence of the representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation on the 30 th March
 2005, the Committee was informed that the domestic air transport industry in India has been facing serious problems
 due to high cost of operations. One of the major reasons for this is the heavy cost of Air Turbine Fuel (ATF).  Even
 though the pricing of ATF is now on import parity basis, the rates applicable for domestic operations continue to be
 significantly higher than that of international operations.  The cost of ATF goes up even further due to high rates of
 sales tax levied by the State Governments/Union Territory administration varying from 20 per cent to 36 per cent which
 affects the viability of domestic airline operations.

 increasing, we tried to absorb it in our own operational expenses by trying to trim costs, by improving
 efficiency, and by improving utilization of aircrafts.  Now we have reached the limits where, I am afraid,
 the airlines will have to come up very shortly with some amount of fare increase to absorb this cost".

 Act) if any designated Indian Carrier purchases Aviation Turbine Fuel for the purposes of its international flights, such
 purchases shall be deemed to take place in the course of the export of goods out of the territory of India.  Appropriate
 amendment would come into effect after the passage of the Finance bill/date of notification by the Government of

 payment of Sales Tax.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the Committee that the ATF prices in India are

 with IATA Regulations.  These tickets are purely on the basis of subject to availability. This means that
 employees/families are allowed to travel only when spare seats are available which could not be sold to the
 public at large and that too at the time of departure of the flight.  These seats would otherwise have gone un-

 the country of the lessor.  Ministry of Civil Aviation further informed that leasing is an ongoing exercise and is resorted
 to by all airlines to cater to short-term capacity needs.  Therefore, the exemption from tax on aircraft rentals was
 required to be extended beyond September 2005.

 aircraft/aircraft engines will, in particular, adversely affect Air India and Indian Airlines as they have a significant
 portion of their fleet as leased aircraft, which are due for renewal and are also planning to induct additional aircraft
 through lease.  Alliance Air, a subsidiary of Indian Airlines is also planning to commence replacement of ageing fleet
 initially through lease route.  Similarly, Air India plans to establish a low cost airline named Air India Express by
 leasing aircraft.  The withdrawal of this facility will also pose an entry barrier to new airlines planning to introduce low
 cost operations as most of these airlines plan to induct aircraft initially through lease route.  All these new initiatives
 will be adversely affected with the withdrawal of income tax exemption, which was available to payment of lease
 rentals on aircraft.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Finance should give special consideration
 to the facts brought out above and in the interest of the civil aviation sector, more so in the interest of the public sector
 operators, provide exemption from tax on agreements to acquire aircraft or aircraft engine on lease beyond September
 2005 also, as suggested by the Ministry of Civil Aviation.

REVAMPING OF TRANSPORT SECTOR IN ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS IN POST TSUNAMI
 SCENARIO
 
129.     On an invitation of Lt. Governor, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, the Chairman, Committee on Transport, Tourism
 and Culture had visited the Islands to have discussion on revamping of Tourism and Transport Sectors in Andaman &
 Nicobar Islands in Post Tsunami Scenario. In the light of the above discussions, the Committee enquired from the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation as to why the Ministry of Civil Aviation was not introducing direct flights to Port Blair from
 other stations in the country apart from Kolkata and Chennai.  In response, the Committee was informed that Indian
 Airlines had been providing air services to Port Blair from Chennai and Kolkata for the past many decades.  Over the
 period of time, Chennai has come to be accepted as a gateway point for travel to Port Blair from South, West as well as
 North India, while Kolkata serves as gateway to Port Blair from East and North India.  Both Chennai and Kolkata are
 as such serving as hub points for operations to Port Blair.  Indian Airlines provides a daily over night connection to Port
 Blair over Chennai/ Kolkata and same day connection in the return direction.  While it would be ideal to have a same
 day onward connection to Port Blair, due to the limitations of Port Blair airfield, the same is not possible and the
 operations to/from Port Blair have to be restricted to morning hours.  In Indian Airlines’ estimate, the existing traffic
 potential to Port Blair from metros such as Delhi and Mumbai and other points is not sufficient to sustain direct services
 with the jet type of aircraft in Indian Airlines fleet.  Also Indian Airlines fleet is fully committed for operating on the
 existing schedule and spare capacity is not available to consider introduction of flights on new domestic routes. 
 Further, Government has laid down Route Dispersal Guidelines with a view to achieve better regulation of air transport
 services taking into account the need for air transport services of different regions of the country.  It is, however, up to
 the airlines to provide air services to specific places depending upon the traffic demand and commercial viability As
 such, the airlines are free to operate anywhere in the country subject to compliance of Route Dispersal Guidelines
 issued by the Government. However, all scheduled domestic airlines have been requested to consider this proposal.
 
130.     The Committee also desired to know as to when Ministry of Civil Aviation planned to allow the airlines
 operating to and from South and South East Asian countries to stop over at Port Blair airport, thereby opening the
 Islands to more tourists.  In response, the Committee was informed that designated airlines of all ASEAN countries,
 i.e., Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Myanmar, Vietnam, Brunei, Philippines, Cambodia & Lao PDR as well
 as Sri Lanka have been permitted unlimited access to Port Blair.  Actual operations are, however, matters of
 commercial judgment of the airlines concerned.

 The Ministry of Civil Aviation informed that with a view to promote tourism to the Island Indian Airlines has
 introduced APEX fares an advance purchase scheme on Kolkata-Port Blair or vice versa and Chennai-Port Blair or vice
 versa sector.  The APEX fares have been offered under three date slabs i.e.   D-7, D-21 and D-28.  The APEX fares

th April 2005

 as ILS CAT-III system.

 commercial terms and tend to follow the bare minimum of what is mandatory for them under the Route Dispersal

 compensate with the losses to be incurred, in case the existing terminal at Hyderabad is closed, by developing shopping
 complexes, housing etc. on commercial basis.   The Committee is opposed to this move of the Government for closing
 the existing airport at Hyderabad for commercial flights once the new Hyderabad International Airport Limited is
 operational and urges the Government to reconsider this decision.
(Para 112)

            The Committee is of the opinion that due protection must be given to the interests of employees of Airports
 Authority of India while proceeding with the commissioning of new international airports at Bangalore and Hyderabad
 and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Committee recommends that all decisions relating to absorption
 of employees of Airports Authority of India by other companies should be taken in a transparent manner in consultation
 with the representatives of the employees of Airports Authority of India.  The Committee cautions that adequate care
 should be taken to protect the interests of the employees of the Authority and it should be ensured that the existing
 terms and conditions of service of the employees of the Authority are not altered after their absorption into the said
 companies.

CREATION OF A EASTERN HUB AT KOLKATA
            The Committee is of the opinion that with the growth of the aviation sector in the country, the pressure and strain
 on Mumbai and Delhi airports is also increasing.  The Committee is apprehensive that with the arrival of private players
 in the airline sector, there will be a further intensification of this pressure.  As accepted by the Secretary of the Ministry,
 the Delhi and Mumbai-centric activity was also becoming unmanageable.  Therefore there exists a need to develop
 alternate destinations, particularing in the eastern part of country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry
 of Civil Aviation should take steps for the creation of an eastern hub at Kolkata.  The Committee also notes that while a
 foreign carrier was fully exploiting the availability of air traffic in Kolkata, our own carriers did not even have a
 presence there. The Committee, therefore, also recommends that Ministry of Civil Aviation should introduce
 international flights from Kolkata.  In the context of look East policy of the Government, the Committee feels that
 locational advantage of Kolkata vis-à-vis South East and Far East Asia can be leveraged. Apart from this, the
 Committee feels that this will reduce the pressure on Delhi & Mumbai airports to a great extent.  On similar grounds,
 the Committee also feels that a Southern hub should be established at Chennai.
(Para 118)
 
PAWAN  HANS HELICOPTERS LIMITED
            The Committee notes that PHHL has been acquiring new fleet of helicopters with a view to extending its
 services in the Domestic Sector for short-haul distances.  The Committee feels that there is a need for reinventing Air
 Transport Services to connect different regions of the country for contributing towards the process of national economic
 growth.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry should explore the possibility for providing regular air
 transport services by PHHL to connect specific places, especially hilly areas which are inaccessible by a fixed wing
 aircraft or other modes of travel.  The Committee further recommends that in order to give a fillip to tourism and for
 unlocking the value of various tourist destinations in the country, the Ministry should operate regular helicopter
 services in certain parts like, North Eastern States, Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh), Nanded, Kohalapur, Shirdi
 (Maharashtra) Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh) and Northern Hill States of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and
 Uttranchal.
 
            The Committee expresses its concern over the rise in helicopter accidents in the country and feels that there is an
 urgent need for revamping the system of safety audits of various helicopter operators.  The Committee is of the view
 that the operations of helicopter companies, especially in the private sector, should be monitored and regulated properly
 in the light of the recent helicopter accidents.  The Committee recommends the Ministry for creation of a dedicated cell
 for carrying out the safety audits for helicopter under DGCA.  The Committee also takes strong exception to the failure
 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation to furnish information sought by the Committee with respect to the proficiency rating
 system of pilots in DGCA.  
(Paras 127 and 128)
 
REVAMPING OF TRANSPORT SECTOR IN ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS IN POST TSUNAMI
 SCENARIO
 
            The Committee notes that transportation of tourists from the mainland has been a major constraint for Andaman
 & Nicobar Islands.  The Committee is of the opinion that affordable air connectivity is a crucial element in sustaining
 tourism in Andaman & Nicobar Islands for the economic sustenance of the islands. Therefore, corrective actions to
 reduce the exorbitant airfares, which deter the increase of the tourist inflow in the region, need to be taken urgently.
 The Committee recommends that LTC facility from Kolkata to Andaman and Nicobar Islands should also be
 introduced and number of seats available under Apex Fare Schemes should be increased in order to encourage more
 and more domestic tourists to visits these islands.  The Committee also recommends that direct flights should be
 introduced to Port Blair from other stations in the country apart from Kolkata and Chennai.  Private airlines should also
 be encouraged to fly to these Islands besides allowing airlines operating from South and South East Asian countries to
 have stopover at Port Blair.  The Committee also recommends for increasing the inter-island air connectivity in
 Andaman and Nicobar Islands in order to boost tourism in these islands.
(Para 133)

R E P O R T
 
The Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004 seeks to address the issue of security pertaining to the
 Merchant Shipping in India and to amend the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and Indian Ports Act, 1908 so as to
 incorporate therein provisions relating to security measures to be adopted by ships and port, port facilities, ship
 identification number, port facility assessment, international ship security certificate, ship security alert system, control
 measures and compliance.
 
2.                     The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill states that India has ratified the International Convention
 on Safety of Life at Sea 1974 (SOLAS 1974) on 16
th June 1976, which came into force on 25 th May 1980.  This
 Convention in its successive forms is generally regarded as the most important of all international treaties concerning
 the safety of merchant ships.  The main objective of the SOLAS 1974 is to specify minimum standards for the
 construction, equipment and operation of ships, compatible with their safety.  There are 11 codes or similar instruments
 that are made mandatory under SOLAS 1974.  Of these, the last Code is the 'International Code for the Security of
 Ships and Port Facility' (ISPS Code).  This Code was adopted as an amendment to SOLAS 1974 by the conference of
 contracting States on 12
th December 2002, by passing 11 resolutions.  Out of those 11 Resolutions, Resolution No. 6
 inter-alia prescribes 1st July 2004 as the application dates for the code.  If the ISPS Code is not implemented it will be
 difficult for the Indian Ships to secure entry in the Ports of other contracting States an also for the foreign ships to visit
 Indian Ports.
 
3.
                                         The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill further states that with a view to implement the
 provisions of the ISPS Code, it is proposed to amend the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.  India being a major seafarer-
supplying nation, it is essential to ensure that our seafarers' employment prospects and movements to other countries are
 not hampered for want of Seafarers' identity document.  Accordingly, it is proposed to incorporate necessary provisions
 in the Bill.
4.
                                         The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill also states that since the implementation of ISPS Code
 also involves ports, it is proposed to consequentially amend the Indian Ports Act, 1908 so as to facilitate a port facility
 in complying with the requirements of the maritime security proposed to be included under the new Part IX B of the

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
 Merchant Shipping act, 1958.
 
5.                                         In their background note furnished to the Committee giving the reasons for the introduction of the Bill,
 the Department of Shipping have brought out in the succeeding paragraphs:-
 
NEED FOR ISPS CODE
5.1                   Part IX of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 relates to 'Safety' of ships.  The provisions of this part
 achieves implementation of International Convention on Safety of Life at sea, 1974 (SOLAS 1974), which came into
 force internationally on 25
th May 1980. India having ratified this on 16 th June 1976 the convention came into force in
 India on 25 th May 1980.  The main objective of the SOLAS Convention is to specify minimum standards for the
 construction, equipment and operation of ships, compatible with their safety.  The Convention has been updated and
 amended on numerous occasions hence is referred to as SOLAS 1974, as amended.  There are 11 Codes or similar
 instruments that are made mandatory under SOLAS 1974.  Of these the last Code is 'International Code for the Security
 of Ships and of port Facility' (ISPS Code).  Following the tragic events of 11 th September 2001, the 22nd session of the
 Assembly of the IMO in November 2001 had unanimously agreed to the development of new measures relating to the
 security of ships and of port facilities for adoption by a Conference of Contracting Governments to the SOLAS 1974. 
 This Code was adopted as an amendment to SOLAS by the conference of Contracting Governments (SOLAS 1974) on
 12th December 2002.  To address the issue of 'Security' in the legislation pertaining to merchant shipping in India, it has
 been proposed to introduce/insert a new part IXB in the Merchant Shipping Act along with minor changes in the long
 title of the Act, new definition of security in Section 3 in part I, amendment of section 31 in Part V.  To complement the
 provisions of new part IXB it was also felt necessary to make corresponding amendments in Indian Ports Act, 1908 by
 providing new Section 68 D.
 
OBJECTIVES OF ISPS CODE
5.2                   The objectives of the ISPS Code are to establish an international framework-involving co-operation
 between contracting States, Government agencies, local administrations and the shipping and port industries to detect
 or assess security threats and take preventive measures against security incidents affecting ships or port facilities used
 in international trade; to establish the respective roles and responsibilities of all concerned at the national and
 international level for ensuring maritime security; to ensure the early and efficient colletion and  exchange of security
 related information; to provide a methodology for security assessments so as to have in place plans and procedures to
 react to changing security levels and; to ensure adequate and proportionate maritime security measures.  If the ISPS
 Code is not implemented, it will be difficult for the Indian ships to secure entry in the ports of other contracting states
 and also for the foreign ships to visit Indian ports. Therefore, it was felt necessary to provide legislative support to
 Indian ships in respect of security and to provide corresponding measures at Indian ports for foreign flag ships.

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
 
5.3                   Similarly, 'Seafarers Identity Document Convention (Revised), 2003', (Convention 185) was adopted by
 International Labour Conference, Geneva, on 19th June 2003.  According to this, access to ships/ports will be restricted
 to only those seafarers who are in possession of Seafarers Identity Document.  Therefore, to bring the Indian seafarers
 at par with international standards, it was felt necessary to introduce corresponding changes in the Merchant Shipping
 Act by insertion of new section 99A in Part VII.  Since India is a major seafarer-supplying nation to international
 shipping, it is imperative that the Indian seafarers are issued the identification documents giving his biometrics and
 personal information, which can be scrutinized, from any port of world for its genuineness.  These provisions would
 ensure that employment opportunity of Indian Seafarers is not compromised.  Similar checks have been employed for
 foreign seafarers at Indian ports at the facilities to meet the requirements of this convention and ensure security of our
 ports and country at large. 
 
SCOPE OF ISPS CODE
6.                                         The scope of ISPS Code is limited to ship and port facilities and the measures included in the Code are
 essentially preventive measures so as to reduce the chances of easy entry for unlawful elements such as and they have
 to be implemented by the port security personnel and the trained ship-staff.  Further, in case of any security incident,
 there would be a better coordination with the agencies in-charge of security and the law and other in the area.  There
 would also be a better awareness towards ensuring safety of ships from acts of sabotage etc.  The measures will also
 ensure that the ships and ports would not be a soft target of the terrorists besides introducing some security measures
 which would assist the port and ship staff in preventing unauthorized entry in ports and on board ships, there are other
 measures to ensure that weapons and unauthorized people are not permitted to enter the port or ships through
 cargo/stores or otherwise.  This necessitates that the port facilities where the ship port interface takes place are
 sanitized.
 
FEATURES OF ISPS CODE
7.                                         The salient features of the ISPS code are as under:-
Ž         To establish an international framework involving co-operation between contracting Governments,
 Government agencies, local administrations and the shipping and port industries to detect and assess
 security threats and take preventive measures against security incidents affecting ships or port facilities
 used in international trade.
Ž          To establish the respective roles and responsibilities of the Contracting Governments, Government
 agencies, local administration and the shipping and port industries, at the national and international level,
 for ensuring maritime security.
Ž         To ensure the early and efficient collection and exchange of security-related information.
Ž         To provide a methodology for security assessments so as to have in place plans and procedures to react to
 changing security levels and

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
Ž         To ensure confidence that adequate and proportionate maritime security measures are in place.
 
FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS OF ISPS CODE
8.                     In order to achieve its objectives, this code embodies a number of functional requirements.  These
 include, but are not limited to:-
Ž                Gathering and assessing information with respect to security threats and exchanging such information
 with appropriate contracting Governments;
Ž                Requiring the maintenance of communication protocols for ships and port facilities;
Ž                Preventing unauthorized access to ships, port facilities and their restricted areas;
Ž                Preventing the introduction of unauthorized weapons, incendiary devices or explosives to ships or port
 facilities;
Ž                Providing means for raising the alarm in reaction to security threats or security incidents;
Ž                Requiring ship and port facility security plans based upon security assessments; and
Ž                Requiring training, drills and exercises to ensure familiarity with security plans and procedures.
APPLICATION OF ISPS CODE
9.                     The ISPS Code shall apply to the following type of ships on International
Voyages and Port Facilities serving such ships:-
Ž                Passengers ships irrespective of size,
Ž                Cargo ships of 500 Gross Tonnage and above not on International voyage.
Ž                All ships of 300 Gross Tonnage on International voyages
Ž                 Port facility serving ships on International voyages.
Ž                Mobile of shore Drilling Units.
 
10.                   The Committee in its meeting held on 17 th January and 23rd February 2005 respectively heard the views
 of Secretary and other officers of the Department of Shipping on the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004. 
 
11.
                The Committee also heard the views of the representatives of the National Security Council and the employees
 unions of Indian National Ports & Docks Workers Federation and All India Port & Dock Workers Federation at its
 sitting held on 14th, 15th  & 23rd February 2005 respectively.  The representatives of National Security Council and of
 the two workers federation while supporting the Bill from maritime security point of view have expressed their
 reservations before the Committee about the implementation of ISPS Code.
 
REASONS FOR ADOPTION OF ISPS CODE AND PROTECTION OF NATIONAL INTEREST
12.
                                     As regards the compulsions for adoption of ISPS Code and protection of National interest, the
 Department of Shipping vide their O.M. No.SR. 20013/2/2003-AG dated 17.02.2005 informed the Committee that in

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
 order to ensure continuity of EXIM trade, the Government has entered into this agreement.  In case ISPS Code is not
 implemented by ships then Indian flagships will not be allowed to carry Cargo to the ports of other countries and
 therefore EXIM trade would suffer.  All the ships involved in international trade are also mandatorily required to keep
 data for last 10 ports of call, all of which must be ISPS compliant.  Therefore, it is necessary for ports also to be ISPS
 compliant; otherwise no foreign ships would call at Indian ports.  Moreover, the measures included in the ISPS Code
 have been arrived at after lengthy deliberations at International Maritime Organization in which India has participated
 actively and they do take into account the views of contracting parties to Safety of Life at Sea Convention.  In ISPS
 Code, there is no such element, which would compromise the national interest.
13.
                                     During the course of evidence tendered on 17.01.2005, the Secretary of Department of Shipping
 deposed before the Committee that;
" Sir, as everybody is aware, after the 11 th September, 2001 incident, there was such an urgency
 to increase security, both in shipping and in ports, in short, in the maritime sector, that the International
 Maritime Organisation called for a diplomatic conference where all the member state Governments were
 present in December, 2002; they made some amendments to the International convention for the Safety
 of Life at Sea, called SOLAS 1974, and the ISPS Code came into existence.  It has Part A and Part B. 
 Part A has mandatory provisions and Part B has guidance provisions.  Sir, it was to be implemented by
 all countries in the world with effect from 1
st July, 2004, and accordingly, all the member state
 Governments have taken steps to update security measure in respect to shipping as well as ports in
 accordance with the ISPS Code.  However, in the Merchant Shipping Act, these provisions had to be
 reflected and, therefore, the Ministry has prepared the Report and submitted it to the Parliament."
 
14.                   The Committee takes note of the fact that in order to ensure continuity of EXIM trade the Government
 has entered into this agreement.  The Committee agrees with the views of the Government that if the ISPS Code is not
 implemented the Indian ships & port facilities may act as a non-tariff barrier for sea borne commerce. It appears to the
 Committee that current assessment of security threat to shipping sector is basically the consequence of 9/11 attack on
 U.S.A.  Terrorism has a much longer history, however, International Maritime Organization ignored that fact and
 suddenly woke up to the threat of security and agreed unanimously to the evolution of new measures relating to ships
 and port facilities post 9/11.  The Committee does not approve the contention of the Secretary that the ISPS Code
 provides both voluntary as well as mandatory provisions.  The Committee feels that security perception is a sovereign
 function and it is country specific. It is not fair, therefore, to confuse between our own security requirements and
 demands of international trade.  Protecting the nation, is a sovereign function of the Government. The Committee,
 therefore, recommends the Department of Shipping to look into the national priorities and interests while implementing
 the ISPS code.
 
15.
                                     The Committee expressed apprehension that Department of Shipping is encroaching upon the law
 making powers of the Parliament so far as framing the laws are concerned.  In response, the Department of Shipping
 informed that the code recognizes the rights of sovereign nations and specifically provides;
"Nothing in this Code shall prejudice the rights or obligations of States under international law"
 

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
16.                The Department of Shipping further informed the Committee that ISPS Code has come into existence through
 an amendment of SOLAS, which came in force internationally on 25th May 1980.  India had ratified this convention on
 16th June 1976.  The aforesaid amendments were deemed to have been accepted on 1st January 2004 unless prior to that
 date more than one third of the contracting Governments to the convention or contracting Governments the combined
 fleet of which constitute not less than 50% of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant fleet have notified their
 objections to the amendments.  Since this has not happened, amendments to SOLAS have come into effect.  Since ISPS
 Code is being implemented under this amendment to SOLAS, no fresh ratification is required.  The present amendment
 Bill is to give legislative backup to ISPS Code.  Therefore, there is no encroachment upon the law making powers of
 Parliament.
 
17.                   The Committee recognizes that our constitution empowers the Government to enter into international
 agreements and no subsequent ratification by the Parliament is necessary.  However, if such agreements warrant any
 legislative change subsequently, then powers of the Parliament are final.  Therefore, the Government should be mindful
 of that flexibility.
 
FORMATION OF MARITIME SECURITY ADVISORY COMMITTEE 
18.                   As regards involvement of Merchant Shipping into the business of security, which is essentially the job
 of the Naval Force or the Armed Forces and formation of a Maritime Security Advisory Committee under the Ministry
 of Defence, the Department of Shipping vide their O.M. dated 17.02.2005 informed the Committee that the role of
 Naval forces or the Armed forces is in no way perceived to be different post-ISPS Code implementation.  In fact,
 International Maritime Organization is not the body to deliberate upon the role of Armed forces in relation to their
 sovereign powers in protecting their national security interests and therefore the Code had no intention to discuss such
 issues.  As already stated, the scope of the ISPS Code and the SOLAS chapter XI-2, based on which the Merchant
 Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004 has been prepared, is confined to only preventive measures to deter and detect.  It is
 clarified that the objective of the code is to establish an international frame work involving cooperation between
 contracting Governments, Government agencies, local administrations, shipping and the port industry to detect security
 threats and take preventive measures against security incidents affecting ships or port facilities only.  The role of
 Armed forces is to respond to any security incident, which may be reported by the ships or port facilities.  Hence the
 objective of ISPS Code in no way clashes with already established role of law enforcement agencies, naval forces or the
 armed forces.  Moreover, jurisdiction of coast guard and navy commences outside the port limit whereas the ISPS Code
 is concerned with port facility security, which is always inside the port limit.  Port Security in the country has been
 traditionally covered by the CISF, Port Police, State Police and in some cases by Private Security i.e. very similar to the
 practice followed by Airports. Port & Ship Security involves screening the cargo, access control, ship port interface and
 interaction with custom etc.  All such issues come under the control of Civilian Authorities.

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
 
19.                                     During the course of evidence tendered on 23.02.2005, the Secretary of Department of Shipping
 deposed before the Committee that;
"Sir, I agree with you on the first point that the National Security Council and the security agencies
 from the Ministry of Defence are ultimately in charge of the security of the country.  In the IMO also,
 this point was clearly conceded that the sovereign Government and the armed forces have their role to
 play once a terrorist threat has been realised.  But the ISPS Code aims at preventing a terrorist
 situation from developing, both in terms of ships and ports.  Therefore, what we did in the Committees
 that we appointed, for the purposes of ISPS Code,  ---- one under my chairmanship and another under
 the chairmanship of the DG Shipping, who is the designated authority -- the representatives from these
 forces have been associated, Navy as well as Coast Guard.  I have the details of names of persons who
 attended these meetings.  That means we have taken the input from them while devising these
 measures and the main objective of the ISPS is to put in place a system.  Sir, the moment there is a
 security threat, it is informed to the security people, whether it is the police at a smaller level or the
 Navy at the larger level.  They will be immediately put on alert."
 
20.
                The Department of Shipping vide their O.M. dated 1.03.2005 further informed the Committee that they have
 formed various levels of interaction with intelligence agencies, defence agencies and appropriate law enforcement
 agencies, and the following Committees have been constituted to implement ISPS Code in India.
(i)        Review Committee, chaired by Secretary (Shipping) comprising of representatives from Ministry of
 Shipping, Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of External Affairs, Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Finance,
 Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gases, Coastguard, Navy Customs, Gujarat Maritime Board, Maharashtra
 Maritime Board, Indian National Ship Owners' Association and Chairman and Managing Director, Shipping
 Corporation of India;
(ii)        Steering Group, chaired by Director General of Shipping comprising of representative from Ministry of
 Shipping, Directorate General of Shipping, Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Home Affairs, Coastguard, Indian
 Navy and Indian National Ship Owners' Association.
(iii)       Port Security Advisory Committee, chaired by Chairman of the Major Ports or Chief executives of
 Maritime Boards comprising of - Port Facility Security Officer and representatives from Coast Guard, Navy,
 State/Centre Intelligence agencies (e.g. Intelligence Bureau), Local Police, Customs, Central Industrial Security
 Force (CISF) or other security Agency incharge of Port Security and Mercantile Marine Department.
 
21.
                                     While carrying out Port Facility Security Assessment, Indian Register of Shipping, the designated
 Recognized Security Organization (RSO), had taken the inputs of Navy, Coast Guard, Intelligence Bureau, and Local
 Police etc. 
 
22.
                                     The Amendments relating to ISPS Code have come into force as part of Safety of Life at Sea
 Convention for which Ministry of Shipping is the nodal agency.  The role of Defence agencies is of advisory nature and
 they have already been included in the Committees.  In addition, the Directorate General of Shipping has been sending

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
 security related information to the National Security Council Secretariat, and the same is discussed in the National
 Security Council fortnightly intelligence summary meetings.  The meeting is attended by officers of Ministry of
 Defence (all the three wings), Coast Guard, IB, MHA, MEA, etc. It is also proposed to request National Security
 Council (NSC) to nominate their representative in the Maritime Security Review Committee, which is functional under
 the chairmanship of Secretary (Shipping).  This would facilitate, to take on board the views of National Security
 Council while implementing ISPS Code.
 
23.
                                     The Committee notes that IMO is not the body to deliberate upon the role of Armed forces in relation to
 their sovereign powers in protecting their national security interest and the scope of ISPS Code is confined to only
 preventive measures to deter and detect and the role of armed forces is to respond to any security incident reported by
 ships or port facilities. The Committee feels that the problem of security is very old and the security requirements are
 becoming far too complex to be handled in the manner they were being handled in the past.  Therefore, an international
 organisation which is primarily engaged in commercial activity through sea route should not have been involved in the
 business of security and some defence related agencies i.e. Navy and Armed forces should have essentially dealt with
 this kind of a code.  The Committee therefore, recommends for creation of a Maritime Security Advisory Committee to
 report on and make recommendations on National Maritime Security matter under the Ministry of Defence so that all
 commerce handled by the Port and Ships would achieve appropriate security coverage.
 
COMPETENCE OF PORT AUTHORITY TO ADDRESS SECURITY ISSUES
24.
                The Committee expressed apprehension that the port authorities all over the world are not competent enough in
 addressing the security issues so far as the terrorist activities are concerned.  In response, the Department of Shipping
 stated that the port authorities are competent to address the security issue so far as terrorist activities are concerned. 
 But it is also a fact that the existing practices on ships and port facility security were not considered adequate at the
 international level.  Prior to adoption of ISPS Code, there were a large number of port facilities all over the world
 including some in India, which did not even have boundary fencing, and effective access control in place.  ISPS Code
 has been implemented to adopt uniform practices understood by each port and ship. 
 
25.                   The Committee notes that the port authorities are competent to address the security issue so far as
 terrorist activities are concerned. But, the existing practices on ships and port facilities security are not considered
 adequate at the international level. The Committee, however, recommends that all port facilities and Indian vessels
 should have comprehensive security plans that are evolved by port authorities and shipping companies in conjunction
 with the Indian Navy and the Coast Guard besides setting up local port security committees for better coordination of
 efforts of central, state and local law enforcement and security agencies.
 
AUTHORITY FOR TAKING DECISION ON THE SECURITY PERCEPTION
26.                   As regards authority for taking decision on the security perception, the Department of Shipping vide their

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
 O.M. dated 17.02.2005 informed the Committee that the contracting Government is the authority for taking decisions
 on the security perception.  Chapter XI-2/3 of SOLAS (obligations of contracting Government with respect to security)
 states:
"Administrations shall set security levels and ensure the provisions of security level information to ships entitled
 to fly their flag.  When changes in security level occur, security-level information shall be updated as the
 circumstance dictates.  Contracting Governments shall set security levels and ensure the provision of security-
level information to port facilities within their territory, and to ships prior to entering a port or whilst in a port
 within their territory.  When changes in security level occur, security-level information shall be updated as the

 primarily, the security levels will be issued by designated authority i.e. D.G. Shipping, based on intelligence inputs
 received from I.B., local police, State Government, Navy, Coastguard etc. However, it is envisaged that security levels
 for the major ports can be declared by the respective Chairman in consultation with the Port Security Advisory
 Committee which consists of representatives from local law enforcement agencies, Navy, Coast Guard, Customs,
 Immigration, etc.  As regards other ports, the security levels will be declared by respective State Maritime Boards in
 similar manner.  The ships generally are required to operate at least at the same security levels as that of the concerned
 port.  In case of any higher threat, it is envisaged that the security level of a particular ship or a group of ships can be
 raised in consultation with or under delegation of D.G. Shipping. The overall security of ports and other areas of
 commercial and strategic importance has been and would continue to be with the appropriate law enforcement
 agencies/Defence services of the country to protect against any internal or external aggression.
 
28.                   The Department of Shipping vide their O.M. dated 1.03.2005 further stated that the security requirements
 under ISPS Code cover prevention and detention aspects and the DG Shipping is competent and equipped to handle
 these aspects.  A Communication Centre in the office of DG Shipping has been specially set up to meet the
 communication and coordination related requirements of ISPS Code on Indian ships, on Indian shores and ISPS
 complaint Indian Ports.  This Communication Centre is manned 24 hours x 7 days basis.  The equipment fitted in the
 Communication Centre is capable of receiving Ship Security Alert from any Indian ship anywhere in the world.  The
 Communication Centre would also receive communication from any foreign maritime administration/agency for
 rendering assistance to their ships in Indian waters.  The Communication Centre is capable of coordinating the efforts
 required in handling any ISPS related security incident.

 paraphernalia to handle the security matters as maintained in the Merchant Shipping Act 1958.  The Committee feels
 that the security concerns are growing day by day and there is a need to institutionalize the security element.  The
 Committee therefore, recommends that, even if, the DG Shipping oversees the functions, for securing maritime
 environment, there should be a Maritime Security Advisory Committee to deal with security matters and to make

 activity, which may not have been covered in the scope of activities identified, and the same will be covered under the

 Committee therefore, recommends that the Department of Shipping should clearly specify and incorporate "any other
 hostile act or influence" in the Bill itself so as to make it more comprehensive and subject to monitoring.

44.                   The Committee desires to know the impact of the Merchant Shipping  (Amendment) Bill, 2004 on the

 implementation of ISPS Code to ports of the country.  For this purpose, a new section 68D is intended to be inserted in

 contrary, it will instill greater awareness amongst them about the maritime security concerns.  Further, the present Bill

 Shipping deposed before the Committee that; 
"Sir, on shore leave, I fully agree with you.  There is a resolution of the IMO also on this that human element
 must be taken into consideration.  In India, you would not find where we have denied shore leave to any other
 flagship.  We are quite humane in that regard.  In difficulty or in terms of illness to the seafarers, our ports'
 people immediately help them.  When our seafarers go to other countries, they are not given that shore leave.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
AT A GLANCE
 
REASONS FOR ADOPTION OF ISPS CODE AND PROTECTION OF NATIONAL INTEREST
 
The Committee takes note of the fact that in order to ensure continuity of EXIM trade the Government has entered into
 this agreement.  The Committee agrees with the views of the Government that if the ISPS Code is not implemented the
 Indian ships & port facilities may act as a non-tariff barrier for sea borne commerce. It appears to the Committee that
 current assessment of security threat to shipping sector is basically the consequence of 9/11 attack on U.S.A.  Terrorism
 has a much longer history, however, International Maritime Organization ignored that fact and suddenly woke up to the
 threat of security and agreed unanimously to the evolution of new measures relating to ships and port facilities post
 9/11.  The Committee does not approve the contention of the Secretary that the ISPS Code provides both voluntary as
 well as mandatory provisions.  The Committee feels that security perception is a sovereign function and it is country
 specific. It is not fair, therefore, to confuse between our own security requirements and demands of international trade. 
 Protecting the nation, is a sovereign function of the Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends the
 Department of Shipping to look into the national priorities and interests while implementing the ISPS code.
 (Para 14)
 
ENCROACHING UPON THE LAW MAKING POWERS OF THE PARLIAMENT

The Committee notes that IMO is not the body to deliberate upon the role of Armed forces in relation to their sovereign
 powers in protecting their national security interest and the scope of ISPS Code is confined to only preventive measures

 complex to be handled in the manner they were being handled in the past.  Therefore, an international organisation
 which is primarily engaged in commercial activity through sea route should not have been involved in the business of
 security and some defence related agencies i.e. Navy and Armed forces should have essentially dealt with this kind of a
 code.  The Committee therefore, recommends for creation of a Maritime Security Advisory Committee to report on and
 make recommendations on National Maritime Security matter under the Ministry of Defence so that all commerce
 handled by the Port and Ships would achieve appropriate security coverage.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture,
 having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this Ninetieth Report on
 “Development of Airport Sector with Special Emphasis on new Modern Airports”.
 
2.      The Committee, at its meeting held on the 8
th September 2004, decided to take up this subject for examination and
 accordingly, heard the Secretary and other officers of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the 8 th November and 28 th
 December 2004 and 6th June and 29th June 2005.
 
3.      The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the Ministry of Civil Aviation for placing before the
 Committee the material and information desired in connection with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by
 the Members.
 
4.      The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 7th August 2005.
 
New Delhi;
August 17, 2005
Sarvana 26, 1927 (Saka)
Nilotpal Basu
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
 on Transport, Tourism & Culture.
 
 
R E P O R T
            Airports are the gateways to a nation.  However, in our country, the state of the airports, both domestic and
 international, leaves much to be desired.  The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
 Tourism and Culture discussed the state of airports in the country and was of the opinion that the situation at the
 airports in the country was a cause of concern.  Air travel has registered tremendous growth due to various factors such
 as higher incomes, more corporate activity, low cost airlines, cheaper fares and absence of adequate rail and road
 transport infrastructure.  At a time when the civil aviation sector was taking wings in the country, the airport
 infrastructure in the country had come under tremendous stress.  The infrastructure available at the airports and the
 amenities inside the airports are grossly inadequate and are in urgent need of replacement or modernization. 
 Accordingly, during the last few years, the Government of India had taken some steps for the modernization of airports
 in the country. The steps initiated by the Government for the development/modernization of airport sector in the

 country drew the attention of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
 Culture and accordingly the Committee decided to take up the various aspects of  'Development of Airport Sector with
 special emphasis on new modern airports' for study and examination.
 
2.         The Committee requested the Ministry of Civil Aviation to furnish a detailed background note on the subject for
 consideration of the Committee.  The Committee also held the oral evidence of the representatives of Ministry of Civil
 Aviation and Airports Authority of India on the 8 th November and 28 th December 2004 and 6 th June and 29 th June
 2005.  The Committee also sought replies to the queries on the subject during the oral evidence of the Secretary and
 other representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation during the examination of Demands for Grants 2005-06 of the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The various aspects of the subject discussed by the Committee and the Committee's
 observations thereon have been brought out in the succeeding paragraphs of the report.
MODERNISATION AND RESTRUCTURING OF DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
 
3.         As per their plans for developmental process of airports, the Ministry of Civil Aviation had taken steps to
 modernize and restructure Delhi and Mumbai airports through Joint Venture route.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation
 provided the following brief consisting of the details of various steps the Government took towards restructuring and
 modernization of Delhi and Mumbai airports:-
 
The Cabinet in its meeting held on 11 th September 2003 accorded its approval for the restructuring of Delhi and
 Mumbai airports by adopting the Joint-Venture route.
 
The AAI Amendment Bill introduced in the Parliament (Budget Session 2003) was passed by the Parliament in
 the Monsoon Session of June 2003.  The Amendment Bill authorizes AAI to transfer the operations and
 management of its existing airports by way of long-term lease to private players.  The Bill inter alia provides for
 exclusion of private airports (like BIAL) from the ambit of AAI Act, excepting security and ATC functions,
 which will continue to be discharged by AAI.  The Bill also authorizes AAI to change Advance Development
 Fee (ADF) for the development/upgradation of existing airports and for the setting up of Greenfield airports.  In
 addition, the Bill also seeks to prevent and remove encroachments of airport land.  The provisions of Airports
 Authority of India (Amendment) Act 2003 became effective w.e.f. 1 st July 2004, as per Gazette Notification
 dated 1st July 2004. 
 
The Cabinet constituted an Empowered Group of Ministers (EGOM) to take up decisions on various issues
 connected with the restructuring of Mumbai and Delhi airports. In this connection the Cabinet also decided to
 constitute an Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) to assist EGOM.  The IMG was accordingly constituted by Ministry
 of Civil Aviation during October 2003 under the Chairmanship of Additional Secretary & Financial Advisor of
 MCA and other Members from the MCA, MoF, Department of Disinvestment and Ministry of Law, Justice &
 Company Affairs and AAI.
 
To assist Ministry of Civil Aviation (MOCA)/Airports Authority of India (AAI) in the restructuring process, AAI
 invited technical & financial bids for the appointment of Financial Consultants.  M/s. ABN AMRO were selected
 as Financial Consultants and they started the work in January 2004.
 
After obtaining the approval of EGOM, Registration of Expressions of Interest were solicited from interested
 parties to acquire 74% equity state in the JVC and the complete documentation, in this regard, was uploaded in
 the websites of AAI and MCA on 17.02.2004.  The last date for submission of EOI was 04.06.2004.
 
Subsequent to formation of the new Government, the Hon'ble Minister of State for Civil Aviation discussed in

 to address these critical issues, the last date of submission of Expression of Interest was extended to 20 th July

The Cabinet in its meeting held on 15 th June 2004 reconstituted the EGOM under the Chairmanship of Defence

The reconstituted EGOM has, inter-alia, approved the 49% cap of FDI, restriction of equity participation by

 modernization process of Delhi and Mumbai airports so that the development and maintenance of the other

 insistence of the Airports Authority of India to provide land free of cost to Airports Authority of India.  In response,
 Ministry of Civil Aviation pointed out that there is a proposal to extend the runway from 7500 ft. to 9000 ft. and for
 which additional land measuring about 102 acres has been requisitioned to State Government.  State Government has
 been requested to provide the land free of cost and free from encumbrances.  Deputy Commissioner, Gaya has

 on certain occasions purchased land for developmental works, such as extension of runway, extension of car parking
 etc. at other airports.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should consider purchasing of
 land required for extension of runway at Gaya airport in similar pattern as they have done in many other cases.

Report
            India is one of the oldest civilizations in the world and its historical heritage and cultural glory has been the
 subject of interest of the entire humanity.  In a country like India, endowed with both tangible and intangible heritage of
 an immense cultural and artistic value, which also has a multi-religious cultural fabric, archaeology assumes a position
 of crucial importance.
2.         Keeping in view the importance of archaeology, the Archaeological Survey of India was established in the year
 1861 with the primary object of surveying and recording the archaeological monuments in India.  It has a long colonial
 history and its mandate has evolved at a very slow pace spread over centuries.  For the first time in the year 1880, an
 organized attempt was made to preserve the monuments from decay by appointing Mr. H.H. Cole as a curator of
 monuments, which also coincided, with the recognition of the fact that the preservation of the monument was the
 permanent responsibility of the State.  In 1899, the Archaeological Survey of India was administratively divided into
 five circles for the preservation, conservation, archaeological exploration and excavation on a permanent basis and with
 well defined polices.  With the advent of Lord Curzon as Viceroy, the Archaeological Survey of India was placed on a
 formal footing during the first decade of the 20
th century.  He appointed Mr. John Marshal as the Director General of
 Archaeological Survey of India, who undertook great excavation at Taxila, Sanchi, Sarnath etc. The concept of
 archaeological conservation of ancient monuments was added during the time of John Marshall.  Hundreds of
 monuments/sites were declared as protected monuments under the purview of the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act
 1904.  In 1944, Dr. R.E.M. Wheeler was appointed Director General of Archaeological Survey of India.  During his
 tenure he incorporated modern methods for carrying archaeological excavations and trained the staff of the Survey in
 excavations at Taxila, Arikamedu and Harappa.  Having indepth understanding and involvement he revolutionized the
 concept of archaeological excavation by introducing importance of stratigraphy.  Wheeler also started Horticulture
 Branch in Archaeological Survey of India to develop suitable gardens to create pollution free ambiance around
 monuments.  Thus, prior to independence a sound foundation was laid for the Archaeological Survey of India. 
CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS IN THE POST INDEPENDENCE PERIOD:
3.         With the promulgation of the Constitution of India from 26
th January 1950, ‘archaeology’ has been made a
 Concurrent subject under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, which reads :
List I (Union List), item 67: ancient and historical monuments and records, and archaeological sites and remains
 declared by or under law by Parliament to be of national importance.
List II (State List), item 12: libraries, museums and other similar institutions controlled or financed by the State; ancient
 and historical monuments and records other than those declared by or under law made by Parliament to be of national
 importance.
List III (Concurrent List), item 40: archaeological sites and remains other than those declared by or under law made by

4.         In fulfillment of the provisions of the Constitution, Parliament passed the “Ancient and Historical Monuments
 and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act” in 1951 by which all the monuments previously protected under the
 Ancient Monuments Preservation Act 1904 were re-declared to be of national importance.  In 1953, after the merger of
 the princely states with the rest of India, the Archaeological Survey of India took the additional responsibility of upkeep
 of the monuments in princely states.
5.         Currently, the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 and Rules, 1959 and the
 Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972 and Rules, 1973 are operational and empowers the Archaeological Survey of
 India in its functioning.  
PRESENT MANDATE OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
6.         The Archaeological Survey of India is the premier organization so far as the archaeological research, study,
 excavation of archaeological sites, conservation/preservation of centrally protected monuments, maintenance of site
 museums and overall regulation of antiquities and art objects are concerned. As an apex body in the field of
 archaeology, the functions of Archaeological Survey of India are very broad and varied which may be classified as
 under :-
Conservation and preservation of monuments/sites and remains;
Archaeological explorations and excavations;
Preservation of monuments and antiquarian remains;
Architectural survey of monuments;
Epigraphical and numismatic studies;
Setting up of the Site Museums;
Training in archaeology;
Archaeologial publications;
Archaeological expeditions abroad;
Implementation of Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972; and
Horticulture operation around ancient monuments and sites.
7.         Since the functions of Archaeological Survey of India are very broad and varied and India is endowed with
 tremendous historical and cultural heritage, the Committee decided to study the functioning of Archaeological Survey
 of India.  In order to get wider views on the subject, the Committee decided to elicit the views of some independent
 experts in the field of archaeology.  Accordingly, the Committee heard the views of Shri S.S. Biswas, former Director
 General, National Museum and Shri Jagatpati Joshi, former Director General, Archaeological Survey of India on the
 17
th September and 1st October 2004 respectively.   On the basis of the information provided by these two independent
 experts and other documents provided to the Committee by the Ministry of Culture, the Committee took the oral
 evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Culture and the representatives of Archaeological Survey of India on the 29
th
 November and 27th December 2004 and the 20th June 2005 to get an indepth insight into the functioning of
 Archaeological Survey of India.

 monuments as of national importance.  All the monuments/sites protected by the Archaeological Survey of India are
 being conserved/preserved on need based requirement.  As regards classification of monuments into different
 categories, the ASI has drawn long term programme to protect all 3663 monuments/sites which are of historical,
 architectural and aesthetic value.  Classification of monuments is an ongoing process and depends upon the

 urgency for structural conservation, preservation and chemical preservation including environmental development and

ORGANISATIONAL SET UP AND THE POST OF DIRECTOR GENERAL OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL
 SURVEY OF INDIA
10.       At present the Archaeological Survey of India is functioning as an attached office under the Ministry of Culture,
 which is headed by the Union Minister for Culture.  The Ministry of Culture has a Secretary level officer, who looks
 after various attached and subordinate office in the Ministry.  Being an attached office, the Archaeological Survey of
 India has its own head designated as Director General.  The Director General, in turn, is assisted by an Additional
 Director General, a Joint Director General and a group of Directors.  At present there are 10 Directors assisting the
 Director General in performing duties.  For administrative convenience and research purposes, the Archaeological
 Survey of India  is divided into 21 Circles headed by a Superintending Archaeologist, who is further assisted by Deputy
 Superintending Archaeologist., Deputy S.A.E., A.S.A., A.S.A.E., Ass & C.As.  There are 6 Excavation Branches, on
 Prehistory Branch, one Building Survey Project, two Temple Survey Projects, two Epigraphy Branches and one
 Science Branch functioning in the Archaeological Survey of India on different field and research project.
11.       The Archaeological Survey of India is headed by a Director General.  Some of the important functions and
 responsibilities of the Director General, Archaeological Survey of India are as under:
To function as the head of the Archaeological Survey of India which is primarily engaged on (a) basic research in
 various disciplines of archaeology, including (i)archaeological excavations and explorations (ii) protection of
 monuments/sites of national importance, their proper maintenance and upkeep and carrying of archaeological
 conservation as well as chemical preservation of these monuments/sites; prevention of vandalism/encroachment at
 these monuments/sites, setting up and maintenance of site, museums, environmental development of monuments/sites;
 (iii) bringing out of archaeological publications (iv) epigraphical research (v) operation of antiquarian law viz. Ancient
 Monuments and Archaeological sites and Remains Act-1958 and Rules 1959; as well as Antiquities & Art Treasures
 Act, 1972 and Rules 1976; (vi) bringing out of archaeological publications (vii) maintenance and upkeep of
 archaeological libraries.
Laying down of archaeological policy in the country, and to issue licences for conducting archaeological excavations by
 various states/research Institution and generally guide archaeological activities in the country.
12.       The Committee noted that the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India was being filled up by
 the Government from Indian Administrative Service (IAS) for a fairly long period.  During its interaction with one
 independent expert on the functioning of Archaeological Survey of India, the Committee was informed that the
 Government had issued a notification in May 2002, according to which  the Director General, Archaeological Survey of
 India should have a Master’s Degree in Indian History/Archaeology/allied subjects and should have eighteen years of
 administrative experience with, at least, five years in the field of archaeology. The Committee noted that the
 notification had not been implemented, and since the last 12 years, the Director General deputed to the Archaeological
 Survey of India had no basic qualification or knowledge in archaeology.
13.       The same independent expert while submitting his views before the Committee on the functioning of
 Archaeological Survey of India also emphasized that the practice of filling up the post of Director General,
 Archaeological Survey of India from Indian Administrative Service on deputation basis had adversely affected the
 functioning of Archaeological Survey of India and stated as under:
“This is relating to the appointment of all the scientific officers, specially the head of the department i.e. the Director
 General who has been coming on deputation basis from the Ministry.  This aspect is very much related to the
 functioning of the ASI.  If the bureaucrats who have little knowledge of it, are manning the scientific department or
 even the academic department, I need not tell you about the results.  If you look at the recruitment rules, you will notice
 this anomaly.  I will give you an example.  Why I am saying this is that these are very important because unless the
 appropriate leader is there, no function can be carried out properly.”
14.       In the backdrop of above information, the Committee enquired from the Ministry of Culture whether there was
 any anomaly in recruitment rules of Archaeological Survey of India with regard to the appointment of Director General

15.       The Committee further enquired from the Ministry of Culture regarding the rationale to fill the post of Director
 General and other scientists, professionals and experts posts in Archaeological Survey of India with bureaucrats from
 outside and whether the recruitment of bureaucrats would not hamper developing Archaeological Survey of India as a
 spearhead of scientific discipline in the country.  In response, the Ministry of Culture in their written reply stated that
 the Archaeological Survey of India is a multidisciplinary agency consisting of archaeologists, scientists, historians,

 will not hamper the development of Archaeological Survey of India as a scientific organisation.  It was also mentioned
 that there is no objective assessment which has established that appointment of officers from outside the Archaeological
 Survey of India has hampered the functioning of Archaeological Survey of India in any way.
16.       The Committee is not in agreement with the argument put- forth by the Ministry of Culture that the appointment
 of generalist administrator as Director General will not hamper the development of Archaeological Survey of India as a
 scientific organisation.  TheCommittee is shocked to note that even after the Gazette Notification of May 2002, the
 Government has not been able to fill up the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India as per the
 requirements of the notification and has been merely filling up the post from Indian Administrative Service on
 deputation basis.  The Committee is constrained to observe that the Government preferred to fill up the highest post of
 an apex institution requiring very high standards of technical qualification with a generalist administrator.  The
 Committee is of the view that a person who has no basic qualification or knowledge of archaeology cannot handle the
 apex responsibility of a Scientific Institution like Archaeological Survey of India.  Unless the leader of the
 Archaeological Survey of India is having the professional expertise, it is very difficult to give a lead.  This has also
 dampened the spirits of the senior officers in the feeder grade of the organization who may never get the opportunities
 to serve as senior most officer of their parent organization.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that steps should be
 taken to fill up the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India as per the requirements of the Notification
 of May 2002, at the earliest.
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA AS A SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL DEPARTMENT
17.       During its interaction with another independent expert on the functioning of Archaeological Survey of India, it
 was brought to the notice of the Committee that the Archaeological Survey of India was declared as a Science and
 Technological Institution w.e.f. 1
st May 1989 by a Gazette Notification.  However, no action was taken to implement
 the notification.  Attention of the Committee was also drawn towards the Mirdha Committee Report submitted in the
 year 1984 in this context and the recommendations made therein.  The second recommendation of the Report stated:-
“The Archaeological Survey of India should not be considered merely an administrative organization, but in view of its
 highly specialized functions, should be accorded the status of a scientific and technical institution, enjoying autonomy
 in its functioning, like other comparable institutions under the Government.”
18.       The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Culture as to when the Archaeological Survey of India was
 declared a scientific and technical Department and whether the notification had been implemented or not.  In response,
 the Committee was informed by Ministry of Culture that, on the basis of the recommendations made by a group set-up
 by the Department of Science and Technology, the Archaeological Survey of India was declared as a Scientific and
 Technological Department vide Notification No.A.36016/2/89-Estt. dated 27.10.1989 issued by Department of Culture. 
 This Notification was operative w.e.f. 1.5.1989.  However, inspite of this, the Archaeological Survey of India continued
 to function as an attached office of the Ministry of Culture. The nature of functions and activities of Archaeological
 Survey of India were of such nature that it could not be so far made into a wholly scientific and technical institution. 
 However, efforts have been made to take advantage of technical and scientific expertise in various disciplines of
 archaeology. 
19.       The Committee further enquired from the Ministry of Culture regarding the action taken by the Ministry of
 Culture to develop Archaeological Survey of India into a scientific and technical department after the issue of the
 notification in this regard.  In response, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Culture that as a follow-up
 action to the declaration of Archaeological Survey of India as Science & Technology Department, a proposal for the
 introduction of the benefits of the Flexible Complementing Scheme to the technical officers of the Archaeological
