 notification in this regard no concrete action was taken by Ministry of Culture and Archaeological Survey of India for
 developing Archaeological Survey of India as a Scientific and Technical Department, which amply indicates the
 administrative apathy towards the whole issue.  The Committee regrets that no internal exercise was undertaken by
 Ministry of Culture and Archaeological Survey of India during the last fifteen years for availing the benefits and
 privileges which could be extended to the Archaeological Survey of India as a Science and Technology department. 
 The Committee observes that there has been deviation in the working of Archaeological Survey of India and that it has
 failed in terms of developing Archaeological Survey of India not merely as an administrative body but also as a
 spearhead for consolidating the scientific discipline of archaeology in the country.  The Committee is of the view that
 the Archaeological Survey of India needs to reinvent itself, not merely as an administrative wing of the Government,
 but as an agency for protecting and safeguarding our national heritage, which involves a lot of scientific and technical
 work.  Unless the Archaeological Survey of India converts itself fully into a scientific and technical organization, the
 basic role and function of the organisation will be defeated.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture
 and Archaeological Survey of India should, without any further loss of time, take necessary follow-up action on the
 recommendations of the Committee chaired by Director General, Archaeological Survey of India so as to avail the
 benefits which accrue to a Science and Technology department.  The Committee also recommends that, if required, the
 Ministry of Culture should also take necessary legislative action to make Archaeological Survey of India Science and
 Technology department in the true sense.
SARASVATI PROJECT
25.       The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, govern excavations in India.  The
 Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India grants licenses to various excavation agencies, both government
 and autonomous, for conducting excavations on the recommendations of the standing Committee of the Central
 Advisory Board of Archaeology (CABA).  The criteria for selecting a site for excavation are as under:
bridging of missing gaps(s) in the cultural sequence of Indian archaeology,
throwing more light on lesser known cultures.
Salvage archaeology in the event of a site being submerged by a dam or being destroyed or damaged due to absolutely
 necessary development works, natural calamities.
26.       The Committee desired to know the details relating to the Sarasvati Heritage Project.  In response the Committee
 was apprised by the Ministry of Culture that the Sarasvati project aimed at conducting a multidisciplinary study of
 River Sarasvati and its basin stretching in India from the Sivaliks to the Arbian Sea, falling in the Indian states of
 Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat and formulating and implementing integrated development programmes in the area by
 creating 15 hub sites as centers of culture, tourism and good civic life.   For providing a proper orientation as well as
 implementation of the Project, the Government of India through its gazette notification S.O. 1329 (E), dated 18
th
 December 2002, New Delhi, constituted a 13 member committee namely, the Advisory Committee, for the
 Multidisciplinary Study of River Sarasvati (ACMS), under the chairmanship of the then Minister of Tourism and
 Culture.
27.       During the oral evidence of the representatives of Ministry of Cultural and Archaeological Survey of India held
 on the 27
th December 2004 the Committee enquired about the origin of the Sarasvati Heritage Project.  In response, the
 Director General, Archaeological Survey of India informed the Committee that “the same report was prepared in
 September 2003 on the basis of the recommendations of a Committee, which was formed in December 2002, with the
 Tourism Minister as the Chairman besides eight other Members who were experts in various fields and one Joint
 Director of Archaeological Survey of India as the Member-Secretary or Convenor of the Committee.” The Committee
 then desired to know about the historical and the scientific basis on which the report was prepared. In response, the
 Ministry informed the Committee   that there was a report of the Remote Sensing Agency in this regard which
 suggested that there was a channel.  But the name Sarasvati was not indicated.

to accomplish environmental upgradation of the sites;
realize all these objectives in all integrated, concerted and planned manner under a special drive during a period of three
 years, to begin with.
29.       However, in the same reply the Ministry also stated that prior to the preparation of the project report, the

 added that they have not framed any special guidelines for implementation of this project.
30.       The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Culture about the procedure followed by the Archaeological
 Survey of India while selecting a site for excavation and whether they consulted any experts and eminent academicians
 in the country before finalizing this project.  The Ministry replied that the archaeological excavations in the country are
 approved by the Standing Committee of the Central Advisory Board on Archaeology (CABA) based on the requests for
 permitting excavations from Universities/Research Organisations.  In light of the above replies submitted by Ministry
 of Culture, the Committee desired to know whether the Sarasvati Heritage Project was recommended by any academic
 body/university which clubbed this omnibus project under the river SarasvatiProject.  The Committee also desired to
 know whether any proper scientific and technical appraisal for defining Saraswati had been taken or not.  In response,
 the Ministry of Culture categorically informed the Committee that "no academic body or university has recommended
 the project".  The Committee was also informed that in the past, scientific surveys were conducted in the dry bed of
 River Ghaggar, identified as River Sarasvati by some geoscientists.  There were also remote sensing studies which have
 established palaeochannels, and the results of such studies have been published in journals like Journal of Arid
 Environments, Journal of Geological Society of India, Man and Environment, South Asian Archaeology, Proceedings
 of the Indian Academy of Science (Earth and Planetary Sciences), etc.”
31.       The Committee further enquired that whether any scientific or technical study had ledto the project or certain
 mythological sources had been used to determine its name. The Committee also enquired as to how a scientific
 department like Archaeological Survey of India proceeded in this matter, and from where did they get the name of the
 river Sarasvati.  To these queries, the Ministry replied that explorations and excavations in parts of Haryana and
 Rajasthan on the dry bed of River Ghaggar and River Chautang (River Drisadvati) havebrought to light several
 settlements ranging from the early Harappan times to the modern ones.  Besides, surveys carried out by various
 universities and research institutions like Kurukshetra University, Deccan College, etc. also brought to light a large
 number of sites.  There were also independent studies by scientists who had made use of the aerial photographs and
 satellite imageries to delineate the palaeo-drainage course of a river.  These studies were published in journals like Man
 and Environment, Geological Society of India Memoirs, etc.  These scientific and archaeological studies had led to the
 formulation of the project and naming it as Sarasvati Heritage Project.
32.       After going through the replies furnished by the Ministry of Culture, the Committee is of the firm view that
 Sarasvati Heritage Project did not conform to the criterion fixed for excavation of archaeological sites since no
 academic body or university had recommended the project.  The Committee also notes that there is an element of
 contradiction in the replies submitted to the Committee by the Department of Culture.  On the one hand, the Ministry of
 Culture has stated that the former Minister of Tourism and Culture was not the Chairman of the Sarasvati Heritage
 Project, while, on the other hand, the Ministry has stated that prior to the preparation of the project report, the

CONSERVATION/PRESERVATION OF MONUMENTS AND REGISTRATION OF ANTIQUITIES
54.       The Committee also enquired about the procedure adopted for conservation/preservation of the monuments.  The
 Committee was informed that whenever an ancient structure or an archaeological site/remain is considered be of
 national importance, a proposal to this effect is initiated by the circle office and sent to the Director General,
 Archaeological Survey of India along with its historical, archaeological and architectural importance.  On receipt of the
 approval of the Director General, Archaeological Survey of India, the proposal is forwarded to the State Government
 with detailed drawings for the counter signature of the Deputy Commissioner/Commissioner concerned.  On receipt of
 the revenue data duly counter signed, the Central Government issues a notification of its intentions to declare the
 monument as of national importance with a two months notice.  On the expiry of notice period and after considering the
 objections, if any, a final Gazette notification is issued for declaring the said monument as a monument of national
 importance.
55.       The State Governments are consulted if the proposed monument is State protected and is proposed to be taken
 over by the Archaeological Survey of India.  In all other cases, State Governments are involved only to the extent of
 preparation of relevant revenue papers required for the notification or subsequently, if land or building compensation is
 involved.
56.       The Committee was further informed that the basic guidelines for conservation have been framed with an
 objective to prolong the life of monuments without the loss of artistic and historical values.  It is important for
 archaeological values to preserve the original fabric of the monument to the extent possible.  Archaeological Survey of
 India follows a Conservation Manual which contains detailed guidelines for execution of conservation works.  The
 conservation and preservation of monuments aim at :
its preservation without disfigurement or alteration of its character;
its maintenance in a proper and attractive condition;
the complete examination of its remains and documentary evidence concerning it; and
 
the preparation of monographs, guide books and reports so that its historical and artistic interest may be perpetuated.
57.       Apart from this the monuments which had garden around them as part of their original design are taken up for
 restoration and maintenance and wherever it was not part of original layout/feature, beautification through landscaping
 is also undertaken.  However, it has been decided to compile a comprehensive conservation manual during the 10
th Five
 Year Plan period incorporating extant guidelines of Archaeological Survey of India and relevant features of
 internationally acceptable conservation guidelines and norms.
58.       The Committee is of the view that beautification and development of archaeological sites no doubt adds to the
 ambience of these sites.  However, the Committee recommends that while taking up work, the focus should be on

 felt that a single Mission structure for both the Missions i.e. for Built Heritage and Antiquities could undertake the

 proposal has been recast into a single Mission proposal.  By merging them together, the financial outlay required for
 undertaking both the Missions has been greatly reduced and the goals are also justified.”

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
MONUMMENTS/SITES UNDER PROTECTION OF ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee notes that the ASI has drawn long-term programme to protect all 3663 monuments/sites of national

91stReport of Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/91streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:19]
 importance out of which 3537 monuments/sites are unticketed.  These monuments have also been classified into three
 categories viz. Group A, B and C for convenience.    The Committee is however aware that there are many
 sites/monuments under the protection/maintenance of Archaeological Survey of India which are located in interior
 areas of various States but are lying unattended. Therefore, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Culture should
 equally treat the revenue earning and not-earning sites and efforts should be made for integrated infrastructure
 development and conservation/ preservation of all monuments/sites with encompassing facilities for tourists, so as to
 give a major fillip to cultural tourism in the country as well as attracting overseas visitors.                               
ORGANISATIONAL SET UP AND THE POST OF DIRECTOR GENERAL OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL
 SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee is not in agreement with the argument put- forth by the Ministry of Culture that the appointment of
 generalist administrator as Director General will not hamper the development of Archaeological Survey of India as a
 scientific organisation.  The Committee is shocked to note that even after the Gazette Notification of May 2002, the
 Government has not been able to fill up the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India as per the
 requirements of the notification and has been merely filling up the post from Indian Administrative Service on
 deputation basis.  The Committee is constrained to observe that the Government preferred to fill up the highest post of
 an apex institution requiring very high standards of technical qualification with a generalist administrator.  The
 Committee is of the view that a person who has no basic qualification or knowledge of archaeology cannot handle the
 apex responsibility of a Scientific Institution like Archaeological Survey of India.  Unless the leader of the
 Archaeological Survey of India is having the professional expertise, it is very difficult to give a lead.  This has also
 dampened the spirits of the senior officers in the feeder grade of the organization who may never get the opportunities
 to serve as senior most officer of their parent organization.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that steps should be
 taken to fill up the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India as per the requirements of the Notification
 of May 2002, at the earliest.
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA AS A SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL DEPARTMENT
The Committee is constrained to note that even after a lapse of fifteen years from the date of issue of the notification in
 this regard no concrete action was taken by Ministry of Culture and Archaeological Survey of India for developing
 Archaeological Survey of India as a Scientific and Technical Department, which amply indicates the administrative
 apathy towards the whole issue.  The Committee regrets that no internal exercise was undertaken by Ministry of
 Culture and Archaeological Survey of India during the last fifteen years for availing the benefits and privileges which
 could be extended to the Archaeological Survey of India as a Science and Technology department.  The Committee
 observes that there has been deviation in the working of Archaeological Survey of India and that it has failed in terms
 of developing Archaeological Survey of India not merely as an administrative body but also as a spearhead for
 consolidating the scientific discipline of archaeology in the country.  The Committee is of the view that the
 Archaeological Survey of India needs to reinvent itself, not merely as an administrative wing of the Government, but as
 an agency for protecting and safeguarding our national heritage, which involves a lot of scientific and technical work. 
 Unless the Archaeological Survey of India converts itself fully into a scientific and technical organization, the basic
 role and function of the organisation will be defeated.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture and
 Archaeological Survey of India should, without any further loss of time, take necessary follow-up action on the
 recommendations of the Committee chaired by Director General, Archaeological Survey of India so as to avail the
 benefits which accrue to a Science and Technology department.  The Committee also recommends that, if required, the
 Ministry of Culture should also take necessary legislative action to make Archaeological Survey of India Science and
 Technology department in the true sense.                                          
SARASVATI PROJECT
After going through the replies furnished by the Ministry of Culture, the Committee is of the firm view that Sarasvati
 Heritage Project did not conform to the criterion fixed for excavation of archaeological sites since no academic body or
 university had recommended the project.  The Committee also notes that there is an element of contradiction in the
 replies submitted to the Committee by the Department of Culture.  On the one hand, the Ministry of Culture has stated
 that the former Minister of Tourism and Culture was not the Chairman of the Sarasvati Heritage Project, while, on the
 other hand, the Ministry has stated that prior to the preparation of the project report, the Government had constituted an
 Advisory Committee with the then Minister of Tourism and Culture as Chairman and that this Committee had
 recommended the Saraswati Heritage Project.  The Committee further notes that the Ministry is not clear as to which
 research agency/scientific survey actually pointed out that the dry beds of River Ghaggar and River Chautang (River
 Drisadvati) are the bed of River Sarasvati.  The Committee understands that existence of River Sarasvati is purely a
 mythological one and a scientific institution like Archaeological Survey of India has not correctly proceeded in the

91stReport of Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/91streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:19]
 matter.   The Committee regrets to note that a major project to the tune of Rs.36.02 crores was prepared which was,
 however, subsequently reduced to Rs.4.98 crores just to excavate a mythological river whereas, several other
 monuments/heritage sites of national importance are languishing in neglect due to acute shortage of funds. The
 Committee recommends that Archaeological Survey of India should strictly adhere to the criterion fixed for selection of
 excavation of sites.  Further, decisions for excavations should be made on the basis of proper scientific and technical
 appraisal and no extraneous factors should go into the decision making.  The Committee also recommends that before
 selecting a site for excavation, the Archaeological Survey of India should very carefully examine the potential of the
 site so that funds earmarked for the same do not go waste. The Committee would like to advise the Archaeological
 Survey of India that it should prevent itself from taking up exercises without a scientific basis which have all
 potentiality for subjective interpretation of historical facts thereby, leading to controversies.          
VACANCIES AND STAFF STRENGTH IN ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee notes with concern that there are large-scale vacancies in various categories in the ASI, which has been
 hampering smooth and effective functioning of the Archaeological Survey of India.  The Committee also notes that the
 Government had been rather lax and inactive in completing the formalities for filling up many of the vacancies, as can
 be seen from the status furnished by the Archaeological Survey of India in respect of these vacancies.  The Committee
 recommends that the Ministry of Culture should take immediate steps to fill up the vacancies in the Archaeological
 Survey of India so that the works being undertaken by the Archaeological Survey of India do not suffer.  The
 Committee also notes that there is an acute shortage of manpower for technical posts for which the Archaeological
 Survey of India had made proposals to create additional posts.  The Committee recommends that the Government
 should favourably consider the proposals submitted by the Archaeological Survey of India for creation of technical
 posts so that the Archaeological Survey of India is efficiently and smoothly able to carry out the voluminous work
 entrusted to it.                     
NON-WRITING/PUBLICATION OF EXCAVATION REPORTS
The Committee is of the view that if excavation reports are not written, then all the taxpayers’ money spent on them
 goes waste.  Also, in absence of timely publication of excavation reports, the achievements of Archaeological Survey of
 India largely remain unnoticed by the public.  The Committee is extremely dissatisfied to observe that despite its
 repeated recommendations, the position in respect of writing of excavation reports has not improved much.  However,
 the Committee is hopeful that the steps now initiated by Archaeological Survey of India for clearing the backlog in
 respect of writing excavation reports would yield some positive results.  The Committee recommends that the
 Archaeological Survey of India should enforce a fixed time frame for writing excavation reports after the excavation
 work has been completed, so that the public at large is not deprived of the vital right to information.  The Committee
 also recommends that the ASI should ensure that officials engaged in a particular excavation work are not transferred
 till such time that they complete the excavations and submit their reports.
ENCROACHMENT AND SECURITY OF MONUMENTS/SITES
The Committee is concerned about the illegal encroachment of monuments/archaeological sites under the protection of
 Archaeological Survey of India.  In this context, the Committee would like to reiterate the recommendation made in its
 85
th Report on Demands for Grants 2005-06 of Ministry of Culture which is as under:
"The Committee expresses its anxiety over the incidents of encroachment upon the land of Centrally Protected
 Monuments.  The Committee is more concerned about the inability of Archeological Survey of India to get back the
 land from encroachers.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that a complete assessment should be made
 regarding encroachment of monuments/sites under the protection of Archaeological Survey of India all over the
 country.  Prompt action ought be taken against the encroachers with the help of State Governments/Local
 Administrations and the matter should be pursued at the highest level.  The Committee also recommends that adequate
 budgetary provisions should be made for security arrangements and protection of monuments, as this is the most crucial
 aspect of preserving our cultural heritage and wherever possible modern gadgets like, electronic surveillance cameras
 should be installed in the monuments.  The Committee feels that security is a sovereign function.  Hence, it is the
 responsibility of Central Government to get the monuments and other important assets protected.  In view of this, the
 Committee is of the opinion that the Union Home Ministry should pay the bills towards the expenses incurred for
 paying the Central Security Agencies under this head.  Accordingly, the Ministry of Culture should pursue the matter at
 the highest level." 
CONSERVATION/PRESERVATION OF MONUMENTS AND REGISTRATION OF ANTIQUITIES
The Committee is of the view that beautification and development of archaeological sites no doubt adds to the ambience
 of these sites.  However, the Committee recommends that while taking up work, the focus should be on actual

The Committee notes the response of the Archaeological Survey of India to the observations made by the Committee in
 its 85

 staff and expertise, Archaeological Survey of India would be able to successfully execute the National Mission for
 Antiquities and Built Heritage and the laudable goals of the Mission would be achieved within the fixed time frame.
The Committee observes that the Ministry of Culture has decided to involve private agencies in handling the National

 deal so that the expenditure to be incurred on the National Mission of Antiquities is spent in the best interest of the
 nation and the valuable information about Indian Antiquities and Monuments are not handed over to foreign hands. 
 The Committee further recommends that strict criteria should be fixed to determine expertise and professionalism in

The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the observations/ recommendations as
 contained in its Eighty-fourth Report on Demands for Grants (2005-2006) (Demand No. 86) of Department of Road

th April, 2005.
 
 2.         Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on 2
nd September, 2005 in respect of all the
 observations/recommendations contained in the Report, which have been categorised as follows: -

4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each item of Action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Department.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Eighty-fourth
 Report, action taken thereon by the Government, and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of
 action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
 
ANALYSIS OF THE TENTH PLAN PROVISIONS AND ANNUAL                                    PLAN 2005-06
(Recommendation at Para 20) 
 
5.         The Committee regrets to note that BE Plan Provision of Rs.7912 crore of Department of Road Transport and
 Highways was brought down to Rs.6766 crore on account of slow implementation of Externally Aided Projects by
 NHAI and the Department.  Further, there was delay in finalization of the loans and obtaining approvals for the
 procurement for the externally aided component of the Corridor Project of NHDP (Phase-II) being financed by the
 Asian Development Bank (ADB).  Also, there was delay in award of works to the contractors and consultants for
 development of NH-34 in West Bengal.  These instances clearly bring out that on the one hand, the Department of
 Road Transport and Highways emphasizes that funds for development and maintenance of National Highways are
 inadequate while, on the other hand, the Department is not able to utilise the higher allocation made to it at BE stage.  
 The Department has failed to make optimal utilization of the funds at its disposal. The reasons for shortfall mentioned
 are delay in land acquisition, poor performance of the contractors, law and order problem etc. are very general in nature
 and are repeated every year. As a result of these, the budgetary allocations of the Department were reduced at RE
 stage.  The Committee is of the view that there is a lack of monitoring system in the Department of Road Transport and
 Highways.  The lack of a proper monitoring system in the Department is exemplified by the delay and non-completion
 of the construction of flyover at Murthal in Haryana and the failure of the Department of Road Transport and Highways
 in verifying the credentials of the contractors who had submitted forged bank guarantees.  The Committee observes that
 the budget allocations of the Department of Road Transport and Highways have been substantially increased during
 2005-06. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should devise
 strategies, whereby they are able to fully utilize the funds at their disposal.  They should also evolve some mechanism
 to identify bottlenecks causing delays and work towards resolving all such hindrances in coordination with all the
 concerned agencies.  This would also help them to avoid time overrun and consequential cost overrun of the projects to
 be executed by them.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
 
6.         The main reason for non-utilization of the approved funds of 2004-05 was non-execution of loan agreements
 with Asian Development Bank (ADB) and World Bank for Projects under NHDP-Phase-II due to procedural delay like
 clearance from ADB / World Bank, high tender rates, delay in signing loan agreement, etc.  However, most of the
 problems have now been resolved. 
 
7.         Out of total length of 6736 kms under NHDP Phase-II, projects consisting of 814 km. are already under
 implementation and the projects for the length of 5722 kms are scheduled for award by Dec., 2005 in phased manner. 
 The projects for the balance 200 kms. shall be awarded in the next financial year 2006-07.  With the award of these
 projects, substantial expenditure is expected to be incurred on their implementation. 
 
8.         Major initiatives and steps to remove constraints and bottlenecks in the implementation of North-South and East-
West Corridor have been undertaken to expedite the implementation of projects and making improvement in the internal

 process on the basis of lessons learnt during the implementation of NHDP Phase-I.  Some of the important initiatives
 and improvements carried out are as under:
(i)                     Process for acquisition of land is being simplified.  The Allocation of Business Rules is proposed to be
 amended in this regard.
(ii)        State Governments have appointed senior officers as Nodal Officers for resolving the problems of pre-
construction activities. Regular follow-up meetings are being held with the officers of State Governments and with

(iv)       One officer of the Railways has been posted at NHAI to co-ordinate all activities relating to approvals on ROBs
 from the Railways.

 Seventeen contractors have been declared as non-performing and banned from further NHAI works, till their
 performance improves.
(vi)       The existing monitoring system is being improved by setting up Wide Area Network (WAN) which will enable

(vii)      A Committee of Secretaries has been constituted to address inter-ministerial and Centre - State issues regarding

FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
9.         The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP)
(Recommendation at Para 29) 
 
10.       The Committee notes that the target date of completion of the Golden Quadrilateral has been revised twice i.e.
 from December 2003 to December 2004 and now up to December 2005.  The Committee had discussed this issue in its
 82
nd Report on Demands for Grants 2004-05 of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and recommended that
 the Government should take all necessary steps to make sure that the works proposed to be completed by December
 2004 are completed within that period.  However, the Committee notes that the progress of four-laning on the Golden
 Quadrilateral project as on December 2004 was only 74%.  Thus, the steps taken by Department of Road Transport and
 Highways for timely completion of the project had not been adequate.  The Committee, therefore, would like to
 reiterate its earlier recommendation made in its 82
nd Report that the Government should take all necessary steps and
 evolve a monitoring mechanism to ensure quality of construction, making officials accountable for failure, transparency
 in implementation process, penalizing defaulting contractors etc. so that the remaining part of the project is completed
 by December 2005 and the need to further revise the target date of completion does not arise.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
 
11.       As on 31.7.2005, 84% of the length of Golden Quadrilateral has been completed.  It is expected that due to
 monitoring and clearance of bottlenecks at the level of Committee of Secretaries (CoS), the Golden Quadrilateral
 Project will be completed substantially (92%) by December 2005 except for re-awarded contracts and contracts which
 are having the completion date after December 2005. 
 
12.       Standardized documents and third-party audits are some measures taken to ensure quality of work.  Apart from
 Engineers India Ltd and Central Road Research Institute, the Highway Research Station, Chennai, and Gujarat
 Engineering Research Institute, Vadodara are being proposed to be engaged in to conduct quality audits. 
 
13.       Major initiatives and steps taken to remove constraints/bottlenecks in the implementation of National Highway
 Projects to expedite implementation of projects have been enumerated in reply to Para 20.

FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
14.       The Committee notes the reply of the Department and desires that there would be continuous efforts in the
 forthcoming phases of NHDP so that there is no time and cost over-run.
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS NOT COVERED UNDER NHDP:
(Recommendation at Para 35) 
 
15.       The Committee notes that in response to its recommendation for an equitable development of non-NHDP
 National Highways, the Department of Road Transport and Highways has formulated projects for development of such
 highways.  The Committee recommends that the Government should give its approval for the Accelerated North-East
 Road Development Project and NHDP Phase IV at the earliest.  Also the projects under NHDP Phase III should be
 taken up at the earliest so that the deadlines set for these projects are met.  The Committee is of the view that
 Department of Road Transport and Highways has now gained sufficient experience during the implementation of
 Golden Quadrilateral.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Department of Road Transport and Highways
 should adopt a proactive approach and take care that the hindrances resulting in delay in timely completion of such
 projects do not recur.  Action should be taken in advance to ensure that such bottlenecks do not impede the timely
 implementation of the projects and the deadlines set for the project are met unlike the Golden Quadrilateral where the
 target date of completion has gone up by two years so far.  
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
 
16.       Stretches of National Highways, state roads and roads of strategic importance being included under the Special
 Accelerated Road Development Programme (SARDP) have been identified.  Approval of the scheme is in advance
 stage.  Proposal for improvement to two lane National Highways, standard with paved shoulders under NHDP Phase IV
 has been finalized and action has been initiated for taking approval of the Government.
 
17.       Under NHDP Phase-III, 10,000 km of National Highways is being developed to 4/6 lane on BOT basis.  In the
 first phase, (NHDP Phase-IIIA), 4,000 km is being taken up.  As on 24.8.2005, 13 packages covering 811 km have
 been awarded.  One project is nearing completion.  The targeted date for completion of NHDP Phase-IIIA is December
 2009. For the remaining 6,000 km NHDP-III B, as an advance action, only preparation of Detailed Project Report
 (DPR) has been approved.  There is no approval yet to take up 4/6 laning work in these 6,000 kms.
 
18.       On the basis of the experience of implementation of NHDP Phase I, major initiative and steps have been taken
 on the identified bottlenecks such as land acquisition, shifting of utilities, construction of Road over bridges, close
 monitoring of projects.    The NHDP Phase III will be implemented mainly on ‘Build Operate & Transfer (BOT)’
 basis.  The Model Concession Agreements are being streamlined for active participation of the private entrepreneurs.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
19.       The Committee notes the reply of the Department and expects that Special Accelerated Road Development
 Programme (SARDP) would be implemented at the earliest.  The Committee is also of the view that the Department
 should expedite all the background work for the ensuing projects based on the experience gained by it while
 implementing the Golden Quadrilateral Project.
 
CENTRAL ROAD FUND
(Recommendation at Para 43) 
 
20.       The Committee takes exception to the fact that funds accruing to the Central Road Fund due to levy of additional
 cess since 1.4.2003 have not been provided to the Department of Road Transport and Highways, inspite of the fact that
 this additional cess of 50 paise per litre on petrol and diesel was levied primarily to support the implementation of
 National Highway Development Project (NHDP).  There has been no positive outcome to this impasse inspite of a
 direction by the Cabinet for implementation of the recommendations of the Group of Ministers.  The Committee
 recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should take up the matter with the Ministry of

 Finance so that the funds due to the Department are provided to it at the earliest and the projects under National
 Highway Development Project do not suffer for want of funds.         
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
21.       During the year 2005-06 an amount of Rs.3269.74 crores has been allocated to NHAI from the Central Road
 Fund. This amount includes the additional cess for the current year.   No fund towards the previous accruals since
 1.4.2003 due to additional cess has been provided. This is being taken up with the Ministry of Finance.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
22.       The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Finance may be impressed upon to release the previous
 fund accruals since 1.4.2003 in view of the high cost of implementation of NHDP.
 
DEVELOPMENT OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS IN NORTH- EASTERN REGION
(Recommendation at Para 56) 
 
23.       One of the objectives of the Tenth Plan for Road Sector is special attention to the development of roads in
 North-Eastern region.  Although three years of the Five Year Plan have gone by, the Government has not taken any
 concrete steps for improving the National Highways network in this region.  Also, the Special Accelerated Road
 Development Programme in the North-Eastern region is still under consideration of the Government. The Committee
 feels that development of road network is very crucial in the context of the development of North-Eastern region of the
 country.  In view of the geographical location and strategic importance of the region, there is a need to provide an all
 weather National Highway network in this region.  The Committee recommends that the Department of Road Transport
 and Highways should pay immediate attention to the development of National Highways in the North-Eastern region. 
 Further, the Special Accelerated Road Development Programme should be expeditiously approved by the Government
 so that work on the project could actually begin and the funds allocated for the project during the year could be
 optimally utilized. 
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
 
24.       This Department is fully aware of the need for expediting developmental works of National Highways in the
 North-Eastern region. Further, the Special Accelerated Road Development Programme for the North-Eastern region is
 under advanced stage of approval.    Adequate funds are being provided for development and maintenance of National
 Highways in North Eastern areas.  During the current year, an amount of  Rs.956.50 crore has been earmarked for
 development of Central Sector Roads which is against the previous year’s (2004-05) provision of Rs.262.21 crores.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
25.       The Committee desires that the substantially higher allocation for the development of Central Sector Roads in
 2005-06 as compared to 2004-05 would actually translate to better condition of roads in the North-Eastern Region. 
 Further, the Committee recommends that the Special Accelerated Road Development Programme (SARDP) should be
 implemented at the earliest in the North-Eastern Region.
 
PARTICIPATION OF PRIVATE SECTOR IN DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE OF NATIONAL
 HIGHWAYS
(Recommendation at Paras 62 & 63) 
 
26.       The Committee feels that in view of the huge resource gap of around Rs. 1,06,000 crore in the road sector during
 the Tenth Plan, there is a genuine need to attract private sector investment in this sector to a large extent.  However, the
 Government has not been able to attract private sector investment to the desired extent.  The Committee recommends
 that the Government project the success of the Golden Quadrilateral to the private sector to encourage them to
 contribute more and more to the development of this sector.  This would definitely help the Government to reduce the
 resource gap position to a large extent.
 
27.       The Committee is apprehensive whether the Government will be able to ensure private sector participation in the

 North-Eastern region of the country to the extent required by them.  The Committee recommends that, in such a

28.       The Government has already encouraged private sector participation in road construction industry in various

29.       The general policy of the Government is to take all the future projects on National Highway Development
 Project (NHDP) on public private partnership basis.  Where the public private partnership is not possible, contracts
 would be awarded on normal construction contract, i.e., Engineering Procurement Contract (EPC) basis.   In line with
 this policy, NHDP Phase-IIIA projects are being taken on Built, Operate and Transfer basis. 
 
30.       The scope of private sector investment is limited at present in the NE region for various reasons.   However,

Eastern Region.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its apprehension on the success of private sector participation in

NEED FOR AN INTEGRATED TRANSPORT POLICY
(Recommendation at Para 65) 
 
32.       The Committee observes that one of the objectives for the Tenth Plan for the road sector is ‘Development of
 roads to be considered an integral part of the total transport system supplementing other modes, integrating the
 development plans with railways and other modes of transport’.   This objective of the Tenth Plan reinforces the need to
 have an integrated transport policy in the country.  The Committee is of the view that the modal-mix in terms of
 transport is very adverse in the country inspite of the fact that we have long inland waterways, a fairly large railway
 network and the recent upsurge in the aviation and road transport sector.  However, in absence of the right kind of
 modal-mix the country is not making optimum utilization of all those resources.  There is, therefore, a need to have a
 more balanced and equitable distribution of passenger and freight traffic in the country.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Government must come forward with an integrated transport policy to make optimum utilization
 of the various transport facilities available in the country.
           
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
 
33.       The Planning Commission had formulated an Integrated Transport Policy in the year 2001.  As a follow-up to
 the above policy, this Department is in the process of formulating a National Road Transport Policy.  A draft National
 Road Transport Policy has already been circulated among the States/UTs and other stake holders inviting their
 suggestions/comments.  The draft National Road Transport Policy has also been posted on the official website
 (www.morth.nic.in
) inviting comments and suggestions.

34.       The Committee further recommends that it should be apprised about the follow-up action on the Draft National
 Road Transport Policy and to incorporate the same in the Integrated Transport Policy of the Government.

(Recommendation at Para 69)

(Recommendation at Para 80) 
 
43.       Road safety is of paramount importance and undermining it can have disastrous results.  This is evident from the
 fact that the rate of accidents as well as number of fatalities in our country are unusually higher compared to most of the
 other countries.  The Committee notes with concern that there may be a shortfall of Rs.1 to 4 crore in this sector.  The
 Committee is of the view that the Department of Road Transport and Highways, as the agency for distribution of funds
 under this head, has the responsibility to ensure optimum utilization of funds.  The Committee recommends that
 Department of Road Transport and Highways should impress upon the concerned agencies / NGOs the need for early
 completion of formalities and submission of relevant documents so that the funds earmarked for the purpose during a
 particular year are not underutilized.    
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
 
44.       As against revised estimate of Rs 32.20 crore, the actual expenditure is Rs 28.49 crore.  The shortfall is due to
 delay in supply of cranes, non-receipt of Final Action Taken Reports in respect of release of final installment of grant-
in-aid under the scheme of ‘Refresher training to drivers in unorganized sector’, etc.  The Committee has also
 recommended that the restriction of spending in the last quarter needs to be relaxed for infrastructure related
 Departments like Road Transport and Highways.
 
45.       The recommendation of the Committee has been noted for compliance.

POLLUTION TESTING AND CONTROL
(Recommendation at Paras 83 & 86) 
 
47.       The Committee understands the reasons for shortfall in respect of Pollution Testing Equipments during 2004-
05.  Since revised emission norms have been introduced from 1.10.2004, the Committee recommends that Department
 of Road Transport and Highways should impress upon the State Governments for early procurement of pollution testing
 equipments during 2005-06 so that, if required, the allocation for the purpose could be increased at RE stage.  
           
48.       The Committee is of the view that vehicular emission has become one of the major sources of environmental
 pollution and the share of the transport sector in total emissions is a matter of serious concern.  The Committee
 appreciates the steps taken by the Department of Road Transport and Highways in controlling vehicular pollution.  The
 Committee recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should impress upon the State
 Governments the need for effective monitoring and enforcement of these norms for on-road vehicles so as to minimize
 its ill effects.                                                                                                             
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
49.       All States/UTs have been advised on 18
th May, 2005, impressing upon the need for taking necessary steps for
 effectively monitoring and enforcement of vehicular emission norms.  They have also been advised about a scheme of
 this Department wherein reimbursement to the extent of 75% of cost of pollution testing equipment can be made by this
 Department to States.

(Recommendation at Para 89) 
51.       The Committee expresses its concern that in the absence of user-friendly public transports, the people in the
 country are resorting to excessive use of private vehicles and this has put the roads under undue pressure.  The
 Committee observes that most of the investment on roads is being extracted from the public itself but the returns
 accruing to the users are not equitable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the efforts of the Government

USE OF RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
(Recommendation at Para 95) 
 
54.       The Committee understands that Automotive Research Association of India, Pune has been set up by the Indian
 vehicle and automotive ancillary manufacturers and it is the Department of Road Transport & Highways's authorised
 certification agency for emissions norms etc.  Almost all vehicle manufacturers and major ancillary manufacturers are
 members of this institute.  The Committee is at a loss to understand as to why Government of India's emission norms
 etc. may be certified by an agency which has vehicle manufacturers as its members and on which the Department of
 Road Transport & Highways does not have any administrative control.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that
 either the Department of Road Transport & Highways should have control on the Automotive Research Association of
 India, Pune or the Association should be divested of the power of fixing emission norms as apex certification agency. 
 It is a direct case of the manufacturers themselves being the regulators, which promotes the scope of corruption in the
 functioning of the Institute.  The Committee desires that a proper enquiry may be instituted in the functioning of this
 institute.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
55.       Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Pune is an authorized testing agency under Central Motor
 Vehicles Rules (CMVR), 1989 to test the vehicles and give type approval certificate as to the compliance of the
 provisions of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Rules thereunder.  There are three other testing agencies namely, Indian
 Institute of Petroleum (IIP), Dehradun, Vehicles Research Development Establishment (VRDE), Ahmednagar and
 Central Farm Machinery Training and Testing Institute (CFMTTI), Budni, which are also authorized under CMVR for
 this purpose.
56.       ARAI is an independent entity governed by Governing Council.  This Department is not a member of Governing
 Council.  Department of Heavy Industry is the nodal agency of Central Government for dealing with ARAI.  Emission
 norms of motor vehicles for various categories of vehicles in different States/areas in the country are being legislated on
 the basis of a road map prepared by Mashelkar Committee on Auto Fuel Policy, set up by Ministry of Petroleum and
 Natural Gas.  The recommendations of this Committee, which have the approval of Union Cabinet form the basis of
 emission norms.  There is also a Standing Committee on Emission (SCOE) under this Department, in which all the
 stakeholders such as authorized testing agencies, Bureau of Indian Standards, Society of Indian Automobile
 Manufactures, Automotive Component Manufacturers Association, Department of Heavy Industry and representatives
 of various State Governments are represented.  Their recommendations are examined in this Department and norms are
 notified following due process of law.  Vehicle Manufacturers represented by Society of Indian Automobile
 Manufacturers (SIAM) do provide their inputs, but they are not in a position to influence the decision making.
57.       New institutional arrangements are being thought of, by both Department of Heavy Industry and this
 Department, which could cover the aspects of technical regulations in future.

ANALYSIS OF ANNUAL PLAN 2005-06
(Recommendation at Para No. 10&11)
 
5.The Committee expresses its concern over the failure of Department of Shipping to spend the approved outlay. 
 During the year 2004-05, out of the budgeted amount of Rs.2419.66 crore the Department could spent only Rs.1400.99
 crore which clearly indicates the poor fiscal management in the Department of Shipping.  The Committee observes that
 even while revising allocations, little consideration has been paid to the actual expenditure incurred in the past.  This
 shows that budgetary and revised estimates have always been made without taking into account the actual requirements
 as experienced in the previous years.
 6.The Committee feels that Department of Shipping has not evolved effective system or planning to systematically
 anticipate, assess and project its actual requirements of funds otherwise the investments could have yielded
 commensurate returns.  The Committee recommends that in future, the Department of Shipping should be transparent
 and realistic while making projections of required funds so that resources may not remain unused and are allocated
 more judiciously.

Ports Wing
7.         The Annual Plan outlay during the year 2004-05 for the Port Sector was Rs.1066.95 crores. Actual expenditure
 was Rs.341.62 crores (Provisional).
8.         The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are accepted and have been brought to the notice of Chairmen
 of Major Ports and heads of other organizations. Allocations for various projects under the Annual Plan are made after
 carrying out an assessment of the requirements on year to year basis. The Annual Plan proposals are formulated about
 five to six months in advance before the commencement of the Annual Plan period after factoring in the anticipated
 expenditure during the current year and the assessed requirements in the ensuing Annual Plan year for on-going
 projects and taking into account the assessed requirement of funds for the new projects to be taken up during the
 ensuing Annual Plan year. Requirements of funds at the Revised Estimates stage is projected after carrying out a review
 of the progress in the expenditure during the year till that time and after taking into account the anticipated expenditure
 during the remaining part of the year. This does not necessarily follow a uniform or standard pattern every year.
 
9.         In view of the time lag between the formulation process for Annual Plan and the implementation period, there is
 generally mismatch between the allocations and the actual expenditure. The ports were advised that there should be
 realistic approach while proposing the Annual Plan outlay for 2005-06 and that only token provision may be kept for
 projects for which administrative approval was yet to be accorded by the Competent Authority. The recommendations
 of the Committee will be kept in view while finalizing the allocation for Annual Plans in future also.

 Therefore, the Committee recommends that the monitoring agency should play rather proactive role and do away with

REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
23.       The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech of 2005-06 have announced that the ‘Dredgers’ would also come
 under tonnage tax regime. However, The vessels registered under Inland Vessels Act 1917 and Coastal Vessels Act,
 1838 are left out and tonnage tax benefit has not been extended  to the vessels covered under these two Act.
24.       This Ministry had already taken up the matter with Ministry of Finance for inclusion of vessels registered under
 Indian Vessel Act and Coasting Vessel Act, which were enjoying the benefits of Section 33 AC but now lost that
 benefits. Simultaneously these have been kept out of tonnage tax benefits also.   As directed by the Committee,
 Ministry of Finance was requested to consider the matter and include the vessels under the above Acts in the tonnage
 tax regime.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
25.    The Committee suggests the Department of  Shipping to pursue the matter persistently with the Department of
 Finance .
SETHUSAMUDRAM SHIP CHANNEL PROJECT
(Recommendation at Para 36)
 26.      The Committee notes the Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project is of great economic and strategic importance
 which will connect the Gulf of Mannar to Bay of Bengal so that the ship moving between East and West coast of India
 could have a continuous navigable sea route within their own territorial waters and the proposed channel save upto 424
 nautical miles of travel and about 30 hours of sailing time for ships.  The Committee notes with satisfaction that
 Ministry of Environment & Forests has also given environmental clearance to the project and a special purpose vehicle
 has been incorporated to raise finance to create and operate navigable channel.  The Committee expects that the project
 once completed will serve the strategic and national security interests besides spuring the overall economic
 development of coastal districts of southern states.  The Committee however, recommends that while taking up the
 implementation of the project, the Department of Shipping must give due attention to the likely effect of natural
 calamities particularly one like as Tsunami which hit southern states during December 2004 and safety measures may
 be incorporated accordingly.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
27.       The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are accepted.The Government sanction for implementing
 Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project at a cost of Rs.2427.40 crores has been issued on 1
st June, 2005. The animation
 models of the Tsunami of 26th December, 2004 available with the Tuticorin Port Trust indicates that the project area
 was the least affected on the east coast by the Tsunami. Hydrodynamic modeling studies recently carried out have
 confirmed the earlier findings that increase in magnitude of the current in the post-channel era will be only along the
 channel in Adam’s Bridge with no change in current status alongside the channel. The issues relating to Tsunami and

APPROACH IN THE 10
TH
 PLAN AND ANALYSIS OF THE ANNUAL PLAN 2005-2006

(Recommendation at Para No.9)
5.
The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation has always been less than the actual requirement and to adjust the shortfall, the allocation has to be subsequently increased.  The Committee is unable to comprehend the
reasons for keeping lower outlays when the actual requirement is far higher.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that every effort should be taken to make realistic estimation of allocation in subsequent plans keeping
in view all the anticipated demand for development of the tourism sector as a whole.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
6.         The Ministry of Tourism has always projected its budgetary requirements based on the actual needs and proposed for revision at the time of formulation of Revised Estimates, if any additional requirement is felt
necessary.  However, the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance are the final authorities for the allocations of funds in the Annual Plans of the Ministry and they have allocated less Budgetary support than the
actual requirements and projected plans.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
7.The Committee is aware of the fact that the Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission are the final authorities for the allocation of funds in the Annual Plans of the Ministry.  However, the Committee recommends
that the attention of the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance may be invited to the observations made by Committee for  allocation of Budgetary support as per actual requirement and projected plans.  Their
response may be submitted to the Committee for its consideration.
(Recommendation at Para No.13)
 
8.         
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism has been allocated a higher amount to the tune of Rs.786.00 crore in the B.E. 2005-06 which is almost 57 per cent over and above the approved outlay for the year
2004-05.  However, the Committee expresses its concern over the under utilisations of funds by the Ministry during the year 2004-05 and notes that the Ministry could spend only 79 per cent of the allocation i.e. Rs.395.1
crore out of the budgeted allocation of Rs.500 crore upto February 2005.  The Committee also notes that larger part of the budgeted amount was spent at the fag end of the financial year, especially, in the months of
February and March, which is much against the financial norms.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the programmes and policies should be implemented in a manner, which ensures regular infusion of
funds in various projects/schemes uniformly in all quarters of the financial year.  The Committee expects that the Ministry of Tourism will be in a better position to suitably revise the plan outlays in future. 
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
9.      The Ministry of Tourism during the year 2004-05 has utilized its 92.30% out of the total budgetary allocation of Rs.503.50 crore.  The Ministry of Tourism has spent Rs.347.95 crore i.e. 69.11% of its total budget
by 31.12.2004.  The reasons for the underutilization during the year 2004-05 were due to late restoration of the cut of Rs.100 crore in B.E. 2004-05 of the Ministry of Tourism by the Ministry of Finance, and non-
approval of re-appropriation proposals.  However, the suggestions of the Committee will be kept in view while formulating its future Annual Plans.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
10.       
The Committee notes the reply furnished by the ministry.
(Recommendation at Para Nos. 18, 19, 23 & 24)
 
11.    The Committee notes that with an aim to improve the existing destinations and circuits and to develop new destinations and tourists circuits of world class standard, the Ministry of Tourism has merged the existing
two scheme of Integrated Development of Tourist Circuit and Product/Infrastructure and destination development into one single scheme as Product/Infrastructure Development of Destinations and Circuits.  However,
the Committee is surprised to note that the tourism potential and uniqueness of some of the important States like Jharkhand, Rajasthan, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh and  Uttranchal for convergence of
resources and development of Circuits and Destinations of international importance has not yet been fully explored by the Ministry.  The Committee recommends that more Circuits and Destinations  region-wise should
be identified in consultation with the State Governments and developed in an integrated and holistic manner for the purpose of convergence of resources and world-class benchmarking, the related Ministries and
Department of State Governments should have sub-plans in their annual plans so that tourism related infrastructure projects receive the highest priority.
 
12.    The Committee also recommends that purposeful domestic and international publicity and marketing support should also be provided to all important tourist Circuits and Destinations so as to create interest of the
tourists in the Indian tourism products besides promoting India as a major tourists destination.
 
13.    The Committee notes with serious concern that the Ministry of Tourism sanctioned 2526 numbers of small isolated projects spread throughout the length and breadth of the country during 8
th
 and 9
th
 plan period,
out of which, 708 projects remained still incomplete.  The Committee feels that delay in implementation of projects not only led to slow progress and cost overrun but at the same time, deprive the tourists of the desired
facilities.  The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism will converge all the resources required for development of tourists infrastructure instead of spreading it very thinly in small isolated projects.  The Committee
recommends that to meet the developmental objectives and convergence of resource, the State and Central Government should work in synergetic manner and provide best facilities at the most economical price besides
addressing the issues of civic governance, management of sites and services, ensuring safety and security and hassle free comfortable stay for the tourists at these projects sites.
 
14.    The Committee also recommends the Ministry to adopt a proactive approach and take care of the hindrances resulting in delay and put in place some institutional mechanism to achieve better coordination, effective
monitoring and timely implementation of these pending projects.                    
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
15.       Identification and development of tourist sites is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments/Union Territories.  The Ministry of Tourism releases Central Financial Assistance for development of
sites/spots identified by the State Governments/Union Territories.  Development of tourist sites is an ongoing process and based on the proposals received from the State Governments/UTs the Ministry of Tourism is
continuously assisting the State Govts/UTs in this process to create world class tourist infrastructure in the country, equipped with best facilities, services, etc. required by the tourists.
 
16.       The Ministry has been promoting and marketing the newly developed/created destinations/circuits sites through its publicity support material and marketing campaigns with a view to create interest among the
discerning tourists.
 
17.       The Ministry of Tourism, with a view to facilitating and expediting the completion process of the incomplete projects of 8
th
 and 9
th
 Plan, had decided to release the balance amount where the State
Governments/UTs complete these projects within 31.3.2005. The Ministry of Tourism has requested all the States/UTs for sending their proposals for release of funds to complete these projects along with required
documents and monitoring/reviewing the progress of implementation of these delayed projects in the ongoing review meetings with the State Governments/UTs.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
18.       The Committee reiterates its observations to the Ministry of Tourism to adopt a proactive approach to remove the bottlenecks which are the root-causes for delay.  The fact that the Ministry, at the threshold of 11
th
Plan is still carrying the backlog of 8
th
 and 9
th
 Plan

s incomplete projects speaks volumes about its inadequacies.
RURAL TOURISM
(Recommendation at Para No.29)
 
19.       The committee observes that Rural Tourism is an important way in addressing the impact of increasing trends of industrialization and helps in moderating the stress of urban life styles and other syndromes and
Ministry of Tourism is paying adequate attention to the development of rural infrastructure in the country in participation with Private Sector with a view to translate the structural changes into benefits at the grassroots
level.  In this regard, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation contained in 79
th
 Report on Demand for Grants 2004-05 of Ministry of Tourism which may be read as under: -

�
The Committee is of the view that Rural Tourism has great potential and prospects in the country as it helps to revive the local peoples
�
 interests and pride in their culture, tradition and values besides generating
the tourists interest in the customs of the indigenous people as it focuses directly on the local people.  The Committee feels that with a growing interest in the intangible culture of different countries (i.e. lifestyle, cuisine,
ceremonies, music, religion, belief, customs and history), there is an enormous potential to encourage global tourism in rural areas.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to develop some institutional mechanism for
supporting, promoting and organizing large number of fairs & festivals and handicrafts & craft melas/bazaars in rural areas which will provide exposure, recognition as well as, additional flow of income to local artisans. 
The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should actively coordinate its efforts for liaising with other Ministries/Departments of Government of India viz. Ministries of Rural Development, Environment and
Forests, Textiles & Culture etc. and other concerned organization/agencies for converging of resource from that Ministry/Department and increase allocation for tourism sector through the state budgets as tourism has a
greater potential for creating a large-scale employment opportunity than any other industry in the country

.

21.       The suggestion of the Hon
�
ble Committee is welcomed. Ministry of Tourism has already written to the Ministry of Rural Development for support under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana and Swarnajayanti
Gram Swarozgar Yojana which will enable successful project outcomes through rural road connectivity and self-employment. Letter has also been sent to Development Commissioner Handlooms with a request to let the

22.       
The Committee notes with appreciation the initiatives taken by the Government in the matter.  The Committee should also be appraised of the achievements of the Government in a detailed manner.
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
(Recommendation at Para No.36)
 
23.       The Committee notes that there are 24 Institutes of Hotel Management and 6 Food Crafts Institutes catering to the requirements of tourism and other industries for trained manpower.  The Committee is of the view
that with the vast expansion and modernisation of the hospitality sector, the Hotel Management and catering education programme gained tremendous popularity and there is great demand for trained manpower not only
in the field of hospitality sector but also it spanned to other sectors like Hospitals, Call Centres, Banks etc.  The Committee observes that as number of hotels/restaurants are going to increase in the future, availability of
trained manpower is a must to meet the growing demand for excellence in the tourism sector.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to set up Institutes of Hotel Management in each State for meeting shortage of
trained manpower in the tourism and other sectors.  The Committee further recommends that in view of the mushrooming of the number of such institutions mostly in the private sector which does not have desired
training level and infrastructure facilities, a statutory status to the National Council for Tourism & Hospitality Education should be granted to better regulate and networking of all resources for institutions in the tourism
and hospitality sectors.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
24.       The  28 Institutes of Hotel Management and Catering Technology (IHMs) and 
7
 Food Craft Institutes (FCIs), which are following courses of NCHMCT, have been set up/being set up in the Country as per break up
given below: 
(i)      21 IHMs functioning under Central Govt.(Ministry of Tourism).

4 IHMs under construction/being set up by Central Government.
(iii)    
3 IHMs functioning under State Govts.
(iv)

(A complete locational list of the above Institutes is available at Annexure I)

26.       The National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology has already decided to offer scheme of affiliation to private sector institutes, which shall go a long way in standardizing the quality of training
in the country.

27.       The Ministry of Tourism has not replied on the Committee's recommendation that a statutory status be granted to National Council for Tourism & Hospitality Education (NCHM & CT).  The Committee again
reiterates that the status of

the growing demand of trained manpower in the field.
PROVIDING A CONSTITUTIONAL STATUS OF TOURISM
(Recommendation at Para No.39)
 
28.       The Committee notes that a proposal to include Tourism in the concurrent list has been mooted by the Ministry for giving Constitutional recognition to tourism and development of tourism in a systematic manner. 
As result of which so far as 29 States/Union Territories have agreed for placing tourism in the concurrent list and 6 States have opposed the proposal.  The Committee feels that India
�
s tourism products will grow only
when the suitable legislative and regulatory support is provided.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry of Tourism to build a strong national consensus for creating awareness about the role of tourism and
harness its benefits as an instrument of economic development and employment catalyst besides removing the hurdles for its growth and every
effort should be taken by the Ministry to include tourism in the Concurrent List of the Constitution.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
29.       The issue of placing 
�
Tourism
�
 in the Concurrent List of the Constitution has been engaging the attention of the Ministry for the last few years, but no final decision could be taken. In this connection all the
State Govt./ UT Admin
�
s and concerned Ministries where consulted.  Whereas 29 States/UTs have agreed for placing tourism in Concurrent list and 6 States have expressed reservations/opposed the proposal. Further, a
number of legal issues are involved in bringing 
�
Tourism
�
 in the Concurrent List of the Constitution, in view of the fact that Tourism is not a single activity, but an amalgam of number of activities like transportation,

30.       The Committee notes the efforts being made by the Ministry in the matter. The Committee may be updated of the further developments in this respect.
 
UNIFORMITY AND RATIONALISATION OF TAXES ON TRANSPORT AND HOSPITALITY SECTOR
(Recommendation at Para No.43)
 
31.       The Committee notes that the major barrier to the growth of tourism in the country is a multitude of Central and State level taxes.  The Committee is of the opinion that uniform taxation is very necessary for
promotion of tourism and recommends the Ministry of Tourism to make consistent effort for building a nationwide campaign on rationalization of taxation issues both in transport and hotel sectors.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
32.       The Ministry of Tourism is aware that one of the fundamental problems plaguing the Indian Tourism sector is a multitude of Central and State Taxes, which make India as an expensive destination as compared to
other competing tourist destinations.  This issue was taken up for discussion during the State Tourism Ministers Conference held in New Delhi on 4
th
 and 5
th
 March, 2005.  Simultaneously the matter has been referred to
the Inter-State Council and on their advice, detailed views of the State Governments and Union Territories have been sought.  The matters like reduction in service tax on tour operators and excise duty on Aviation Turbine
Fuel are being taken up with the Ministry of Finance.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
33.       The Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Government to rationalize the tax structure concerning the different departments of tourism sector.  However, it suggests them to strive to evolve consensus
on the subject. 
DOMESTIC TOURISM AND PUBLICITY
(Recommendation at Para Nos. 48 & 49)
34.       The Committee notes that during the year 2003, around 6 million Indians have visited abroad against a total incoming flow of 2.73 million foreign tourists, and more and more countries are queuing up to attract the
Indian tourists, which has led to foreign exchange outflow.  The Committee observes that by diverting Indian tourists going abroad to Indian destinations, massive potential for domestic tourism can be explored and this
requires focussed approach for its growth.  The Committee is of the view that the growth of global tourism depends upon the domestic tourism and it is easier to target the domestic tourism market as compared to the
international market.  The Committee feels that a relative change in the marketing strategy is required for tapping the domestic and international tourism markets and recommends that special emphasis must be laid for
accessing the market by consolidation of efforts to arrest the increasing trend of outbound tourists.
 
35.       The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry for launching a multi-pronged promotional campaign in all key markets across the world under the brand name of

Incredible India

.  The Committee hopes
that the campaign will continue to focus on the diverse and varied tourism products of the country and will be able to create awareness about varied attractions amongst the travelers.  The Committee notes that the outlay
on publicity for 2005-06 has been increased to Rs.70 crore which is almost five times as compared to that of last financial year.  The Committee hopes that with the increased outlay, the Ministry of Tourism will be able to
make effective publicity to promote domestic tourism.  However, the Committee recommends the Ministry to chalk-out a concrete plan for targeting domestic middle class tourists.

 replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the earliest.
