 believed in a common economy, export substitution and import substitution. As a result, ports did not
 significantly contribute in our exports and imports. Therefore, you would see that over a period of 55 years,
 after independence, we have only 12 ports, and luckily, 187 ports have come in the non-major sectors. But, Sir,
 today, what is happening is, with 8.1 to 10 per cent growth of the Indian economy, 150 billion dollars export
 and the export growth rate of 25 per cent, 95 per cent of Exim trade goes through the ports. There will be
 inevitable pressure on the ports. If they do not export, then the minor ports will export it. Minor ports like Essar
 and Reliance are expanding. They are expanding in a very big way. It is not that we are trying to have equitable
 distribution of cargo because that is not possible among the 12 major ports. Our ports are responding to the
 commercial opportunity that is available there. But the time has come when we will have to make an all out
 effort to develop our ports. Now, the trade is not going to be Atlantic oriented. The future belongs to the Pacific
 Rim States. Therefore, it will be eastward. That is the logic as to why Kolkata has a future on account of that
 kind of a substitute for Singapore. If we take that kind of geo-strategic outlook and concentrate on the Pacific
 area, then, Sir, I am sure, all these things will fall in line. For that, Sir, we need your full support, the
 Government's full support and the Parliament's full support'.
 
27.       The Committee observes that the international trade is witnessing an increasing trend towards containerization. 
 However, the Committee is constrained to note that the major ports did not significantly contribute to export-import trade and
 about 70 percent of containers are trans-shipped at neighbourhood international Ports such as, Colombo, Dubai and Singapore
 Ports, making thereby India's export costlier and imports less competitive.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
 Government should establish hub ports in the country preferably, in East and West Coast for trans-shipment of containerized
 cargo for the growth of sea-borne overseas trade and economic development. 
 
SETHUSAMUDRAM SHIP CHANNEL PROJECT
28.       Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project envisages dredging of a ship channel in the shallow portion of sea to connect the
 Gulf of Mannar and Bay of Bengal through Palk Bay so that the ships, depending on draught required, moving between east
 and west coast of India could have a continuous navigable sea route around the peninsula within India's own territorial waters. 
 This will save up to 424 nautical miles (one nautical mile is equal to 1.852 kms.) of distance and up to 30 hours of sailing time
 for ships between east and west coast. The project will also enhance the national security and world lead to overall economic
 development of the region. 
29.       As regards allocation and utilization of outlay, the Department of Shipping  informed that total allocation for
 Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project in BE 2006-07 is Rs. 304 crore comprising Rs. 204 crore budgetary grant and Rs.100
 crore internal and extra-budgetary resources(IEBR). The budgetary grant component is towards the payment of equity share by
 the Government to Sethusamudram Corporation Limited (SCL), the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) for implementation of the
 project. The IEBR component is towards payment of equity share to SCL by the other partners in the SPV, namely Chennai
 Port Trust, Tuticorin Port Trust, Visakhapatnam Port Trust, Paradip Port Trust, Ennore Port Limited, Shipping Corporation of
 India Limited and Dredging Corporation of India Limited. The amount is likely to be utilised for carrying out the dredging and
 other associated works for the project.  
30.       The Committee pointed out about the environmental impact of the project and wanted to know about the details of study
 undertaken for the purpose, the Department of Shipping  submitted that taking into consideration the environmentally sensitive
 nature of the project, in view of its location and also the main component of work, namely, dredging and disposal of dredged
 material, an initial Environmental Examination of the project was made through National Environmental Engineering Research
 Institute (NEERI) Nagpur.  The final report of NEERI was received in 1998 in which they had suggested a new alignment of
 the channel, prima facie, acceptable from environmental considerations. The alignment of the channel now proposed is
 completely in the sea and thus the term 'channel' instead of 'canal' is being used in respect of this project.  A presentation of the
 Initial Environment Examination Report was made to the Ministry of Environment & Forests in April, 1999 for 31 ft. draft.

 mode of transport on its own and for its development requires fiscal support from the Government.
41.       The cost benefit analysis also implies relief should be provided to these sectors as the revenue lost to the exchequer is
 only about Rs. 1.50 crore per annum, since there are only about 400 small vessels constituting tonnage of 0.012 million GT
 registered under Inland Vessels Act and about 120 Vessels of 0.018 million GT registered under Coastal Vessels Act, which
 needs to cover under the Tonnage Tax regime.  This sector have been unintentionally got adversely affected because 33 AC
 benefits have been withdrawn from them in Financial Bill 2004-05 without extending tonnage tax benefit to them.  The
 rationale for extending Tonnage Tax benefit to this sector is to unfold the infrastructural potential of these sectors which will
 ultimately benefit Indian economy much more than the tax which can be realized with the present taxation structure.  The

INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
 61.      Inland waterways comprising of rivers, lakes, canals, creeks, backwaters etc. extend to about 14500 km in the country. 
 However, potential of this important mode of transport has not been exploited so far.  In several countries of the world where
 development of this mode was given required importance and attention, Inland Water Transport (IWT) has substantial share in
 inland water transport net work.  So far, following three waterways have been declared as national waterways:-
National Waterway No.1 (NW-1)
Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system from Allahabad to Haldia (1620 kms) - declared as national waterway in 1986.
National Waterway No.2 (NW-2)
The Brahmaputra river from Sadiya to Dhubri (891 kms) - declared as national waterway in 1988.
National Waterway No.3 (NW-3)
The west coast canal from Kollam to Kottapuram alongwith Champakara and Udyogmandal canais (205 kms) -
 declared as national waterway in 1993.

69.       The Committee pointed out that the entrepreneurs are not flocking in to take advantage of the incentives being provided
 to IWT sector and wanted to know the reasons from the Department of Shipping. The Department of Shipping informed the
 Committee that Inland waterways require regular development and maintenance for becoming/ remaining a competitive mode
 of transport in the dynamic situation of economic development. However, Inland Water Transport sector remained neglected
 for a long time in the country,  while the other modes namely rail and road developed substantially. There also has been
 significant improvement in technology of providing and maintaining infrastructure in rail and road sectors both for creation of
 basic facilities as well as rolling stock.    However, due to the neglect, IWT sector not only remained dormant but actually de-
generated and lost its significance in  many areas. Due to its inherent advantages in terms of fuel efficiency, lower cost of
 transportation and environment friendliness, this sector still remained important in some areas where it continued to remain
 competitive to the other modes.  Such of these areas are Goa, West Bengal, Assam, Kerala, Orissa,  Mumbai etc.  When the
 IWT mode is also developed like the other two modes, this mode also would play its role in the overall transport mix of the
 country as an alternative and supplementary mode of inland transport.
70.       Non development of IWT sector not only made many waterways non navigable for bigger sizes of inland vessels, it also
 drove away many operators and shippers who had no alternative but to utilize road and rail modes.  Bringing them back to
 IWT sector requires many actions including up-gradation of basic IWT infrastructure, fiscal incentives, vessel building subsidy
 as well as freight subsidy etc.  While some of these have been put into place, it will take some more time for these activities to
 develop to a level where the private sector feels confident to invest in the sector.  It may be noted that while Government may
 provide the basic infrastructure namely fairway, terminals and navigational aids, the ownership and operation of cargo and
 passenger vessels have to be primarily in the private sector for long term success of this mode.  We are hopeful that by
 providing basic IWT infrastructure on various waterways significant cargo can be shifted to IWT mode.  We have already seen
 substantial increase in transportation of cargo on Indo-Bangladesh routes in 2-3 years where it has gone up from the level of 2-

71.       As regards the proposal to give institutional framework for development of IWT in the country the Department of
 Shipping informed the Committee that Institutional arrangement for development of IWT is already in place.  While Inland
 Waterways Authority of India is a Central Government agency for development and regulation of inland waterways, its
 primary responsibility is development  and regulation of national waterways for shipping and navigation.  At State level, most
 of the riverine States have got some setup responsible for development of IWT.  These set ups however, need to be up-graded/
 strengthened in many States.  Under Centrally Sponsored Scheme for IWT development, the Government of India also
 provides grant of 100% to north-eastern States including Sikkim and 90% to other States.  IWAI assists the Department of
 Shipping for examination and monitoring of projects being prepared and implemented by the States under this scheme.
72.       IWT sector is currently underdeveloped in terms of requisite infrastructure. Hence the thrust is on developing requisite
 infrastructure so that IWT mode becomes a preferred option for transportation of cargo. Once requisite infrastructure is in
 place and IWT development in the country has crossed the threshold level, commercial IWT operations can be expected, in
 which case cost recovery through users charges will also be possible.
73.       The Committee observes that the Government is giving step-motherly treatment to the Inland Water Transport Sector
 and this approach is reflected in the pattern of budgeting as well as utilization of funds in the IWT Sector. The Committee is
 dismayed to note that an outlay of Rs. 150.00 crore was allocated in BE 2005-06 for the IWT Sector  but it was reduced to Rs.
 101.25 crore at RE stage and an expenditure of Rs. 47.87 crore was made only upto February, 2006. The Committee notes that
 Inland Water Transport is one of the oldest, economically, environmentally sustainable mode of transport but the potential of
 Inland Water Transport remains largely unexploited due to the detrimental policies of the Government.    The Committee
 observes that although the Department of Shipping is committed to step up the share of IWT in the country's total trade still
 this sector remains under developed at present for want of requisite infrastructure and therefore, is not viable for commercial
 operations.  The Committee feels that inadequate policy support, interest and investments are some of the factors which are
 aggravating the problems of the Inland Water Transport and this sector is loosing a competitive edge with other modal mix in
 the country.  The Committee is of the view that growth of the Inland Water  Transport sector will entirely depend upon the
 quantum of investments, made through public-private partnership and a multi-dimensional approach for creating the required
 infrastructure primarily through Government Support.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of Shipping to
 provide some institutional framework for creating a vibrant Inland Water Transport sector in the country and  IWT should be
 included under the National Maritime Development Programme for augmentation of IWT fleet, creation of inter-modal
 linkages and upgradation of cargo handling technologies etc.

            The Committee notes that the Department of Shipping is implementing the schemes for enhancing the capacity and
 productivity of all major ports and to encourage the private sector participation for the development of ports infrastructure and
 accordingly, comprehensive policy guidelines have been issued.  The Committee also notes that the Government has allowed
 cent percent FDI for construction and maintenance of ports in order to mobilise substantial resources as well as to improve
 efficiency, productivity and quality of services of Ports.  The Committee, however, observed that as against the capacity of
 408.60 million TPA, the major ports handled a total traffic of 310.80 mt. upto December 2005.  This way, the aggregate
 capacity of major ports exceeds the traffic target marginally. Therefore, there is need to increase capacity of ports on urgent 
 basis. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of Shipping to take action for development of infrastructure in
 major ports so as to face global competition of sea-borne trade and enhance private sector investment including FDI in the
 sector by addressing the procedural rigidity expediting well integrated and coordinated policy framework and approach.

PORT LABOUR REFORMS
 
            The Committee  notes that in the changed fiscal regime the Government is committed for labour reforms  and desires to
 allow private sector investment for creation and augmentation of  capacity building in the port infrastructure. The Committee
 also notes with concern that enhancement of private sector investment for development of port infrastructure may deter the
 interest of employees unions/federations. Therefore, the Committee feels that the port labour reforms are necessary before
 exposing the labour sector to open market mechanism.  In view of this, the Committee recommends the Department of
 Shipping to de-regulate and de-centralize the commercial environment for collective bargaining to improve the productivity
 levels at ports while taking adequate care of labour interests.(Para 21)
PORT CONNECTIVITY
            The Committee observes that the lack of proper port connectivity has hampered the development of ports. The
 Committee also notes that projects involving 117.73 km. for improving road accessibility to Ports have been completed and
 projects involving 313.85 kms. of road length are under implementation. The Committee is of the view that development of
 other modes of transport viz. railways, highways and inland water transport is also essential for improving the accessibility to
 ports and to keep pace with the growing requirements of overseas trade. The Committee feels that the availability of such
 modal mix will result in considerable saving in cost and time for cargo containers assessing these ports. The Committee
 therefore, recommends the Department of Shipping  to take steps for better road and rail connectivity infrastructure in all the
 major ports for the growth of the container cargo. The cost of connectivity could be shared in public sector by the strategic
 partners or alternatively,  the private public partnership (PPP) or joint venture partnership (JVP) could also be explored.
(Para 23)
CONTAINERIZATION IN MAJOR PORTS
            The Committee observes that the international trade is witnessing an increasing trend towards containerization. 
 However, the Committee is constrained to note that the major ports did not significantly contribute to export-import trade and
 about 70 percent of containers are trans-shipped at neighbourhood international Ports such as, Colombo, Dubai and Singapore
 Ports, making thereby India's export costlier and imports less competitive.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
 Government should establish hub ports in the country preferably, in East and West Coast for trans-shipment of containerized
 cargo for the growth of sea-borne overseas trade and economic development.  (Para 27)

 from many corners regarding the environmental repercussions of the Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project whereas, the

 in 2003-04 despite the increase in capacity of Air India and major capacity induction by other carriers into India.  The
 Ministry has cited the reason of ageing fleet of Air India as compared to the state-of-the-art aircrafts available with

 international sector, the market share of the national carriers have remained stagnant at around 30% from 2002-03 to
 2004-05.

 leveraged to diversify the international air services and to avail the entitlements of new traffic rights to the full extent.

ROUTE DISPERSAL GUIDELINES
 
122.     The Route Dispersal Guidelines (RDG) issued by the Government in 1994, require all scheduled airlines to
 deploy at least 10% of the capacity deployed by them on major trunk routes (i.e. CAT-I routes) on the routes to/from
 North East, Jammu & Kashmir,  Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands (i.e. CAT II routes).  Out of the total
 capacity so deployed in CAT-II routes, 10% of the capacity is required to be deployed for connectivity within North
 East, Jammu & Kashmir, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.  Further, the airlines are also required to
 deploy 50% of the capacity, deployed on CAT-I routes, on non-trunk routes i.e. CAT-III routes.  The Director General
 of Civil Aviation monitors the compliance with the Route Dispersal Guidelines on a monthly basis.  The Committee
 inquired about the status of the proposal of the Ministry to review the Route Dispersal Guidelines (RDG) and the
 reasons for the inordinate delay in taking action on the recommendations of the committee set up under the
 Chairmanship of Director General of Civil Aviation contained in its report submitted on 18.3.2005.  In their reply, the
 Ministry stated that the Government had set up a Committee under the Chairmanship of Director General of Civil
 Aviation vide Order dated 23-09-2003 to review the existing Routes Dispersal Guidelines.  The Committee has
 submitted its report on 18-03-2005, which is under active consideration of the Government.  In the context of news
 reports regarding a proposal to impose a cess of Rs.500 on air travel in lieu of phasing  out Route Dispersal Guidelines,
 the Committee sought the explanation of the Secretary during the course of the oral evidence tendered by him.  The
 following submissions were made by the Secretary: -
 
“Sir, briefly I would respond to the issues that you have raised. You referred to the press report that the Government is
 going to levy a fee of Rs.500 on passengers which would be financing the construction and modernisation of non-metro
 airports. Sir, let me explain that, firstly, there is no decision of the Government to impose such a fee. This came because
 of one thought that is being discussed in the Ministry and also it is our effort to see in what form it would be part of the
 civil aviation policy. I would take two minutes to explain it.
 
Sir, today, we have what are known as route dispersal guidelines under which all airlines have to fly to the North-East,
 Jammu & Kashmir & Islands, a percentage of total kilometres they fly on the main routes. This is to ensure that
 services to some of the far-away regions, difficult and remote areas of the country, particularly in the North-East, island
 territories of the country and the State of Jammu and Kashmir, are served where, otherwise, on purely commercial

 operations.

Adequate size of terminal building to handle international and transit passengers.

 the scope and extent of concessions/exemptions with the Commerce Ministry/Finance Ministry for deriving the
 anticipated benefits from the announcements made in the Annual Supplement, 2006 under the Foreign Trade Policy
 2004-09.   The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should initiate suitable steps in advance to facilitate
 the National Carriers to avail the full benefits of the announcements.(Para 25)
 
The Committee notes that Air India had approached only M/s. Jet Airways in July, 2005 to negotiate the wet-lease of
 one A340-330E aircraft.  The Committee is of the opinion that Air India could have approached other Airlines
 organisations.  The procedure followed by Air India was against the practice of open competitive tendering process and
 therefore lacks transparency.  The Committee feels that the impending shortage could have been anticipated early had
 there been a constant assessment of the available aircraft capacity. The Committee further recommends that adequate
 contingency plans should be prepared including standing arrangements for lease of aircrafts during exigencies by
 following the proper tendering process.(Para 27)
 
INDIAN AIRLINES LIMITED
 
The Committee notes that there is a scope for further improvement in the overall load factor of Indian Airlines and
 recommends that there is a need to focus attention of all the factors that are responsible for acting as constraints in the
 achievement of the desired level of overall load factor.   The Committee also notes with concern that the market share
 of national carriers has decreased despite the overall increase in the growth rate of domestic passengers traffic, which is
 also reflected in the decline in the reported profits of Indian Airlines.  The Committee recommends that adequate steps,
 in addition to the acquisition of aircrafts, should be taken to enable Indian Airlines to tap the market opportunities in the
 domestic as well as international markets.(Para 32)
 
The Committee feels that the issue of wage revision of employees of Indian Airlines has been pending for a long
 time. In this connection, the Committee would like to draw the attention of the Ministry to the recommendations
 made by the Committee in its 96
th Report, which is reproduced below: -
“The Committee expresses its anguish over the evasive comments of the Ministry offered in response to the
 recommendation of the Parliamentary Committee.  The Committee is extremely unhappy about the lackadaisical
 approach of the Ministry on the issue of revision of scales of pay of employees of Indian Airlines.  The Committee is of
 the view that the satisfaction level of the personnel in the matter of service conditions is a major factor affecting the

 performance of any organisation.  The total inaction on the part of the Ministry in the matter of pay revision of
 employees of Indian Airlines is surprising, especially in the present age of poaching and stiff competition by other
 Indian scheduled carriers.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Ministry should expedite its decision in the
 matter in the overall interest of the employees and the organisation.”   The Committee once again reiterates the above
 recommendation and expects an early action thereon.(Para 34)
 
ACQUISITION OF AIRCRAFTS BY INDIAN AIRLINES LIMITED & AIR INDIA LIMITED
 
The Committee expects that the Ministry would take necessary steps to ensure that the time schedules fixed for the
 delivery of aircrafts to Indian Airlines and Air India are adhered to so that the National Carriers are able to take
 maximum benefits of exemption from payment of tax under Section 10(15A).  The Committee hopes that the Ministry
 would not hesitate to invoke the penalty clauses in the terms and conditions of the purchases in the event of failure to
 adhere to the agreed timeframe of delivery of aircrafts.  The Committee recommends the Government to ensure that the
 commitments made by the M/s. Boeing and M/s. Airbus Industrie to set up training centers for flight and maintenance
 training, investment in areas such as Pilot training, aircraft maintenance and repair etc. may be in place well in time.  It
 is further recommended that the matter regarding the extension beyond 1
st April, 2007 of the exemption from payment
 of tax on lease rentals payable to a non-resident foreign lessor under Section 10(15A) should be pursued with the
 Ministry of Finance.  The Committee also recommends that Government should explore the possibility of extending its
 space/defence aeronautical endeavours to the manufacturing of civilian aircrafts to reduce the dependency on foreign
 companies for the supply of aircrafts.(Para 64)
 
ALLIANCE AIR
 
The Committee notes with concern the deterioration of flight connectivity in the North Eastern region due to the
 constraints faced by Alliance Air on account of exodus of pilots, in view of the fact that the North Eastern region has
 got strategic importance.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the efforts being made to induct pilots should be
 intensified to normalize the operations of Alliance Air in the North-East. The Committee also recommends that the
 assurance of putting more aircrafts on routes in the North-East after the acquisition of aircrafts by Indian Airlines
 should be fulfilled immediately after the delivery of the first batch of aircrafts.(Para 68)
 
AIR INDIA EXPRESS
 
The Committee feels that the operations of Air India Express has been of immense help to the expatriate Indian workers
 in the Gulf region.  The Committee recommends that the operations of this budget airlines should be carefully planned
 with a view to achieve the objective of offering low cost air connectivity to skilled/unskilled Indian workers employed
 in the Gulf region and other parts of the world.  The Committee expects that the Ministry will take suitable steps so that
 aspirations of the people for increasing the frequency of operations as well as providing connectivity to new regions
 will be fulfilled.(Para 73)
 
PAWAN HANS HELICOPTERS LIMITED
The Committee feels that there is tremendous scope of utilizing the helicopter facility to connect the remote tourist
 places.  The Committee recommends that Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited should prepare specific plans to
 diversify/connect to important tourist places as a part of diversification of its operations. The Committee expects that
 the approved outlay for new fleet acquisition will be fully utilised in the current financial year.  The Committee notes
 that a substantial number of the grounded operating fleet of Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited was rendered
 unserviceable during the torrential rains/floods at Mumbai in July 2005.  The Committee recommends that suitable
 contingency plans should be evolved to prevent the recurrence of such mishaps.  The Committee also recommends that
 efforts should be made to make the damaged Dauphin fleet serviceable in a time bound manner.
(Para 78)
 
AIRPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA
The Committee notes that the approximate financial implication for the development of 35 Non-Metro Airports would
 be Rs.4662.50 crore over a period of five years starting from 2006-07 to 2010-11 and that the Ministry is considering a

 proposal to levy ADF/ UDF on passengers at these 35 Non-Metro Airports for funding the part development cost and to
 make the project financially viable as per the proposal.  In this context the Committee desires to draw the attention of
 the Ministry to the assurance given in the Action Taken Replies furnished by it on the recommendations contained in
 the 90th Report of the Committee that after the restructuring of the Delhi and Mumbai airports, Airports Authority of
 India will be better off financially and it will not only be able to maintain other airports in the country but also upgrade
 and modernize these airports.  Further, it was also submitted that Airports Authority of India is planning to modernize
 35 Non-Metro Airports to world-class standards by using reserves including internal reserves.  The Committee further
 recommends that the proposal should be expedited and implemented in a specific time frame.
 
The Committee notes that there is a spurt in the commercial activities in Mangalore, which is likely to benefit the civil
 aviation activities in the region.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to harness the potential benefits,
 the necessary steps, including discussions with the State Government, for the early commissioning of the Mangalore
 airport and commencement of international flights should be taken by the Ministry.(Paras 92 & 93)
 
The Committee notes that utilisation of funds and physical progress in the projects under implementation in the North
 Eastern region is very poor barring a few projects.  The Committee recommends that Airports Authority of India should
 give focussed attention to the projects under implementation in the North Eastern Region and fix achievable targets for
 early completion of the same.   The Committee recommends that the preparatory steps for the construction of an airfield
 in Arunachal Pradesh should be completed at the earliest so that people of that State can be provided with air
 connectivity to rest of India. In the matter of provision of adequate finances, the Committee recommends that the
 Ministry should pursue the matter with the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region.  The Committee also
 recommends that  the Ministry should explore the possibility of allocating more funds from the internal resources to
 fund the airport developmental project in the North Eastern region.(Para 99)
 
RESTRUCTURING DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
 
The Committee recommends that the Tripartite Committee with the representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation,
 Airports Authority of India and AAI Employees Joint Forum should hold regular meetings and finalise its Report in a
 time bound manner in view of the importance of the issues relating to modernization of airports by Airports Authority
 of India and the stake of the employees including job security.(Para 102)
 
KOLKATA & CHENNAI AIRPORTS
 
The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Ministry with regard to construction of international airports at
 Kolkata and Chennai. The Committee is of the opinion that with the growth of the aviation sector in the country, the
 pressure and strain on Mumbai and Delhi airports is also increasing.  The Committee is apprehensive that with the
 arrival of private players in the airline sector, there will be further intensification of this pressure.  As accepted by the
 Secretary of the Ministry, the Delhi and Mumbai-centric activity was also becoming unmanageable.  The Committee,
 therefore, feels that there exists a need to develop alternate airports and recommends that work of international
 terminals at Kolkata and Chennai should be completed at the earliest.(Para 104)
 
PRIVATE SCHEDULED AIRLINES
The policy of opening up of international skies to Indian scheduled airlines was adopted to ensure full realization of the
 objective to enhance utilisation of traffic rights available to India.  The Committee, however notes that despite the
 permission granted to private carriers to operate services to USA and Belgium, the services have not commenced and it
 is surprising that the Ministry has left the matter to the commercial judgement of the concerned airlines.  The
 Committee is of the view that there should be proper monitoring of the permissions granted by the Ministry and
 recommends that it must be ensured that actual operations are started by the operators so that the stated objective of
 optimum utilisation of traffic rights is achieved.  The Committee also reiterates its recommendations contained in its
 96
th Report, which is reproduced below: -
 
“The Committee notes from the reply of the Ministry that there are only two minimum eligibility criteria prescribed for
 selection of scheduled domestic airlines to be allowed to operate on international routes, namely, a minimum fleet

 strength of 20 aircrafts and a minimum experience of five years operations on domestic routes.  The Committee also
 notes that the basic policy of the Government to allow the scheduled carriers to operate on international routes has been
 framed after due consideration of the Report of Naresh Chandra Committee, which was submitted to the Ministry in
 December 2003.  The said committee had reportedly revealed that we are presently using only 40% of our bilateral
 rights.  However, the Committee feels that the steep restrictions imposed by the Ministry are impediments in achieving
 the basic objectives behind the new policy to mitigate under capacity in the international segment and to enhance global
 connectivity to and from different states in the country.   The Committee recommends that in view of the irreversible
 nature of the new policy, the Ministry should review its prescribed standards regarding fleet strength, maintenance
 facilities, safety systems etc. for granting licences to new airlines in the domestic sector, taking into consideration the
 requirements for the international sector also.  Such a review would enable the relaxation of the existing stringent
 restrictions on Indian scheduled airlines for international operations. The Committee also notes that the stringent
 restrictions have not been able to avoid the denial of flights to one of the private airlines to destinations in the United
 States of America.”(Para 108)
 
SHORTAGE OF TRAINED MANPOWER IN CIVIL AVIATION SECTOR
 
The Committee notes that the civil aviation sector in the country is growing at a fast rate and more and more private
 carriers are joining the field.  There is also a proposal for large-scale aircrafts acquisition by Indian Airlines and Air
 India.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the various efforts at augmenting the number of trained Pilots, Air
 Traffic Control (ATC) Personnel and Service and Maintenance Engineers should receive focussed attention, so that
 there are no slippages in the targets sought to be achieved.   The Committee also recommends that   the capacity of
 upgradation of Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Academy (IGRUA) and the construction of the new Flying Training
 Academy at Gondia should be completed within a stipulated time frame.(Para 118)
 
MERGER OF AIRLINES
 
The Committee observes that of late there have been changes in the strategy of private airlines operators by way of
 consolidation of their operations.  The Committee feels that these conditions can lead to monopolistic situation in civil
 aviation sector and there is a need to check this trend.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that while formulating
 the new Civil Aviation Policy, all the consequences of merger of airlines including the matter regarding reallocation of
 infrastructural facilities at airports should be addressed properly.(Para 121)
 
ROUTE DISPERSAL GUIDELINES
 
123.     The Committee is surprised to note that no final decision has been taken by the Ministry to review the existing
 Routes Dispersal Guidelines although the internal Committee set up under the Chairmanship of Director General of
 Civil Aviation had submitted its report on 18
th March 2005. The Committee also notes that although no decision has
 been taken on the proposal to impose a surcharge to fund the minimum subsidy to be given to the successful bidder
 who offers to operate in North Eastern region, island territories and the States of Jammu & Kashmir, the proposal was
 initiated on the demands made by airlines operators for amending/scrapping of the Route Dispersal Guidelines as they
 find it uneconomical to operate to the said regions on purely commercial considerations.  The Committee is of the view
 that the demands of the private operators are unjustified as the national carriers are also operating to the said regions on
 purely social considerations. The Committee is of the opinion that the private carriers should also share the social
 obligations.  In view of the boom in the domestic passenger traffic, the Committee feels that the hitherto non-
commercial or unviable routes have been transformed into profit making routes.  The Committee recommends that the
 Ministry should make an analysis of the profit/loss on the so-called non-commercial routes before taking a final
 decisions in the matter.   The Committee is also of the opinion that the profits generated by the private carriers are used
 by them to operate flights in the non-commercial routes, if any.  In this scenario, the Committee recommends that the
 Ministry should also make a study as to whether the grant of minimum subsidy to airline operators will result in
 corresponding reduction in airfares on the main routes.(Para 123)

129.     The Committee notes that despite the efforts made by the Ministry, the private airlines operators have not yet
 trained their pilots for ILS Cat-III operations.  The Committee also notes that the Director General of Civil Aviation has
 been asked to thoroughly examine the legal and operational issues related to making the training in Cat-II / III A & B
 operations mandatory. The Committee recommends that the Report of Director General of Civil Aviation should be
 expedited and suitable steps should be taken in time to enhance the utilisation of ILS Cat-II/III A & B installed at Indira
 Gandhi International Airport, Delhi by private carriers.  In this context, the Committee reiterates its earlier
 recommendations contained in its 88

“The Committee recommends that in order to improve the operational efficiency during the extreme foggy conditions,
 the Ministry should amend 'Aircraft Rules' to incorporate a provision for making training of pilots compulsory by the
 private airlines on CAT-III System so that the investment made by the Government on the installation of the system
 through the tax payers' money is not underutilized.”
 
“The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that in order to improve the operational efficiency during the
 extreme foggy conditions, training of pilots should be made compulsory by the private airlines on CAT-III System. 
 The Committee further recommends that utilization of CAT-II and CAT-III systems by private airlines should be made
 compulsory by training a fixed minimum proportion of their pilots and it should be enforced by the Government
 strictly.”(Para 129)
 
BENCHMARKING OF AIRPORTS
 
The Committee notes that the although there are certain pre-requisites for declaration of an airport as international
 airport, the term world class airport is an objective term depending on the availability of facilities comparable to major
 airports in the region.  The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the airports declared as international airports in
 the country will not certainly be of world class standards unless passenger friendly facilities are developed.  In this
 context, the Committee notes that the customer satisfaction survey has revealed that overall satisfaction level with
 Mumbai International Airport, Delhi International Airport and Delhi Domestic Airport are well below the desired
 standard of 3.5 on a five point scale and also the average obtaining in airports in the Middle East/Asia Pacific region. 
 Only the figures in respect of Mumbai Domestic Airport are near to the desired standard of 3.5 and the average
 obtaining in airports in the Middle East/Asia Pacific region.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that there is a
 need to develop suitable institutional mechanism to assess the performance standards on continuous basis and take steps
 to upgrade the same to world-class standards.(Para 133)
 
ALLOTMENT OF PARKING BASES
 
The Committee notes that the Airports Authority of India is in the process of developing a policy on the allotment of
 night parking bays to various airlines and additional parking bases are being constructed at various airports in the
 country to meet the demand.  The Committee recommends that the policy should be formulated at the earliest and the
 work relating to construction of additional parking bases at various airports should be completed within a stipulated
 time frame.  The Committee also expects that the airline operators would avail the concessions offered by the Ministry
 to decongest the bigger airports.(Para 135)
 
PACKAGES FOR OFFICIAL TRAVEL AND LEAVE TRAVEL CONCESSION (LTC)
 
The Committee notes that Air India has initiated discussions with the various Ministries in the Government of India and
 is formulating a very attractive package for Government of India personnel travelling abroad.  The Committee
 recommends that the signing of the Memoranda of Understanding with various Ministries to ensure that a large part of
 Government of India personnel travel on Air India should be completed at the earliest so that the hitherto assured
 revenue will remain with the organisation.   The Committee notes that the special package of Leave Travel Concession
 to Government of India personnel to visit Jammu and Kashmir expires in June 2006 and therefore recommends that the
 Ministry should provide additional flights till such period to the extent possible in view of the non-availability of
 accommodation in the present flight schedule.(Para 139)

SARASVATI PROJECT
(Recommendation at Para 32)
 
14.       After going through the replies furnished by the Ministry of Culture, the Committee is of the firm view that
 Sarasvati Heritage Project did not conform to the criterion fixed for excavation of archaeological sites since no
 academic body or university had recommended the project.  The Committee also notes that there is an element of
 contradiction in the replies submitted to the Committee by the Department of Culture.  On the one hand, the Ministry of
 Culture has stated that the former Minister of Tourism and Culture was not the Chairman of the Sarasvati Heritage
 Project, while, on the other hand, the Ministry has stated that prior to the preparation of the project report, the
 Government had constituted an Advisory Committee with the then Minister of Tourism and Culture as Chairman and
 that this Committee had recommended the Saraswati Heritage Project.  The Committee further notes that the Ministry is
 not clear as to which research agency/scientific survey actually pointed out that the dry beds of River Ghaggar and
 River Chautang (River Drisadvati) are the bed of River Sarasvati.  The Committee understands that existence of River
 Sarasvati is purely a mythological one and a scientific institution like Archaeological Survey of India has not correctly
 proceeded in the matter.   The Committee regrets to note that a major project to the tune of Rs.36.02 crores was
 prepared which was, however, subsequently reduced to Rs.4.98 crores just to excavate a mythological river whereas,
 several other monuments/heritage sites of national importance are languishing in neglect due to acute shortage of funds.
 The Committee recommends that Archaeological Survey of India should strictly adhere to the criterion fixed for
 selection of excavation of sites.  Further, decisions for excavations should be made on the basis of proper scientific and
 technical appraisal and no extraneous factors should go into the decision making.  The Committee also recommends
 that before selecting a site for excavation, the Archaeological Survey of India should very carefully examine the
 potential of the site so that funds earmarked for the same do not go waste. The Committee would like to advise the
 Archaeological Survey of India that it should prevent itself from taking up exercises without a scientific basis which
 have all potentiality for subjective interpretation of historical facts thereby, leading to controversies.                      
                                                
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNEMNT
 
15.       The criteria for selection of ancient sites for archaeological excavation generally include (a) the site should hold
 promise of revealing an unknown culture or aspects of a lesser known culture, (b) the site needs to be cleared to
 facilitate conservation/preservation/area development in case of centrally protected site, and (c) the site is under threat
 of submergence owing to construction of dams, etc. The decision of excavation of site is made on the basis of site
 survey for surface studies, exploration around the site, topographical details, study of site location maps, sampling of
 surface finds, trial-trenching, and so on. It is according to the scope of work that the funds for excavation of the site are
 earmarked, and at times even augmented if required. For more scientific basis, the ASI has now been increasingly
 resorting to new scientific techniques like Ground Penetrating Radar, Satellite Imageries, Computer-Aided Survey by

 thermoluminescence dating, archaeo-botany, archaeo-zoology etc. for obtaining objective inputs.

NON-WRITING/PUBLICATION OF EXCAVATION REPORTS
(Recommendation at Para 46)
 
20.       The Committee is of the view that if excavation reports are not written, then all the taxpayers’ money spent on
 them goes waste.  Also, in absence of timely publication of excavation reports, the achievements of Archaeological
 Survey of India largely remain unnoticed by the public.  The Committee is extremely dissatisfied to observe that
 despite its repeated recommendations, the position in respect of writing of excavation reports has not improved much. 
 However, the Committee is hopeful that the steps now initiated by Archaeological Survey of India for clearing the
 backlog in respect of writing excavation reports would yield some positive results.  The Committee recommends that
 the Archaeological Survey of India should enforce a fixed time frame for writing excavation reports after the
 excavation work has been completed, so that the public at large is not deprived of the vital right to information.  The
 Committee also recommends that the ASI should ensure that officials engaged in a particular excavation work are not
 transferred till such time that they complete the excavations and submit their reports.

25.       The Committee is concerned about the illegal encroachment of monuments/archaeological sites under the
 protection of Archaeological Survey of India.  In this context, the Committee would like to reiterate the

th Report on Demands for Grants 2005-06 of Ministry of Culture which is as under:

 Monuments.  The Committee is more concerned about the inability of Archeological Survey of India to get back the
 land from encroachers.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that a complete assessment should be made
 regarding encroachment of monuments/sites under the protection of Archaeological Survey of India all over the
 country.  Prompt action ought be taken against the encroachers with the help of State Governments/Local
 Administrations and the matter should be pursued at the highest level.  The Committee also recommends that adequate
 budgetary provisions should be made for security arrangements and protection of monuments, as this is the most crucial
 aspect of preserving our cultural heritage and wherever possible modern gadgets like, electronic surveillance cameras
 should be installed in the monuments.  The Committee feels that security is a sovereign function.  Hence, it is the
 responsibility of Central Government to get the monuments and other important assets protected.  In view of this, the
 Committee is of the opinion that the Union Home Ministry should pay the bills towards the expenses incurred for
 paying the Central Security Agencies under this head.  Accordingly, the Ministry of Culture should pursue the matter at
 the highest level."

            I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture,

2.     The Committee, at its meeting held on the 7
th October, 19 th October, 2005, and 5 th July, 2006, respectively
 considered the subject and heard the Secretary and other officials of Department of Tourism and ITDC.
 
3.     The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of Department of Tourism and ITDC  for placing before
 the Committee the material and information desired in connection with the subject and for clarifying the points raised
 by the Members. 
4.     The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 18
th September, 2006.
5.         A note of dissent to the Report of the Committee has been received. The chronology with regard thereto is as
 follows:
 
(i)         While adopting the Report on 18
th September, 2006 suggestions were also invited from the Members.  In the
 meanwhile, a letter was received from Shri Vedprakash Goyal which was neither a note of dissent nor concrete
 suggestions for carrying out changes in the particular paras of the Report. Only objections were raised on the comments
 of the Committee in the report on disinvestment of ITDC hotels. Copy of the letter given by Shri Vedprakash Goyal
 was also signed by four other Committee Members which was handed over to Committee Secretariat on 6 th October,
 2006 when the Committee met for other purposes. Thereafter, I discussed the issues with Shri Vedprakash Goyal and
 when there was no unanimity in our views, he was asked to give a note of dissent and accordingly a note of dissent to
 the Report has been given which has been appended to the Report.
 
(ii)        Incidentally, it is worth mentioning that the study on the “Functioning and Performance of India Tourism
 Development Corporation Limited”  was taken up by the previous Committee on 7
th October, 2005. Most of the
 meetings and evidences were recorded during the tenure of that Committee except one meeting which was held with the
 Secretary, Department of Tourism and CMD of ITDC by the present Committee. Neither I nor my distinguished
 colleague Shri Vedprakash Goyal was Member of that Committee. The present Committee has only adopted the Report
 which was prepared on the basis of studies made by the previous Committee. As such the present Committee has only
 carried over the unfinished work of previous Committee.
(iii)       Since the note of dissent contained aspersions on the Committee itself or inferences or ironical expressions or

 the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States order for removal of such lines or words or

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
            Over the past two decades, tourism has been identified as one of the world's largest industries with a growth rate
 of 5 per cent, per annum. The year 2003 saw tourism in our country emerging as a major sector of our economy,
 although it constitutes only a fraction of its vast potential.  A survey conducted by Conde Nast UK, the leading
 international travel magazine, ranked India amongst the top ten destinations of the world.  A poll conducted by Lonely
 Planet has ranked India as one of the top five destinations in the world. This Committee i.e. the Department-related
 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture discussed the kind of development that is taking

108th Report of Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/108threport.htm[28-08-2018 13:19:51]
 place in the economy and particularly, in the aviation and tourism sectors where new priorities and initiatives have been
 actuated  and was of the view that the functioning of ITDC becomes very crucial in this kind of situation and
 particularly when it aimed to provide leadership and play a catalytic role in the development of tourism infrastructure in
 the country, thereby, promoting India as a tourist destination.  The Committee therefore, decided to take-up the subject
 "functioning and performance of ITDC" for examination and report.
2.         The Committee requested the Department of Tourism to furnish a detailed background note on the subject for
 consideration of the Committee.  The same was received on 7
th June, 2005.  The Committee also took oral evidences of
 the Secretary and other senior officials of the Department of Tourism and ITDC on the 7 th October, 19th October, 2005
 and 5 th July, 2006 respectively and sought replies to the queries on the subject.  The various aspects of the subject
 discussed by the Committee and Committee's observations thereon have been enumerated in the succeeding paragraphs
 of the report.
FORMATION AND OBJECTIVES OF ITDC
3.         The ITDC was established on the 1
st October, 1966 under the Company's Act, 1956 with the amalgamation of
 three undertakings namely Hotel Corporation of India Ltd., India Tourism Transport Undertaking Ltd. and India
 Tourism Corporation Ltd. into a unified Corporation.  The Corporation was incorporated with the sole objective of
 developing and expanding tourism infrastructure in the country thereby promoting India as a tourist destination.
 Subsequently, two Government companies namely the Ashok Hotels Ltd. and Janpath Hotel Ltd. were merged with
 ITDC on 20th March, 1970.  The mission of ITDC is to provide leadership and play catalytic role in the development of
 tourism infrastructure in the country and to achieve excellence in its strategic business units through professionalism,
 efficiency, value for money and customer focussed service.  Broadly, the main objectives of the Corporation are:
construction, management and marketing of hotels  and catering units.
providing tourist transport facilities and money changing facilities.
providing duty free shopping facilities to the tourists.
providing entertainment facilities to the tourists.
providing consultancy-cum-management services and training for tourism related projects.
production, distribution and sale of tourist publicity material.
promoting tourism through food festival, fairs and joint ventures in India and abroad.
ROLE OF ITDC
4.         The Committee was informed that ITDC is disseminating the benefits of its skills and experience for
 development of tourism in the country.  It is offering consultancy and management services both to private and public
 sectors and also undertaking the joint venture hotel projects in collaboration with the State Governments/State
 Corporations.  In addition, ITDC is popularizing Indian Cuisines abroad by participating in food-cum-cultural festivals. 
 Further, Corporation has diversified its activities by providing Management and Consultancy Services in collaboration
 with the Government both at Central and State levels, relating to tourism and engineering projects.  The Corporation
 has been playing a crucial and strategic role in ensuring proper dispersal of socio-economic benefits of tourism,
 promoting national integration and international understanding, helping removal of regional imbalances, generating
 employment opportunities, augmenting foreign exchange earnings and also acting as a catalyst in the development of
 tourism.  ITDC, thus, represents a major public sector effort towards the development of tourism within the country and
 abroad.      
5.         During the course of oral evidence, the Secretary, Department of Tourism has deposed before the Committee
 that:
"Sir, we entirely agree with the observation of the Committee that there has been a complete change, as a matter of fact,
 in the context in which the ITDC is now operating.  At this moment, everybody knows and recognizes that the economy
 has changed.  The economy has become very, very complex and has much more developed than it was in the early 50's
 or 60's.  The hospitality industry itself has grown beyond recognition. Remarkable growth has taken place in this sector
 and it is also poised for further growth in the years to come. At the same time, the private sector has come on its own. 
 Tourism industry in the private sector has established itself and, as a matter of fact, some of them have set world-class
 benchmarks for others in the world to emulate.  Besides, earlier, even the Department of Tourism itself was not very
 active.  Now the Department of Tourism has taken on itself the role of promoting tourism. The Department of Tourism
 is meant not only for the ITDC, but also for the entire tourism sector, which also includes the private sector in a major
 way, so, that is why, now it has been a Government effort, but driven by the private sector in a major way.  That is how
 the change is taking place."
6.         The Committee notes that with the transformation of Indian economy to keep pace with globalization, the ITDC

 is striving to achieve its objectives of developing and expanding tourism infrastructure in the country and promoting
 India as a tourist ­­­­­­­­­­­destination of the globe by providing all tourism related services under a single roof.  The
 Committee feels that though ITDC is functioning on commercial lines it should also help in removing the regional
 imbalances by proper diffusion and uniform percolation of socio-economic benefits amongst all stratas of the society. 
 The Committee feels that in this manner, it would pave the way for more employment generation in the tourism sector
 and act as a catalyst for development of Tourism across the country. 
ORGANIZATIONAL SET-UP
7.         The present organizational set up at the corporate level comprises of C&MD, Functional Director and heads of
 business groups viz. Ashok Groups of Hotels & Catering.  Ashok International Trade, Ashok Travel & Tours, Ashok
 Reservation & Marketing Services, Ashok Creatives, Ashok Institute of Hospitality & Tourism Management and
 Engineering Consultancy and Business Development.  Besides, there are some support/service departments namely
 Human Resource Management, Finance & Accounts, Public Relations, Secretarial and Vigilance & Security.
BOARD OF DIRECTORS
8.         To a query regarding the criteria for selection of non-official Government Directors on the Board of ITDC and
 their contribution in the functioning of ITDC, the Department of Tourism has submitted that the posts of part-time non-
official Directors on the Board of ITDC are lying vacant at the moment as the Government is in the process of filling up
 these posts.  The ITDC Board of Directors, presently consists of five Directors.  In addition, there is one functional
 Director and three Government Directors. 
9.         ITDC, being a Public Sector Enterprise, the appointment of Directors – both executive and non-executive is
 made by the Government of India.  Presently, the Board of Directors comprises of CMD.  Director (Finance) and three
 part-time official Directors representing Government of India namely Shri Parvez Dewan, CMD, Shri P. P. Singh,
 Director (F), Shri P. K. Mishra AS&FA(Tourism), Shri Atul Chaturvedi, Director (T) and Shri Manoj Sethi, Finance
 Controller(Tourism).  The following criteria is adopted for selection and appointment of such Directors:
(a) Qualification Minimum qualification for part-time non-official Directors would be
 graduate degree from a recognized university.
(b) Experience Not less than ten years at the level of Joint Secretary and above in the
 government; CMD/MD in Corporate Sector/PSU; Professor level in
 academic institution or eminent professional of repute.
(c) Age The age band should be between 45-65 years (minimum/maximum limit).
 
10.       As per guidelines issued by Department of Public Enterprises, the Board of Directors of Public Sector
 Enterprises consist of Functional Directors, Government Directors and Non-official Directors.  The Functional
 Directors are full time operational Directors and are appointed through selection by Public Sector Enterprises Selection
 Board.  The Government Directors are appointed by administrative Ministries and are the officers dealing with
 concerned enterprises.  The Non-official Directors are also nominated by the administrative Ministries and are to be
 drawn from public-men, technocrats, management experts and consultants and professional managers in industry and
 trade with proven ability and managerial expertise with the objective of making the Board more professional.
11.       Regarding monthly remuneration the Department informed that no pay structure is in vogue in respect of the
 non-official Directors.   They are paid for attending the meetings @Rs.1000/- per meeting plus TA/DA as per
 Department of Public Enterprises Guidelines.  During the year 2004-05, six meetings of the Board of Directors were
 held to transact the business of the company.
12.       The Committee notes with concern that the re-constitution of the ITDC's Board of Directors with appointment of
 non-official part time Directors remains under consideration of the Department.  The Committee feels that presence
 of    non-official Directors on the Board will make the Board more professional.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the posts of part time non-official Directors on the Board of ITDC should be filled up by the
 Government from the concerned areas without fail.
GEOGRAPHICAL SPREAD OF ITDC
13.       Giving the details of logistics available with the ITDC and its role in the development of remote rural areas in
 the country, the Department of Tourism informed that since its inception, ITDC has been playing both the promotional
 as well as commercial role for the development of tourism infrastructure across the country. A statement showing the
 various units of ITDC spread all over the country zone-wise is given below:

14.       The ITDC never confined its activities to only the metropolitan cities but also promoted remote areas.  In tune
 with its promotional role, it has ventured into new destinations in remote/backward regions where private sector was
 initially shy to invest due to low returns and high risk. It operated Kaziranga Forest Lodge, Kanha Forest Lodge etc.
 which were subsequently transferred to State Governments.  It opened Chaupal at Ashok Hotel providing rural
 ambience with the objective to promote rural tourism. 
15.       The Department of Tourism further informed that in the changed tourism scenario, ITDC has diversified into
 new service oriented business activities and is playing the role of a facilitator to various agencies including Department
 of Tourism in undertaking execution of tourism & engineering projects at Jharkhand, Somnath, Noida, Delhi,
 Kanyakumari, Gulmarg etc. and mounting of SEL Shows at Udaigiri, Kumbalgarh, Madurai, Sabarmati Ashram,
 Vivekanand Rock Memorial, Kanyakumari, Hampi, Chandigarh etc. However, consequent upon the implementation of
 the disinvestment policy ITDC stopped setting up new hotels/resorts in the country. ITDC had also set up a Tourism
 Task Force to promote camping and adventure tourism in the remote areas in collaboration with local
 Governments/authorities.  During 1991-93, it set up camps at the following places with the financial support from the
 Department of Tourism:
Adventure Camp at Narwar (Madhya Pradesh)
 Desert Camp at Jaisalmer (Rajasthan)                                                                       
Mountain Camp at Bir (Himachal Pradesh)
Beach Camp at Union Territory of Diu
Island Camp in Andamans
Jungle Camp at Coorg
Mountain Camp at Solangh Nallah (Himachal Pradesh)
16.       Such camps can again be set up in future at rural areas of the country with the financial support from Department
 of Tourism. Besides, the Engineering Division of ITDC has contributed in the development of villages in the following
 ways:
Preparation of Detailed Project Reports for development of villages under Rural Tourism Development Scheme of the
 Department of Tourism, Government of India  Sesawng (Mizoram), Bhitar Gram (UP), Kamaleshwarpur (Chattisgarh),
 Rengo village (Arunachal Pradesh) and Leshumi (Nagaland), Sasatgre (Meghalaya).  The reports have been submitted
 to Department of Tourism for approval and release of funds for execution of works. The execution of work will also be
 undertaken by ITDC, if these are assigned to ITDC.
ITDC has taken up the work under Chaudhary Charan Singh Scheme in Jyotisar (Haryana), Balia (UP) & Barsana
 (UP).  The works at Hundru (Jharkhand) and Johna (Jharkhand) have also been undertaken on behalf of Department of
 Tourism, Government of Jharkhand.
ITDC has also undertaken works of construction of Chaupals in Kotla Mubarakpur, Nagali Rajapur, Sarai Kale Khan in
 Delhi.
17.       The Committee notes that ITDC has been playing active role, both as promotional and commercial for the
 development of tourism infrastructure spreading all over the country. The Committee also notes that ITDC has set-up a
 Tourism Task Force for promotion of camping and adventure tourism in the remote areas in collaboration with the local
 Governments/authorities.  The Committee finds that consequent upon the implementation of disinvestment policy, the
 presence of the Corporation in the country has shrunk and ITDC stopped  setting up of new hotels/resorts in the
 country.  The Committee feels that this has not only confined the activities of ITDC to metropolitan cities but also
 diminished the geographic spread of ITDC.  The Committee, however,  recommends that the geographic spread of
 ITDC should not be confined only to metro cities of the nation but it should further be expanded to rural areas and
 hinterlands to provide required logistics to foreign and domestic tourists and the Department of Tourism should provide
 all support/help to ITDC in this regard.  The Committee further recommends that Department of Tourism should
 consider the detailed project reports prepared by ITDC under Rural Tourism Development Scheme and release funds
 for execution of works.  The Committee also recommends that ITDC should monitor the execution under the Rural
 Tourism Development Scheme.   This will create infrastructure in the villages, which in turn will play catalytic role for
 attracting private investment there.

REASONS FOR LOW PERFORMANCE AND MEASURES TAKEN FOR IMPROVEMENT IN THE

23.       The Committee desired to know the reasons for low performance by the ITDC in earlier years and whether any
 measures have been put -in place for improvement of performance and future plans to meet such eventualities, the
 Department of Tourism in their written replies informed the Committee that Tourism scenario in the country was
 adversely affected by following national and international events/factors which resulted into low performance of ITDC
 :
Lower turnout of international business travellers due to following international and domestic reasons:
Terrorists attack in USA on 11
th Sept., 2001.
Conflict in Afghanistan.
Terrorists attack on Indian Parliament on 13
th Dec., 2001
Gujarat Riots
Tension on Indo-Pak Borders and advisories issued by a number of foreign countries against visiting India.
Media publicity on  ITDC disinvestment adversely affected business inflow into hotels from prospective clients and
 potential markets.
Lack of refurbishing/upgradation of hotel properties because of the process of disinvestment.
Uncertainty and psycho-fear created in employees due to disinvestment in ITDC.
Substantial increase in the license fee and royalty in respect of duty free shops payable to AAI.
Increase in availability of hotel rooms in approved sector resulting in cut-throat competition and price war.

Consolidation in the existing facilities/services of the ITDC and sub-contracting some services.
To have strict control over wastage and pilferage.
Recovery of outstanding dues form public/private parties.

83.       As regards, impact of disinvestment, the Department submitted that ITDC started feeling the adverse impact as
 soon as the Government decided to disinvest ITDC Hotels.  Renovation schemes were put on hold rendering ITDC
 properties non-competitive. The psycho-fear created by uncertainty kept the morale of the employees very low
 affecting the services.  The business providers were hesitant to do business with ITDC due to the uncertainty.  Media
 publicity on ITDC disinvestment had also played a major role affecting business adversely.  In the initial stage itself,
 ITDC was directed by the Department of Disinvestment to avoid making any long-term commitment which resulted in
 drifting of its Conference Business as well as room bookings from prospective clients and potential market.  As a result
 of the impact of disinvestment, ITDC suffered losses during four consecutive years from 1999-2000 to 2002-03 leading
 to financial crunch in ITDC. After disinvestment of 18 hotel properties, the largest Hotel Chain of Ashok Group of
 Hotels was broken and ITDC's presence as a hotelier is now confined only to certain areas, its geographical spread
 achieved earlier stood diminished.

 information/data/material to the Advisor, Ministries of Disinvestment and Tourism and to implement decision of the
 Government for disinvestment of hotels.  The apex corporation in the field of tourism was not even given a reasonable
 opportunity for making presentation and defending its case before the Disinvestment Commission or pleading its case.
 The Committee strongly denounces the move of the Government for not giving any opportunity to the ITDC for being
 heard before disinvestment of its properties although it was performing well.  Further, by putting few other ITDC hotels
 in the disinvestments list for some years and subsequently removing those therefrom, also dampened the spirit of the
 employees working in these hotels and of the Corporation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a thorough
 probe in the matter of disinvestment of ITDC Hotels be undertaken by the Government to know the entire sequence of
 disinvestment of ITDC's properties and reasons for doing so by some independent agency. The probe should also
 include as to what was the end use of the money collected through disinvestments of ITDC properties.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS – AT A GLANCE
ROLE OF ITDC
            The Committee notes that with the transformation of Indian economy to keep pace with globalization, the ITDC
 is striving to achieve its objectives of developing and expanding tourism infrastructure in the country and promoting
 India as a tourist ­­­­­­­­­­­destination of the globe by providing all tourism related services under a single roof.  The
 Committee feels that  though ITDC is functioning on commercial lines it should also help in removing the regional
 imbalances by proper diffusion and uniform percolation of socio-economic benefits amongst  all stratas of the society. 
 The Committee feels that in this manner, it would pave the way for more employment generation in the tourism sector
 and act as a catalyst for development of Tourism across the country.                                   (Para 6)
BOARD OF DIRECTORS
            The Committee notes with concern that the re-constitution of the ITDC's Board of Directors with appointment of
 non-official part time Directors remains under consideration of the Department.  The Committee feels that presence
 of    non-official Directors on the Board will make the Board more professional.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the posts of part time non-official Directors on the Board of ITDC should be filled up by the
 Government from the concerned areas without fail.
                                                     (Para 12)
 GEOGRAPHICAL SPREAD OF ITDC
            The Committee notes that ITDC has been playing active role, both as promotional and commercial for the
 development of tourism infrastructure spreading all over the country. The Committee also notes that ITDC has set-up a
 Tourism Task Force for promotion of camping and adventure tourism in the remote areas in collaboration with the local
 Governments/authorities.  The Committee finds that consequent upon the implementation of disinvestment policy, the
 presence of the Corporation in the country has shrunk and ITDC stopped  setting up of new hotels/resorts in the
 country.  The Committee feels that this has not only confined the activities of ITDC to metropolitan cities but also
 diminished the geographic spread of ITDC.  The Committee, however, recommends that the geographic spread of
 ITDC should not be confined only to metro cities of the nation but it should further be expanded to rural areas and
 hinterlands to provide required logistics to foreign and domestic tourists and the Department of Tourism should provide
 all support/help to ITDC in this regard.  The Committee further recommends that Department of Tourism should
 consider the detailed project reports prepared by ITDC under Rural Tourism Development Scheme and release funds
 for execution of works.  The Committee also recommends that ITDC should monitor the execution under the Rural
 Tourism Development Scheme.   This will create infrastructure in the villages, which in turn will play catalytic role for

            The Committee notes the reasons put-forth by the Department of Tourism for low performance from 1999-2000

 difficult for the Corporation to maintain even the present level of business. The Committee is also of the view that it is

 the Department to conduct a detailed study by some outside agency for analyzing the reasons for low performance of
 ITDC vis-a-vis its profitability.                                                                                                                 (Para 40)
NETWORK OF ITDC SERVICES – ASHOK GROUP OF HOTELS AND CATERING ESTABLISHMENTS
            The committee notes that after incurring losses since 2002-03, the Ashok Groups of Hotels has emerged as a
 profit making centre in the year 2004-05.  The Committee also notes that Ashok Hotel being the flagship, has a brand
 image but that image is no longer there as compared to the hotels in the private sectors.  The Committee feels that there
 is a need for restoration of this image in the market so that they can contribute towards the hospitality industry at large
 and earn revenue for themselves. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to make concerted efforts to
 turnaround ITDC Ashok Groups of Hotel with world class facilities and re-position it as an brand ambassador in its
 group. The Committee also recommends that in order to make ITDC a leading organisation for the future, the
 Government should grant matching equity support to ITDC on 1:1 basis for upgradation and major renovation of Ashok
 Groups of Hotels and energising other divisions too.  The 50% investment should be in the form of equity and 50%
 investment by way of loan from the Financial Institutions.              (Para 45)
ASHOK INTERNATIONAL TRADE DIVISION
The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Ashok International Trade Division  achieved  highest turnover during
 the year 2004-05 from retail sale of duty free goods to the direct consumers.  However, it notes with dismay that due to
 the impact of extraneous factors like SARS etc. there was a drop in the inbound as well as outbound tourists which
 further affected the tourism scenario in the country and particularly the ITDC.  The Committee feels that the vicious
 circle could have been broken if the local tourism is given enough encouragement and recommends the ITDC to
 enlarge the activities of Ashok International Trade Division, so as to counter the adverse impact of extraneous factors
 on the business and profitability.
            The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the privatization of Delhi and Mumbai airports due to which
 there prevails uncertainty in the operation of Duty Free Shops in these airports which contributed about 75% turnover
 of the Ashok International Trade Division (AITD).  However, the Committee notes that ITDC has been successful in
 securing and executing agreements with private management of Delhi and Mumbai Airports for extensions of licence
 for a further period of six months for operations of Duty Free Shops at these airports on the similar terms and
 conditions as was there with AAI previously.  The Committee feels that although the future status of AITD is uncertain
 and will much depend on the policy of the private managements in the selection of Duty Free operators but at the same
 time, ITDC can get the contract  with a mix of marketing strategies, right merchandising, competitive pricing and
 sustained product promotions.  The Committee is hopeful that given a fair and competitive environment, AITD will be
 able to secure the contract in these airports in the future besides operating Duty Free Shops in Chennai, Kolkata,
 Trivandrum, Goa, Calicut, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad and Bangalore airports.  The Committee recommends the
 Department to make all out efforts in securing the contract for operating Duty Free Shops in these airports.
            The Committee notes with dismay that the issue of rent/royalty between AAI and ITDC has not yet been settled
 and the case is under mediation.  The Committee is of the view that ITDC though a commercial entity is exposed to
 business risk but at the same time, the incidence of high rate of rent have adversely affected the product pricing,
 profitability and competitive edge of the AITD.  The Committee opined that inspite of the contract, the dispute be
 resolved on the basis of equity between AAI and ITDC and some concessions may also be offered.  The Committee
 recommends the Department to pursue the matter with the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Ministry of Finance for early
 settlement of issue of royalty.                 (Para 50, 52 & 54)
ASHOK TRAVELS & TOURS
            The Committee notes with dismay that Ashok Travel and Tours Division of ITDC is continuously incurring
 losses because of the highly competitive market conditions.  The Committee is of the view that the deficit can be
 balanced by the ITDC from its corporate earnings.  The Committee recommends the Department to suitably restructure
 the Division to function as a major tour operator in the country and take advantage of market conditions and prevailing
 boom in the tourism sector.                                                (Para 58)
ASHOK RESERVATIONS AND MARKETING SERVICES
            The Committee notes that Ashok reservations and marketing services division of ITDC has been appointed as
 event manager by various Ministries/Organisations for handling conferences, events and exhibitions. The Committee
 recommends the Department to resort to aggressive marketing plans so that ITDC becomes the leading event manager
 of the country.                                      (Para 61)
