ASHOK CREATIVES
            The Committee notes that Ashok Creatives is the only specialised tourism communication agency in the country
 offering a range of tourism and travel related services to Department of Tourism.  The Committee recommends that this
 Division should excel in capturing the booming sector like Advertising by taking advantage of the experience and the
 creative talent of in-house people and continue to expand its activities by undertaking tourism development projects for
 the Department of Tourism/State Government Tourism Departments and other external agencies.                  
                                                ( Para 66)
 ENGINEERING & CONSULTANCY - BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT DIVISION
            The Committee notes that the Engineering Division of ITDC has been entrusted with the job of development of
 tourism infrastructure and various other projects by the Department of Tourism and State Government besides
 providing Engineering Consultancy services including preparation of feasibility reports, tourism master plans and
 detailed project reports.  The Committee feels that there is a need for re-organisation of this Division, as it has to play a
 major role for providing consultancy and assistance to various State Governments and other regions of the country. 
 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Engineering & Consultancy Division of ITDC should be strengthened
 and motivated so that they can implement projects of infrastructure development with the State Governments at a rapid
 rate.                                                              (Para 71)
ASHOK INSTITUTE OF HOSPITALITY & TOURISM MANAGEMENT
            The Committee notes that Ashok Institute of Hospitality & Tourism management  is imparting training for
 hospitality, travel and tourism Industry and emerged as a separate strategic business unit and education provider in
 human resource development for the hospitality and tourism sector.  The Committee is of the view that there is a great
 demand for trained manpower in the hospitality & tourism sector and availability of trained manpower is a must to
 meet the growing demand for excellence in the tourism sector.  The Committee is of the firm opinion that contemporary
 relevance of ITDC is more in terms of its demonstrative ability of showcasing new ideas that are emerging in the field
 of tourism and it should set standards to deal with the challenges in the field of tourism.  The Committee however,
 recommends the ITDC to expand the scope of activities of Ashok Institute of Hospitality &Tourism Management to
 other regions in the country and impart quality education for meeting the shortage of trained manpower in the tourism
 and other sectors.                                                                                                            (Para 75)
SOUND & LIGHT SHOWS
            The Committee notes that after incurring losses since 2002-03, the Ashok Sound & Light Show has turnaround
 during 2004-05 and earned profit. The Committee feels that in order to showcase India's rich cultural  heritage, history
 and values to the masses,   there is a need to produce such Sound & Light Show in every State.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends the Department to explore the possibility of mounting sound and light shows in every
 State.                    (Para 77)
ASHOK TOURIST SERVICE STATION
            The Committee notes that that Ashok Tourist Service Station is an Indian Oil retail outlet-cum-service station
 run by the ITDC.  The Committee also notes that this service station is running into losses.  The Committee
 recommends the Department to restructure the service station suitably besides, implementing sales-promotion schemes
 for recovering from the burgeoning losses in the future.                       (Para 79)
DISINVESTMENT OF ITDC HOTELS
            The Committee is at pain to note that the role of ITDC was limited only upto providing
 information/data/material to the Advisor, Ministries of Disinvestment  and Tourism and to implement decision of the
 Government for disinvestment of hotels.  The apex corporation in the field of tourism was not even given a reasonable
 opportunity for making presentation and defending its case before the Disinvestment Commission or pleading its case.
 The Committee strongly denounces the move of the Government  for not giving any opportunity to the ITDC for being
 heard before disinvestment of its properties although it was performing well.  Further, by putting few other ITDC hotels
 in the disinvestments list for some years and subsequently removing those therefrom, also dampened the spirit of the
 employees working in these hotels and of the Corporation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a thorough
 probe in the matter of disinvestment of ITDC Hotels  be undertaken by the Government to know the entire sequence  of
 disinvestment of ITDC's properties and reasons for doing so by some independent agency. The probe should also
 include as to what was the end use of the money collected through disinvestments of ITDC properties.             
            The Committee notes that disinvestment and its impact on the ITDC has made the organisation crippled.  The
 Committee finds that during 1999-2003, ITDC made a total loss of Rs. 159.52 crore and before and after that period,
 ITDC has generally been performing well.  The Committee observes that during the process of disinvestment, ITDC
 also faced certain difficulties because of some external factors and suffered losses during four consecutive years leading

Phalguna 18, 1928 (Saka) Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture
 
                                                              
                          
 
 
 
 
 
* Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II, Section-2, dated 07.08.2006.
* *Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, No. 43442 dated 05.09.2006.
R E P O R T
The Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 7 th August, 2006.  The Bill was
 referred to this Committee for examination and report.  Under the mandate, the Committee has examined the Bill and
 finalised the Report after hearing the views of various stakeholders, experts and Ministries/Departments.  The Bill seeks
 to enable the Government to regulate the foreign registered aircrafts which are being operated in India, to give powers
 to Government for the purpose of licensing of personnel engaged in air traffic control, certification, inspection and
 regulation of communication, navigation and surveillance and air traffic management, safeguarding civil aviation
 against acts of unlawful interference and to ensure civil aviation security and investigation of "incident" along with
 "accident". This Bill also proposes to give more powers to the Director General of Civil Aviation for performing safety
 oversight functions and to impose penalty for contravention of the provisions of the Chicago Convention. 
 
2.         The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill states that a sea change has occurred in the aviation sector
 during the last two decades.   The Central Government are already exercising their control over the manufacture, use
 and operation of civil aircrafts under various provision of the Aircraft Act 1934 and also under various rules and
 instructions issued under that Act. The management and operation of domestic airports, navigation and communication
 facilities and air traffic control at all airports was transferred from Government to the National Airports Authority in
 1986.  The National Airports Authority was merged with the International Airport Authority of India w.e.f. 1
st April
 1995 to form a single entity named Airports Authority of India.  The Government opened the domestic air transport
 services to the private sector in 1994.  With drastic developments in the fields of technology, communication,
 navigation, surveillance etc. the air traffic management system is also switching over from ground based to satellite
 based technology in the near future.  With unprecedented growth of the civil aviation sector it has become all the more
 important to provide  safeguards for civil aviation security.
 
3.         The statement of objects and reasons further states that the safety and security provisions and international
 standards as mentioned in the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) is to be implemented in the present
 scenario and it also states that the various provisions of the Convention on International Civil Aviation popularly
 known as Chicago Convention are to be given effect. 
 
4.         The Ministry of Civil Aviation in their background note furnished on the 25
th September 2006 to the Committee
 have brought out the following points as reasons for the introduction of the Bill:- 
 
I           Regulation of Foreign Registered Aircraft
 
5.         The Aircraft Act 1934 is not having any provision for extending the applicability of the act to foreign registered
 aircrafts which may be for the time being in or over India.  There is no regulatory power with the Government over the
 foreign registered aircraft when they are operating in India.  However, Clause (b) of Sub-rule (2) of Rule 1 of the
 Aircraft Rules, 1937, which have been made in exercise of the powers conferred by Sections 5, 7 and 8 of the Act,
 provides that these rules shall also apply to all aircraft and to persons on aircraft for the time being in or over India.  In
 order to remove this anomaly, it is considered necessary to have a similar express provision in the Act, so as to exercise
 regulatory control on foreign registered aircraft operating in or over India.  It is, therefore, proposed to insert a new
 clause in sub-section (2) of Section 1 of the Act to make this point explicit and clear.

II          Accident and Incident
 
6.         Section 7 of the Aircraft Act deals with the investigation of an accident only.  However, the word ‘incident’ is
 mentioned along with ‘accident’ in annexure 13 of Chicago Convention and it has made a clear distinction between
 accidents and incidents.  An accident is said to have taken place when a person is fatally or seriously injured during a
 flight or the aircraft sustains substantial damage or structural failure or the aircraft is missing or is completely
 inaccessible.  An incident, on the other hand, is an occurrence other than an accident associated with the operation of
 the aircraft that affects or could affect the safety of operations.  Since the Parent Act is silent over the incident aspect,
 the present legislation proposes to include the word incident along with the word accident in Section 7 of the Act.
 
 
 
 
 
III   Supervisory control over ATM standards/ATC personnel
 
7.       The Government after the enactment of Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 , has entrusted the job of
 management of civil airports in the country to the Airports Authority of India which includes the air traffic control and
 navigational and communication facilities.  But the basic responsibility of ensuring air safety lies with the Government
 only and for that purpose it needs to exercise supervisory control on the airports and its ground aids, communication
 and navigation and management facilities etc.  The proposed amendment will give powers to the Government to grant
 license to the personnel engaged in air traffic control in order to maintain the desired standards and level of
 proficiency.  Annexure 1 to the Chicago Convention also provides for such licensing by States in the air traffic control.
 
IV  Civil aviation security
 
 8.    With the opening of Indian skies to the private players and arrival of a large number of foreign players in the civil
 aviation sector, the need for reviewing of civil aviation security is also emphasized.  The expression “safety of aircraft
 operations” mainly covers the maintenance and airworthiness aspects of the aircraft and the proficiency of flight crews,
 ground engineers, etc.   There is no mention about the threat due to unlawful acts of interference.  The International
 Civil Aviation Organization has recognized the distinct importance of safety and security and they have laid down
 separate standards for security of civil aviation against unlawful interference.  In this context, necessity arises to enlarge
 the scope of Section 5 of the Act to give more powers to the Central Government to make rules to safeguard civil
 aviation against unlawful acts thereby ensuring civil aviation security. 
 
V         Powers to DGCA
 
9.         Section 5A of the Aircraft Act speaks about the powers given to DGCA or any other Officer empowered by
 Government to issue directions from time to time in consistent with the provisions of the act and rules.  Clause (b), (c),
 (e), (f), (g), (h) and (m) of sub section (2) of Section 5 give powers of licensing, inspection of aerodromes, inspection of
 aircrafts, the conditions under which  aircraft may be flown, the licensing of persons employed in the operation or
 maintenance of aircrafts, the permission to fly on an air route.  However, the fast growing air traffic scenario and the
 past experience have shown that there is a necessity to enlarge the above powers to cover some grey areas.  As such it is
 proposed that the regulation of air transport services, prohibition of flight over specified areas and prohibition of
 slaughtering and flaying of animals within 10kms radius of the airports will be included in the section 5 (2) of the Act. 
 The proposed amendments in Clause 5A of the Bill will give more powers to the DGCA over the air traffic control and
 operation of CNS. 
 
VI        Safety Oversight Functions
 
10.       Safety Oversight is a function to ensure effective implementation of safety related Standards and Recommended
 Practices and associated procedures contained in the Annexure to the Convention on International Civil Aviation and
 related ICAO documents.  Section 4 of the Aircraft Act, 1934 provides power to Central Government to make rules to
 implement the Convention.  Safety Oversight function is currently being performed by DGCA but the Act does not

109th report of commitee on Transport,tourism & culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/109threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:16:50]
 specifically delegate this function to DGCA.  It is, therefore, proposed in the Bill to add a Section in the Aircraft Act to
 specifically provide for Safety Oversight functions to be performed by Director – General of Civil Aviation or any
 other officer specially empowered in this behalf by Central Government.
 
VII       Penalties for violations of provisions of the act
 
11.       The aircraft operators who are violating various provisions of the Act are punishable under Sub Section 1A of
 Section 10 of the Act.  This punishment includes imposition of fine and imprisonment.  These punishments vary
 depending upon the act or rule it is violating.  These penalties were laid down several decades ago and the quantum of
 fine or imprisonment in this Section has now become out dated and it will not have much deterrent effect on the
 operators.  As such it is inevitable to raise the quantum of punishment in the existing scenario. 
 
VIII      Quantum of punishment for rules framed under Chicago 
            Convention
 
12.       Section 4 of the Act gives powers to the Government to frame rules for the implementation of Chicago
 Convention.  However, the violation of Rules is not punishable under Sub Section 2 of Section 10 of the Act.  It is
 therefore, proposed to amend Sub Section 2 of Section 10 to make such violations punishable.

Overall recommendation
 
18.       The Committee is of the view that this Bill is a piece meal effort on the part of the Government.  A lot of
 ambiguities exist regarding the role of Airports Authority of India, its powers and functions. In Clause 4A it is not clear
 as to who will be solely responsible to perform the safety oversight functions.  The Committee feels that with the
 coming of new private airports, green field airports, chartered airways and many other private and foreign airlines
 entering into Indian skies, Government should become more futuristic while bringing any new legislation. 
 Simultaneously the Committee is equally concerned about the fact that issues which have been incorporated in the

 civil aviation sector etc. in the proposed Bill. The proposed Bill should not leave any area uncovered pertaining to civil

(Para 17.39)
Overall recommendation
The Committee is of the view that this Bill is a piece meal effort on the part of the Government.  A lot of
 ambiguities exist regarding the role of Airports Authority of India, its powers and functions. In Clause 4A it is not clear
 as to who will be solely responsible to perform the safety oversight functions.  The Committee feels that with the
 coming of new private airports, green field airports, chartered airways and many other private and foreign airlines
 entering into Indian skies, Government should become more futuristic while bringing any new legislation. 
 Simultaneously the Committee is equally concerned about the fact that issues which have been incorporated in the
 present Bill and which require urgent attention should not be kept pending.  Therefore the Committee adopts the
 Clauses 2,3,7,8,9,10,11,12,13 and 14 and recommends that clauses 4,5 and 6 be redrafted as per the recommendations
 made at Para 17.17 above.  The Committee feels that the objectives behind the Bill i.e. ".....Now, with vast
 developments in technology, communication, navigation, surveillance and air traffic management are switching over
 from ground based to satellite based technology.  As a result of these developments, a need has arisen to lay down
 appropriate safeguards to ensure protection of civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference" are commendable but
 the legislation introduced for the purpose is found to be lacking in many accounts.  The Committee feels that no proper
 thinking has gone into the preparation of the Bill and that it has been very hastily drafted.  The Committee strongly
 feels that it is a piecemeal legislation and therefore, urges upon Government to carefully consider all the points
 mentioned above and recommends that the Government should come up with a comprehensive legislation incorporating
 all the suggestions made in the preceding paragraphs of the Report and covering all the issues concerning our Civil
 Aviation sector such as overcrowding at the airports and sky, requisite infrastructure, safety issues, flight regulations,
 social responsibilities of airlines of the public and private sectors, clear demarcation of various authorities handling
 civil aviation sector etc. in the proposed Bill. The proposed Bill should not leave any area uncovered pertaining to civil
 aviation.
(Para 18)

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            At present the Central Government through various provisions of the Aircraft Act, 1934 and the rules made
 thereunder exercises control in respect of manufacture, possession, use, operation, sale, import and export of civil
 aircrafts and licensing of aerodromes.
            2. In the last two decades, significant developments have taken place in the civil aviation sector in India.  The
 domestic air transport services were opened to the private sector in 1994 and the management and operation of the
 airports, the navigation, communication facilities and the air traffic control at airports were transferred to the Airports
 Authority of India with effect from the 1
st April, 1995.  Now, with vast developments in technology, communication,
 navigation, surveillance and air traffic management are switching over from ground based to satellite based
 technology.  As a result of these developments, a need has arisen to lay down appropriate safeguards to ensure
 protection of civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference.
            3. Keeping in view the above aspects as well as standards laid down by the International Civil Aviation
 Organisation (ICAO) for safety and security of civil aviation and also to give effect to various provisions of the
 Convention on International Civil Aviation popularly known as Chicago Convention, certain amendments are proposed
 to be made to the Aircraft Act, 1934.
            4. The Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006, inter-alia, seeks –
(a)
    to regulate foreign registered aircraft which is for the time being operating in or over India;
(b)   to empower the Central Government for –
(i)                  licensing of personnel engaged in air traffic control;
(ii)                certification, inspection and regulation of communication, navigation and surveillance
 and air traffic management;
(iii)               safeguarding civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference and to ensure civil
 aviation security; and
(iv)              investigation of incident along with accident.
(c)    to empower the Director General of Civil Aviation for performing safety oversight functions
(d)   to impose penalty for contravention of the provisions of the Chicago Convention;
(e)    to enhance quantum of existing penalties for violation of rules relating to carriage in aircraft of arms
 or explosives of providing false information or abetment of offences or non-compliance of directions
 with a view to achieve desired deterrent effect which would go a long way in raising the compliance
 level;
(f)     to enlarge the scope of the powers of Director General of Civil Aviation.
5. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
 Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred and
 Tenth Report of the Committee on the Central Road Fund (Amendment) Bill, 2006*.
 
2.         The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 18
th December, 2006. In pursuance of rules relating to the
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the
 Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha, referred** the Bill to the Committee on the 26 th December, 2006 for examination and
 report.
 
3.         The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary, Department of Road Transport and Highways and Secretary,
 Ministry of Rural Development at its meeting held on the 9
th March, 2007.
 
4.         The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill and considered the draft Report on the Bill
 and adopted the same on the 19.03.07 .
 
5.         The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways for the assistance provided during deliberations on the provisions of the Bill.

The Central Road Fund (Amendment) Bill, 2006 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 18 th December, 2006. On
 26th December, 2006 Hon'ble Chairman Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha referred the
 Bill to the Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture for examination and Report.  Under the mandate, the
 Committee has examined the Bill and finalised the Report after hearing the views of the nodal Ministry, i.e. , Road
 Transport and Highways and the only stakeholder i.e., Ministry of Rural Development.  The Bill seeks to amend the
 Central Road Fund Act, 2000 which provides for levy and collection by way of cess, excise and customs duty on petrol
 and high-speed diesel oil for development and maintenance of National Highways, rural roads, State roads and
 improvement of safety at railway crossings.  Under Section 9 of the Act the Central Government has the power to
 administer the fund and allocate and disburse such sums as are considered necessary to the concerned departments
 responsible for the development and maintenance of rural roads.  Under section 10, the Central Government is
 responsible for allocation of fifty percent of the cess on high-speed diesel oil for the development and maintenance of
 National Highways, rural roads, State roads and construction of roads over or under railways.  The fund available under
 Section 10 is utilized for the provision of all-weather connectivity to rural habitations through centrally sponsored
 scheme “Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana”.  Under the Scheme, a target has been set to provide road connectivity to
 all rural habitations having a population of 1000 and above (500 and above in hilly and tribal areas) by 2009.  This will
 require an investment of about Rs.48,000 crores.  To bridge the funding gap, the Government intends to borrow
 Rs.16,500 crores over a period of four years. Since the Central Road Fund Act, 2000 does not have any provision for
 borrowing for rural roads and utilization of the proceeds of future cess for repayment of loans, the Central Road Fund
 (Amendment) Bill, 2006 seeks to amend the Parent Act to enable the Central Government to take such measures as may
 be necessary to raise funds for the development of rural roads, and it may use the share of the fund for the repayment of
 any loan taken for the purpose of development of rural roads in any State or Union territory.
2.         The Central Road Fund was in existence since 1929.  It was being governed by the Parliamentary Resolution of
 1977 according to which an amount not less that 3.5 paise per litre of petrol consumed was to be set apart out of the
 custom and excise duty levied on petrol for development of roads.  The amount was being distributed between the State
 and the Central Schemes at the ratio of 80:20 after defraying the cost of administration of the Fund.  The two Houses of
 the Parliament passed a revised Resolution in May 1988 according to which an amount not less than 5 per cent of the
 basic price of petrol and diesel was earmarked for the development of Road Sector.  However, this resolution could not
 be implemented due to reservations expressed by Ministry of Finance and difficult resources position.
3.         In recognition of the need for funds for the road infrastructure sector the Union Budget for 1988-89 provided for
 a levy of additional excise duty and additional customs duty of one Rupee per litre of petrol.  Subsequently, an
 additional duty of one Rupee per litre on imported and domestic high speed diesel was proposed in the Budget  for
 1999-2000.  The revenue from these two levies was to accrue to the dedicated Central Road Fund.  It was also decided
 that 50 per cent of the cess on diesel will be given to the Ministry of Rural Development for Rural Roads.  A legal
 instrument was necessary for administration of the Fund.  Accordingly, due to urgency of the matter the Central Road
 Fund ordinance was promulgated on 1.11.2000 for this purpose.  Subsequently the ordinance was replaced by the
 Central Road Fund Act, 2000.
4.         With regard to utilisation and apportioning of the fund, the Department of Road, Transport and Highways
 informed the Committee as follows:-

(i)                  Development and maintenance of National Highways
(ii)                Development of rural roads
(iii)               Development and maintenance of other State roads including roads of inter-state and

(iv)              Construction of roads either under or over the railways by means of bridge and erection
 of safety works at the unmanned rail-road crossings; and
(v)                Disbursement in respect of such proposals as may be prescribed.
(B)            According to Sub-Section (viii) of Section 10 of the Act, the money accrued to the Fund will
 be apportioned in the following manner.
(a)                Fifty per cent of the cess on high speed diesel oil for the development of rural roads in
 such manner as may be prescribed; and
(b)               The balance amount of fifty per cent of cess of high speed diesel oil and the entire cess
 collected on petrol is allocated as follows:-
(i)                  An amount equal to fifty seven and one half percent of such sum for the development
 and maintenance of National Highways.
(ii)                An amount equal to twelve and one half per cent for the construction of roads either
 under or over the railways by means of bridge and erection of safety works on un-manned
 rail-road crossing.
(iii)
               The balance thirty per cent on development of roads other than National Highways and
 out of this amount, ten per cent, that is three per cent of the total share of State roads shall
 be kept as reserve by the Central Government for allocation to States for implementation
 of ,State road schemes of inter-state and economic importance' to be approved by the
 Central Government.
            Under Section 9, the Central Government shall have the power to administer the Fund and shall -
(a)
                take such decisions regarding investment on projects of national highways and
 expressways as it considers necessary;
(b)               take such measures as may be necessary to raise fund for the development and
 maintenance of the National Highways;
(c)                allocate and disburse such sums as are considered necessary, to the concerned
 departments responsible for the development and maintenance of -
(i)                  National Highways;
(ii)                rural roads;
(iii)               State roads; and
(iv)              Construction of roads either under or over the railways by means of a bridge and erect
 suitable safety works at unmanned rail-road level crossings.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
The Central Road Fund Act, 2000 provides for levy and collection by way of cess, excise and customs duty on
 petrol and high-speed diesel oil for development and maintenance of National Highways, rural roads, State roads and
 improvement of safety at railway crossings.  Under section 9, the Central Government has the power to administer the
 fund and allocate and disburse such sums as are considered necessary to the concerned departments responsible for the
 development and maintenance of rural roads.  Under section 10, the Central Government is responsible for allocation of
 fifty percent of the cess on high-speed diesel oil for the development and maintenance of National Highways, rural
 roads, State roads and construction of roads over or under railways.  The allocation under section 10 is utilized for
 provision of all-weather connectivity to rural habitations through centrally sponsored scheme “Pradhan Mantri Gram
 Sadak Yojana”.  Under this, a target has been set to provide road connectivity to all rural habitations having a
 population of 1000 and above (500 and above in hilly and tribal areas) by 2009.  This will require an investment of
 about Rs.48,000 crores.  To bridge the funding gap it has been decided to borrow Rs.16,500 crores over a period of four
 years.
 
2.         Since the Central Road Fund Act, 2000 does not have any provision for borrowing for rural roads and utilization
 of the proceeds of future cess for repayment of loans, the Central Road Fund (Amendment) Bill, 2006 seeks to amend
 the Act to enable the Central Government to take such measures as may be necessary to raise funds for the development
 of rural roads, and it may use the share of the fund for the repayment of any loan taken for the purpose of development
 of rural roads in any State or Union territory.

5.      The Committee finds that despite its earlier recommendations on the aspect of funds utilization and the
 need for constant monitoring of projects, the Department of Road Transport and Highways has done precious
 little to improve the situation. This is evident from the reply of the Department with regard to non-utilisation of
 funds that the allocation for road sector is based on anticipated implementation of projects every year. The
 trend from the year 2002-03 onwards would reveal that the actual utilization has been more or less steady and
 consistent. The slippages occur when major projects do not get implemented for the years they are projected for
 implementation. For instance, allocations for programmes of NHDP Phase-III and SARDP-NE did not
 materialize fully because the approvals were not available in the time-frame projected. The Committee desires to
 know as to why approvals were not available in time and whether any responsibility has been fixed in the
 matter. The Committee observes that the budgetary allocation of the Department of Road Transport and
 Highways was substantially increased from 2004-05 (revised estimates) of Rs. 8566.00 crore  to Rs. 13293.75
 crore during 2005-06 and for 2006-07 (budget estimates) the allocation has again been increased to Rs 15307.31
 crore. The Committee, therefore, re-emphasises that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should
 devise strategies, in such a way so that they are able to fully utilize the funds placed at their disposal. They
 should also evolve some mechanism to identify bottlenecks causing delays and work towards resolving all such
 hindrances in coordination with all the concerned agencies. This would also help them to avoid time overrun and
 consequential cost overrun of the projects to be executed by them.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6.      The reason for non-utilisation  of funds cannot be solely attributed to the delayed implementation of projects. It is
 also due to the fact, particularly, in case of NHDP Phase-III that the projects awarded have actually not yet been started
 owing to the reason that the stipulated time of 180 days given to the concessionaires for achieving financial close is yet
 to be over. The disbursement of grants will start only after the appointed date. Besides, in most of the projects, the
 bidders have offered negative grant against the grant anticipated by NHAI to be paid to the concessionaire. This has
 resulted in low level of expenditure which gives impression of less utilization of the allocated funds.
7.      Slow progress in some of the projects has also resulted into the less utilization of funds. The reasons for the slow
 progress include tardy performance of the contractors, delayed acquisition of land, delay in shifting of utilities, delay in
 forest/environment clearances etc. However, as suggested by the Committee, the bottlenecks causing delays have
 been/are being identified on project to project basis and remedial/corrective actions are also being taken wherever

 Investment Board (PIB) in its meetings held on 4th and 17th February, 2005 and approved on 21st February, 2005. It
 was decided by the Government that the matter might, in the first instance, be considered by Committee of Secretaries
 (CoS). The proposal was subsequently considered by the CoS on 5th April, 2005, 15th July, 2005 and 3rd August,
 2005. The phase-A of ‘Special Accelerated Road Development Programme’ in North Eastern region (SARDP-NE)
 comprising improvement to 1310 km. length of National Highways, State Roads and GS Roads at an estimated cost of
 Rs. 4618 crore was approved on 22.9.2005. Subsequent to the approval by CCEA, implementing agencies
 (NHAI/BRO/State PWDs) were directed to prepare Detailed Project Reports (DPRs). The DPRs were in progress by
 the implementing agencies tilll the end of 31st March, 2006; therefore, funds earmarked for SARDP-NE during 2005-
06 could not be utilized.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
9.      The Committee takes a serious view of the non-utilization of funds earmarked for SARDP-NE during 2005-
06. The National Highways serve not only as life line but also are strategically important taken into account the
 location of North East States. Therefore, the Committee again emphasise that the Government must take
 measures to ensure that funds earmarked for road sector are utilized optimally. The Committee also
 recommends that Department of Road Transport and Highways should take step so that the implementing
 agencies submit DPRs in time.
 
(Recommendation at Para 24)
10.    The Committee notes that in the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Five Year Plan, it is recommended that
 the Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport and Highways should prepare a detailed programme for the next two
 years keeping in view the level of budgetary support available and the need for leveraging to the maximum
 extent by adopting a proper mix of Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) and Build Operate and
 Transfer (BOT) projects. In view of the repeated under-utilization of budget allocation year after year, the
 Committee feels that the Department should not feel aggrieved by the fact that the budget provision for 2006-07
 has been enhanced by only 10 per cent from the budget provision for the year 2005-06 despite enhancement of
 11.2 per cent in the cost of construction during 2005 following increase in price indices of the basic ingredients of
 the road sector-steel, cement and bitumen. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways should devise effective institutional mechanisms to constantly monitor the progress of
 the projects under implementation and to ensure optimum utilization of funds. This mechanism should also
 involve means to fix responsibility at Project Head Level for the delay in completion of projects thereby acting as
 a deterrent for cost and time over-runs. The Committee recommends that the Department should also explore
 the possibility of opening of more budget / accounting offices keeping in view the increasing number of projects
 under implementation.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
11.    As per the recommendations in the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Five Year Plan, a comprehensive month-
wise and project-wise monitorable  target has been fixed, both for the physical and financial progress. The actual
 achievement against these targets is constantly being monitored and the reasons for slippages are critically analyzed to
 avoid their recurrence and to improve the progress of work. Dy. Chairman, Planning Commission also hold meetings
 on quarterly basis to review the progress against the monitorable  targets. As suggested by the Committee, the projects
 are being awarded by adopting a mix of EPC and BOT projects for NHDP Phase-II and BOT projects for NHDP Phase-
Ill onwards as per the policy decision taken by the Government that all future projects would be awarded only on BOT
 basis (either based on the toll or annuity or a suitable toll / annuity hybrid), with EPC award being made in specified
 exceptional cases only.
12.    To ensure optimum utilization of funds, effective institutional mechanisms are already in place in NHAI both at

15.    The Committee is constrained to note that the Golden Quadrilateral Project which was initially scheduled
 to be completed by the end of 2003 will now stretch upto 2007-08 and only 557 km. of North South - East West
 (NSEW) Corridor Project of 7,300 km. has been completed against the deadline for completion of entire project
 by December, 2007. The Committee recommends that action for revised estimates awarding the Ganjam
 -Icchapuram section of National Highway 5 of 50.8 km. length in Orissa, which is a part of the Golden
 Quadrilateral project are yet to be awarded, should be completed at the earliest and it should be ensured that
 the actual construction work is completed within the stipulated time-frame. The Committee takes exception to
 the fact that in NS-EW Corridor project, the target for award of contracts of 5,722 km. by December, 2005 in a
 phased manner could not be achieved by the Department and the target date has been shifted to March, 2006. In
 this context the Committee is surprised to note that the BE allocation for NHAI has been scaled down
 considerably during 2004-05 and 2005-06 in the respective revised estimates. The reasons for slowing down of
 the pace of construction put forward by the NHAI is unacceptable to the Committee in view of the fact that
 although Golden Quadrilateral Project is in the final stage of completion, but considerable work is still pending
 in NS-EW Corridor Project. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should play a pro-
active role in ensuring strict compliance of the targets fixed for completion of awarded projects and also the
 schedules for award of contracts in the pending projects. The Committee is of the view that proper verification
 of bank guarantees submitted by contractors should be undertaken at the initial stage itself to avoid termination
 of the contracts at a later stage. The Committee notes that increasing number of contracts are under
 implementation and being awarded. Therefore, it is recommended that the Department should be vigilant in
 respect of each contract and should strictly  enforce the compensation conditions in the contracts in respect of
 non-performing contractors. The Committee, further, recommends that the Department should not wait for the
 targeted date of completion to initiate action but should fix short-term targets for the contractors so that the
 projects can be monitored constantly and immediate and early remedial action may be taken in case of
 anticipated delays. The Committee also feels that the Department should draw-up a database of the performance
 of the contractors involved in NHDP and encourage outstanding contractors, who strictly comply with the
 construction standards and quality control and also complete the projects well within the targetted date, to
 undertake more and more projects as incentives.

22.    The present guidelines for approval of road/bridge works under the Centrally sponsored scheme of Inter State
 Connectivity and Economic Importance (ISC and EI) broadly cover following categories of works:—
              (i)    Inter-State roads/bridges necessary for ensuring through communication;
              (ii)   Roads/bridges connecting National Highways;
              (iii)   Roads/bridges required for opening up new areas for economic growth where railway facilities cannot be

              (iv)  Roads/bridges which would contribute materially to rapid development, e.g. in hilly areas and areas having

35.    The Committee feels that the encroachment of land under National Highways is a serious issue as it
 hampers the smooth development of highways and is also an irritant in the timely completion of various
 projects. The Committee recommends that suitable action should be taken to prevent encroachment in the first
 place. The Committee is surprised to note that there was considerable delay in enforcing the Control of National
 Highways (Land and Traffic) Act, 2002. Further, the Presiding Officers for only two of eight National Highway
 Tribunals have been appointed so far. The Committee notes that the National Highway Administrations have
 been empowered to remove encroachments on National Highways under its jurisdiction and the power of appeal
 vests with National Highway Tribunal, which is the Appellate Authority on all such matters. The Committee is
 of the view that the number of National Highway Tribunals (NHT) is disproportionate to the number of
 National Highway Administrations set up so far. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the number of
 National Highway Tribunals (NHT) should be increased and preferably one in each State should be opened. The
 Committee also recommends that the existing vacancies of Presiding Officers should be filled up at the earliest.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
36.    The Control of National Highways (Land and Traffic) Act, 2002 has come into effect from 27.1.2005. In order to
 implement the various provisions of the Act, 192 National Highway Administrations and 8 National Highway Tribunals
 have been set up. As per the Act, Highway Administrations should be in possession of the land registers showing the
 details of the land under their jurisdiction within the Right of Way of the National Highway. The work relating to the
 preparation of land registers has been very slow due to non-availability of proper records. As a result, the action on the
 part of the Highway Administrations to remove encroachments from the National Highway land has been slow. Till
 now, cases have come up only in the Chandigarh Branch of the Tribunal. The slow progress in the implementation of
 the provisions of the Act is due to the problems involved in the preparation of the land registers and not due to
 inadequate number of National Highway Tribunals. Efforts are on to speed up the process of preparation of land
 registers. The proposals approved by the Government in connection with the enactment of the Control of National
 Highways (Land and Traffic) Act, 2002 have provisions for the setting up of 233 National Highway Administrations
 and 28 National Highway Tribunals. Therefore, as .and when the work load increases, the number of National Highway
 Tribunals can be increased. Considering the present status, it has been proposed to set up 8 Tribunals initially. For
 filling up the existing vacant posts of Presiding Officers of the National Highway Tribunals, fresh recruitment process
 has been started.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
37.    The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Department of Road Transport and Highways that slow
 progress in the implementation of National Highways (Land and Traffic) Act, 2002 is due to the problems
 involved in the preparation of land registers and not due to inadequate number of National Highway Tribunals.
 The Committee feels that preparation land registers are important but from enforcement point of view role of
 National Highway Tribunal is all the more important because in the process of removal of encroachments the
 power of appeal vests with National Highways Tribunal, which is the Appellate Authority on all such matters.
38.    The Committee notes the reply of the Department that “when the work load increases number of National
 Highways Tribunal can be increased” and is at dismay that Department has just ignored the considered advice

REPORT
        The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the observations
 recommendations as contained in its One Hundred and Third Report on Demands for Grants  (2006-07) (Demand No.
 20) of the Department of Culture, which was presented to the Parliament on  22nd May, 2007.
2.     Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on 15th January 2007 in respect of all the
 observations/recommendations contained in the Report. These have been categorized as follows:-
 (i) Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government:  
  Para Nos. 11, 15, 21, 29, 37, 55 and 61 Total-7
 (ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
 view of the Government replies:
 
  Para No. 65 Total-1
 (iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
 not been accepted by the Committee:
 
  Para Nos. 32 and 49 Total-2
 (iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government
 are still awaited:
 
  Para Nos. 18, 24, 40, 44 and 71 Total-5
3.     The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as
 interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the earliest.
4.     On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each item of the action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry. The recommendations of the Committee contained in the One Hundred and
 Third, action taken thereon by the Government and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of
 action taken have been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
THE APPROACH IN THE TENTH PLAN AND ANALYSIS OF THE ANNUAL PLAN 2005-06
(Recommendation at Para 11)
5.     The Committee is of the view that fixing of the Revised Estimates ceiling by the Ministry of Finance on the
 basis of the level of expenditure attained upto the month of September/October creates problem for the
 Department of Culture. The Committee observes that most of the cultural functions and festivals take place in
 the month of October and November, after the monsoon. The Archaeological Survey of India also incurres
 major expenditure after the monsoon. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government must review
 the budgeting procedure and evolve some mechanism to ensure that the Plan allocation for the Department of
 Culture is not reduced. The Committee recommends that if the review of the budgetary allocation is done in the
 month of December, instead of the month of September then the cut in the budgetary provision could be
 avoided. The Committee observes that the major allocation for conservation work is being done under Non Plan
 Allocation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that conversation activity should be brought under the Plan
 Head so that conservation is not affected for want of funds, which is causing problem to the Department of
 Culture who wish to increase the conservation activities, hence need more expenditure.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6.     In pursuance of the recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing Committee, budget provision for conservation
 will be brought under Plan heads while preparing the Budget Estimates for 2007-08 onwards.
7.     In Archaeological Survey of India, field officers are asked regularly to programme  the activities in such a manner
 that flow of expenditure is proportionately distributed in the months and 67 per cent expenditure is achieved by end of
 December. But as the conservation work of Archaeological Survey of India is seasonal in nature and in extreme
 summer and monsoon seasons, the pace of work and the flow of expenditure will be slow and the flow of expenditure
 will not strictly be proportionate every month. Archaeological survey of India is explaining the above to Planning
 Commission and Ministry of Culture every year to minimize the budget reduction on this ground.
8.     With regard to review of Budgetary  allocation in the month of December instead of September, the
 recommendations of the Committee have been forwarded to Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission for

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/112.htm[28-08-2018 13:22:57]
 obtaining their comments/decision.
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
(a)    Release of the Revenue Collected as Admission Fees to Archaeological Survey of India
(Recommendation at Para 15)
9.     The Committee feels that execution of conservation and preservation works need an expertise and timely
 funding of projects. But with its meager resource, it is difficult for the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) to
 protect and maintain all the 3667 monuments/sites. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 100 per cent of
 the revenue collected as entry fees from ticketed monuments should be released to ASI for stepping up the
 activities and to augment resources of ASI. Coordinated efforts should also be taken by the Department to bring
 more monuments under central protection and also efforts should be made to raise the number of monuments
 for ticketing purpose to generate more revenue. The Committee strongly feels that there exists a requirement for
 creation of a non lapsable fund out of the amount generated by the ticketing of monuments which can be used
 for preservation and development of monuments in a dedicated manner.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
10.   A proposal for creation of a Non-lapsable fund for conservation and preservation activities on National monuments
 of Archaeological Survey of India, out of revenue obtained by sale of entry ticket was made to Ministry of Finance
 after consultation with Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission. In this regard the Minister for Tourism and Culture
 had written to Minister of Finance vide letter dated 3.9.2005. Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs
 vide their letter dated 27.12.2005 had asked for further details which were furnished by Archaeological Survey of India
 vide letter dated 16.3.2006. The proposal is now under consideration of Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic
 Affairs.
11.   In the year 1999 the total number of protected monuments was 3597 while now it has increased to 3667. Though
 the manpower resources of Archaeological Survey of India is a limiting factor in taking more monuments for central
 protection, Archaeological Survey of India continues to take more monuments of outstanding architectural/historical
 importance for protection under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. All field
 officers have been directed to review the number of ticketed monuments with the objective of bringing more
 monuments under ticketing.
(b)    The Post of Director-General in Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)
(Recommendation at Para 18)
12.   The Committee regrets to note that the promotional post of ADG, ASI could not be filled up as there was no
 suitable candidate in the country and ultimately the post was abolished as per the rules/regulations of the
 Department of Expenditure because the post could not be filled within prescribed time limit. It is pity that we
 are having more than hundred year old premier institute like ASI, but there is no archaeologist to be fit for
 promotion to the post of ADG. It clearly shows the callous attitude of the Government so far as management of
 the affairs of ASI is concerned. The Committee is of the view that there is no dearth of talent in the country.
 However, there is need to do away the rigidity in the eligibility criteria for the posts of Joint Director General,
 ADG and then DG, ASI. The Committee hopes that the vacant post will be filled up at the earliest as promised
 by the Secretary during the course of his evidence.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
13.   The post of Additional Director General (Archaeology) is the only feeder post which provides promotional avenues
 to the departmental officers for the post of Director General in the Archaeological Survey of India. The post of
 Additional Director General (Archaeology) in the Archaeological Survey of India has already been revived and the
 UPSC has been asked to fill up the post.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
14.   The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and hopes that UPSC will take due care to fill up the vacant
 post at the earliest. The Committee however, hopes that recruitment condition for the post of Additional
 Director General (Archaeology) must have been framed taking into account the availability of manpower in this
 connection so that there are enough candidates available for the post.
(c)    Conservation and Preservation of Monuments by the ASI

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

(Recommendation at Para 21)
15.   The Committee is happy to note that more and more corporate houses are coming forward to help the ASI
 in conservation of monuments by way of contributions to National Culture Fund. The Committee recommends
 that the Department of Culture should continue its efforts to ensure more involvement of private sector
 companies/firms. But at the same time the Committee also cautions that private involvement should not lead to
 commercial use of the monuments putting their safety and sanctity at stake.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
16.   The National Culture Fund (NCF) was constituted as a Trust in 1996 for infusion of private and corporate capital
 for cultural activities. Several projects have been initiated under NCF for conservation, preservation and environmental
 development of heritage monuments which are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.
17.   Under the prevailing scheme, Archaeological Survey of India enters into an MoU with the National Culture Fund
 and the private/public sector company for taking up projects of conservation and preservation of monuments. The
 provisions of the MoU would detail conditions under which the projects are taken up, and due care is always taken to
 ensure that there would be no commercialization of the monuments and the safety and sanctity of the monument are not
 affected in any way.
(Recommendation at Para 24)
18.   The monuments like Taj Mahal, Agra and Sun Temple at Konark which are famous all over the world and
 attract millions of tourists to the country should be conserved/preserved  very carefully and the Archaeological
 Survey of India should pay utmost attention towards this. The Committee recommends the Department to make
 adequate budgetary provision for this purpose. The Committee also recommends that the findings of the expert
 Committee on Konark Sun Temple should be implemented immediately in order to enable this famous
 monument survive.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
19.   Though the budgetary allocation of the Archaeological Survey of India has increased over the period, the available
 allocations are always inadequate to meet the demand of conservation and preservation of the ancient monuments.
 Archaeological Survey of India provides maximum allocation for the important monuments like Taj Mahal, Agra and
 Sun Temple, Konark, which are visited by large number of tourists from all over the world. However, there is an
 overall shortage of funds for the conservation of other centrally protected monuments.
20.   Archaeological Survey of India has constituted an Expert Committee for making detailed study of the structural
 issues at Sun Temple, Konark. The services of CBRI, Roorkee has already been availed. Archaeological Survey of
 India would ensure that the recommendations of the Expert Committee and the CBRI are fully implemented.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
21.   The Committee is constrained to note that Government failed to meet the requirement of funds necessary
 for conservation and preservation of centrally protected monuments and recommends that the Department of
 Culture should continue raising its demand for adequate resource allocation for protection of all monuments of
 national importance.
NATIONAL MUSEUM AND MUSEUM SECURITY
(Recommendation at Para 29)
22.   The Committee agrees with the Department that Museum security is the major area of concern and
 therefore enhancement of security arrangements is very much required. The Committee while recognizing the
 importance of security arrangements of National Museum also recommends that adequate steps should be taken
 to enhance the security of the State Museums also. The Committee considers that the cut imposed by the Finance
 Ministry at RE stage is unreasonable due to which modernization project of major museums in the country had
 to be postponed and some major international exhibitions planed during the year could not be
organised and recommends the Department to take up the matter with the Finance Ministry to avoid such cuts in
 future.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
23.   The recommendations of the Security Committee constituted by the Ministry of Culture have been communicated
 to all State Governments to help them upgrade the security of their Museums. A provision has been made in the
 Ministry’s Scheme for ”Promotion and Strengthening of Regional and Local Museums” for grant of financial assistance
 to State Government Museums to purchase equipment for Security System from 2005-06.

NATIONAL ARCHIVES OF INDIA
(Recommendation at Para 32)
24. The Committee appreciate that the National Archives has undertaken computerization programme in a big
 way. However, the Committee is simultaneously disappointed about the fact that no much attempt has been
 made to acquire documents/manuscripts in the post independence era. The Committee expressed its dismay that
 despite being pointed out by the Committee earlier the Department of Culture has also failed to fill-up the post
 of Director-General of Achieves. The Committee once again recommends that this post should be filled up
 without any further delay.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
25.   The National Archives of India continues to acquire records from the various Ministries and Government
 Undertakings. In order to improve the acquisition, special meetings were held with the concerned officers of the various
 Ministries to ascertain the practical difficulties involved. Special steps were initiated to shift the records to NAI.
 Besides, special meetings were held with the Public Sector Undertakings and Central Government offices located at
 Mumbai, Bangalore , Kolkata, Chennai and Hyderabad to chalk out plans for early declassification and subsequent
 transfer of public records to the NAI. As a result of these steps, there has been steady improvement in the acquisition of
 records during the year 2005-06 as well as the current year.
26.   The post of the Director General, NAI was advertised by the UPSC and interviews were held. However UPSC did
 not recommend any name. Subsequently the post was again advertised. The last date for receiving the applications is
 over and UPSC is expected to conduct the interview soon. It is hoped that UPSC will select a suitable candidate for the
 post.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
27.   The Committee notes that NAI is concentrating upon acquisition of official records only from various
 Government sources. Whereas, the Department of Culture has not given any information on acquisition of
 ancient manuscripts and other documents which are still in the private hands and are facing the threat of
 extinction. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that NAI should attempt to acquire more and more
 manuscripts/documents and take steps for their preservation.
28.   The Committee is however, constrained to note that there is no progress in the matter of filling up the post
 of Director General, NAI. The Committee fails to understand as to what short of recruitment conditions have
 been framed that no candidate is available for the post fulfilling such conditions. The Committee, recommend
 that recruitment conditions be relaxed or modified to make them realistic so that the post of Director-General,
 NAI is filled up at the earliest so that the functioning of the premier Achieves is not affected.
LIBRARY SECTOR
(National Library, Kolkata and other Libraries)
(Recommendation at Para 37)
29.   The Committee observes that there exists a dire necessity to strengthen literary activities in the length and
 breadth of the country and for that purpose these leading libraries like, National Library, Kolkata, Raja
 Rammohun Roy Library and Delhi Public Library play a crucial role. The Committee recommends that the
 budgetary allocation made for these libraries should be spent in a time bound manner. The Committee further
 recommends that the Delhi Public Library should widen its scope of activities and timely purchases should be
 made in order to save this important public organisation from languishing in neglect.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
30.   The Annual Action Plan of National Library, Raja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation and Delhi Public Library
 has been drawn and is being implemented. National Library, Kolkata has taken up the projects related to Digitization,
 Computerised Cataloguing. Networking and providing Internet facilities to users. The Raja Rammohun Roy Library
 Foundation, Kolkata  has drawn and adopted a new formula for assisting the libraries under their matching scheme.
 According to this new formula the libraries in developed States would get State and Central assistance in the ratio of
 50:50 and those in developing and backward States excluding North-Eastern States the ratio of RRRLF and State
 Government assistance will be 60:40. In respect of North Eastern States, the Central assistance will be 90 per cent.
 RRRLF also provides for assistance entirely from Central Plan Grants under its non-matching schemes.
31.   As regards Delhi Public Library, a Review Committee was set up to look into the activities of the Library and its
 Report is under consideration of the Government. During the financial year 2005-06, 55406 books worth Rs.95 lakhs
 were purchased by the Delhi Public Library. The Library has also kept the provision of Rupees One Crore in financial

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

 year 2006-07 for acquisition/replenishment of all type of reading materials. The progress of implementation of Action
 Plan of all libraries is being monitored on the quantitative and financial parameters on monthly basis.
SAHITYA AKADEMI
(Recommendation at Para 40)
32.   The Committee observes that the Sahitya Akademi is the premier institution in the country for literary
 dialogue, publication and promotion of literature. The Committee recommends that the projected budgetary
 allocation i.e., Rs. 10.64 crore should be released to the Akademi. The Department of Culture should also ensure
 that the construction of the proposed office building is completed in time.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
33.   Sufficient grants are provided for the Sahitya Akademi to take up the various activities of the Akademi. As regards
 their new building project, the initial formalities on the building project are yet to be completed. Sufficient provision
 will be made in the budget as and when required.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
34.   The Committee observes that it is an interim reply and the Department of Culture should keep the
 Committee informed of the progress in the matter.
NATIONAL SCHOOL OF DRAMA
(Recommendations at Para 44)
35.   The Committee expresses its happiness over the fact that the National School of Drama has been declared a
 ‘Deemed University’ under Section 3 of the University Grants Commission Act, 1956 and desires that with this
 the scope of activities of the School will be further broadened.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
36.   The Broad-based Committee constituted to look into all the aspects of National School of Drama’s future vision
 including its being a ‘Deemed to be University’. The recommendations of the Broad Based Committee were approved
 by the National School of Drama Society. These recommendation will have to be considered by the Government.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
37.   The Committee desires that the proposal to give ‘Deemed to be University” status to NSD should be pursued
 by the Ministry until the recommendation to that effect is accepted by Government.
INDIRA GANDHI NATIONAL CENTRE FOR THE ARTS
(Recommendation at Para 49)
38.   The Committee is not happy with the manner in which the Department of Culture is handling the affairs of
 Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA). Though the Tenth Five Year Plan is going to end this
 year, however the corpus fund of Rs. 90 crores which was proposed in the Tenth Plan for the IGNCA has not
 been released so far. The Committee recommends that the Department of Culture should take sincere steps and
 do away the problems of IGNCA.. The Department of Culture should also ensure the early release of an amount
 of Rs.90 crore as envisaged during Tenth Plan and it should not be linked to any other project.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
39.   In 2003 the Cabinet resolved that the project based funding would be given to IGNCA and they have to manage
 their own affairs from the interest that they earned from Corpus Fund.
40.   IGNCA has submitted proposal for Rs.2.90 crores for inclusion in the current year’s plan which is under
 consideration. In a meeting taken by the Principal Secretary to the PM on 21.5.2006 the following decisions were
 taken:
              (i)   CPWD in consultation with the IGNCA should access the requirement of funds for completion of buildings
 and also for their maintenance and furnish their revised cost estimates for consideration and approval of
 EFC.
              (ii)   The required funds would be provided in the budget of Ministry of Culture through Supplementary Grant.
              (iii)   Regarding augmentation of Corpus of IGNCA, it was decided that IGNCA will re-assess the need for
 further augmentation of their Corpus and submit it to Ministry of Culture for their scrutiny/examination.
              (iv)  Ministry of Culture after seeking approval of EFC will place the matter for consideration of the Cabinet.

41.   The Committee observes that Department of Culture is silent on the aspect of release of the corpus fund of

SCIENCE CITIES
(Recommendation at Para 55)
42.   The Committee feels that holding back 60 per cent of the total budgetary amount i.e., Rs.12.00 crore out of
 total Rs. 20.00 crore , for Pushpa Gujral Science City is unjustifiable. More so, when the Pushpa Gujral Science
 City, Kapurthala was not in a position to utilize the same amount due to pending audit objections. Science City
 project which is very crucial for popularizing science amidst masses, therefore, the Committee recommends that
 the Department of Culture should give adequate emphasis to regional Science Centres at Dharwad, Raipur,
 Pimpri, Chinchwad, Pune as well as Sub-Regional Science Centres, at Solapur and Kelimpong and promote
 their activities further.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
43.   It may be submitted that the Ministry of Finance had imposed an overall huge cut in September/October, 2005 on
 Department’s budget. Accordingly the budget under each and every Head had been proportionately reduced. The B.E.
 under ‘Science Cities’ for 2005-06 was reduced to Rs. 8.00 crores. Adequate attention is being paid in respect of
 Regional Science Centre at Dharwad, Raipur, Pimpri Chinchwad, Pune as well as Sub-Regional Science Centres at
 Solapur and Kelimpong and for promotion their activities. Details of progress in each case is explained below:
Regional Science Centres

REPORT
        This Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the observations/
 recommendations as contained in its One Hundred and Fourth Report on Demands for Grants (2006-07) (Demand No.
 92) of the Department of Tourism, which was presented to the Parliament on 22nd May, 2006.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
